nodes.title: INTRODUCTION
nodes.heading: INTRODUCTION
nodes.start_phrase: The following is Management’s discussion and analysis of the financial condition and results of operations (“MD&A”) of JPMorgan Chase & Co. (“JPMorgan Chase” or the “Firm”) for the second quarter of 2023 .
nodes.summary:
- Introduces the MD&A for JPMorgan Chase’s Q2 2023 Form 10-Q, to be read alongside the 2022 Form 10-K, with references to a glossary and line-of-business metrics for definitions.
- Includes forward-looking statements with cautions about risks and uncertainties; directs readers to specific Risk Factors and Forward-looking Statements sections; notes no obligation to update such statements.
- Provides a company overview: JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE: JPM), incorporated in 1968, a leading U.S.-based global financial services firm with $3.9 trillion in assets and $312.5 billion in stockholders’ equity as of June 30, 2023, serving U.S. consumers/small businesses and global corporate, institutional, and government clients under the J.P. Morgan and Chase brands.
- Outlines structure and key subsidiaries: principal bank subsidiary JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (branches in 48 states and Washington, D.C.); principal non-bank subsidiary J.P. Morgan Securities LLC; major overseas subsidiaries J.P. Morgan Securities plc (U.K.) and J.P. Morgan SE (Germany); global operations via branches, subsidiaries, representative offices, and foreign banks.
- Describes management reporting segments: Consumer & Community Banking (CCB), Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB), Commercial Banking (CB), Asset & Wealth Management (AWM), plus a Corporate segment; references to Business Segment Results and related notes.
- Notes the May 1, 2023 acquisition of certain assets and assumption of certain liabilities of First Republic Bank from the FDIC, with a reference to Note 28 for details.
- Explains availability of SEC filings (Forms 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K) and other investor information on the Firm’s and SEC’s websites, free of charge, and clarifies that website information is not incorporated by reference into the Form 10-Q.

nodes.title: EXECUTIVE OVERVIEW
nodes.heading: EXECUTIVE OVERVIEW
nodes.start_phrase: This executive ov erview of the MD&A highlights selected information and does not contain all of the information that is important to readers of this Form 10-Q.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Executive overview of JPMorgan Chase’s MD&A for the Form 10-Q, highlighting select items; advises reading the full 10-Q and 2022 10-K for complete trends, risks, and critical accounting estimates. Comparisons are Q2 2023 vs Q2 2022 unless noted.
- Firmwide results (Q2 2023): Net income $14.5B (+67%); diluted EPS $4.75 (+72%); ROE 20%; ROTCE 25%.
- Key one-time/transactional items: Estimated $2.7B bargain purchase gain in Corporate from the First Republic acquisition; $1.2B net addition to the allowance for credit losses tied to the acquisition; $900M investment securities losses in Treasury and CIO; $599M of expenses associated with the acquisition.
- Revenue: Total net revenue $41.3B (+34%).
  - Net interest income (NII) $21.8B (+44%), driven by higher rates and, to a lesser extent, the First Republic acquisition; partially offset by lower Markets NII and lower average deposit balances. NII excluding Markets $22.4B (+63%).
  - Noninterest revenue (NIR) $19.5B (+25%), supported by the First Republic acquisition, higher Markets NIR, and absence of prior-year Payments equity investment losses; partially offset by higher Treasury/CIO securities losses.
  - Markets revenue declined overall due to lower Markets NII, largely offset by higher Markets NIR.
- Expenses: Noninterest expense $20.8B (+11%), driven by higher compensation (additional headcount, wage inflation), First Republic-related costs, higher technology and marketing investments, and higher legal expense.
- Credit: Provision for credit losses $2.9B (+163%); pre-provision profit $20.5B (+71%).
- Capital, book value, and returns: CET1 ratio 13.8%, Tier 1 15.4%, Total capital 17.3% (ratios reflect CECL capital transition); book value per share $98.11 (+14%); tangible book value per share $79.90 (+15%).
- Memo/managed basis metrics: NII ex-Markets $22.37B (+63%); NIR ex-Markets $13.01B (+28%); Markets revenue $7.02B (-10%); total net revenue (managed) $42.40B (+34%).
- Definitions/notes: NII and NIR denote net interest income and noninterest revenue; Markets comprises CIB’s Fixed Income and Equity Markets businesses; capital ratios reflect CECL transition provisions and refer to further detail in Capital Risk Management sections of the 10-Q and 2022 10-K.

nodes.title: Firmwide overview
nodes.heading: Firmwide overview
nodes.start_phrase: For the second quarter of 2023 , JPMorgan Chase reported net income of $14.5 billion, up 67%, earnings per share of $4.75, ROE of 20% and ROTCE of 25% .
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Executive overview of JPMorgan Chase’s MD&A for the second quarter of 2023; directs readers to the full Form 10‑Q and 2022 Form 10‑K for complete trends, risks, and critical accounting estimates.
- Headline results (Q2 2023 vs Q2 2022): net income up 67% to $14.5B; EPS $4.75; ROE 20%; ROTCE 25%.
- Revenue: total net revenue up 34% to $41.3B, driven by:
  - Net interest income up 44% to $21.8B on higher rates and, to a lesser extent, the First Republic acquisition; NII excluding Markets up 63% to $22.4B.
  - Noninterest revenue up 25% to $19.5B, reflecting the First Republic bargain purchase gain of ~$2.7B (Corporate) and stronger Markets NIR, partially offset by ~$900M of investment securities losses in Treasury and CIO.
  - Markets revenue declined, with lower Markets NII largely offset by higher Markets NIR.
- Expenses: noninterest expense up 11% to $20.8B, driven by higher compensation (headcount and wage inflation), ~$599M of First Republic–related expense, increased technology and marketing investments, and higher legal expense.
- Credit costs: provision for credit losses of $2.9B, including a $1.5B net ACL build and $1.4B of net charge-offs.
  - ACL build includes ~$1.2B to establish allowance for First Republic loans and commitments; additional builds in Card Services and wholesale (CB) largely offset by a reduction in Corporate.
  - Net charge-offs rose, mainly in Card, as 30+ day delinquencies normalized to pre‑pandemic levels.
- Allowance and asset quality: total ACL $24.3B; allowance-to-loans coverage ratio 1.75% (vs. 1.69% prior year); nonperforming assets ~$7.8B, flat year-over-year with mix shift toward wholesale nonaccruals.
- Balance sheet trends: firmwide average loans up 13% to ~$1.2T (CCB and CB, including First Republic); firmwide average deposits down 6% to ~$2.4T due to AWM migration to higher‑yielding investments, attrition in CIB/CB (including deliberate reductions), and higher CCB spending, partially offset by First Republic inflows in CCB and Corporate increases tied to international consumer initiatives.
- Capital and liquidity:
  - CET1 capital ~$236B; Standardized CET1 ratio 13.8% and Advanced CET1 ratio 13.9% (reflecting CECL transition); Tier 1 15.4%; Total capital 17.3%; SLR 5.8%.
  - Tangible book value per share $79.90 (up 15%); book value per share $98.11 (up 14%).
  - Liquidity: HQLA ~$792B and unencumbered marketable securities ~$620B, totaling ~ $1.4T of liquidity sources.
- Additional context:
  - Pre-provision profit up 71% to $20.5B.
  - Managed basis total net revenue $42.4B; Markets revenue $7.0B; memo metrics provided for NII/NIR excluding Markets.
  - Non-GAAP measures cited include pre-provision profit, ROTCE, TCE, TBVPS, NII/NIR excluding Markets, and managed-basis revenue; reconciliations referenced in the MD&A.
  - Comparisons are Q2 2023 vs Q2 2022; references provided to sections on capital, liquidity, consolidated results, business segment results, and First Republic acquisition details.

nodes.title: Selected capital and other metrics
nodes.heading: Selected capital and other metrics
nodes.start_phrase: •CET1 capital was $236 billion , and the Standardized and Advanced CET1 ratios were 13.8% and 13.9% , respectively.
nodes.summary:
- Provision for credit losses was $2.9B, comprising a $1.5B net addition to the allowance (including $1.2B to establish allowance for First Republic loans and lending-related commitments) and $1.4B of net charge-offs. The allowance build included $233M in consumer (primarily Card Services) and $79M in wholesale (CB +$389M largely offset by Corporate -$243M). Net charge-offs rose $754M, predominantly in CCB/Card as 30+ day delinquencies returned to pre-pandemic levels. Prior year had a $428M allowance build and $657M net charge-offs.
- Total allowance for credit losses was $24.3B at June 30, 2023; allowance for loan losses to retained loans coverage ratio was 1.75% vs. 1.69% prior year.
- Nonperforming assets totaled $7.8B at June 30, 2023, relatively flat year-over-year: lower consumer nonaccruals from prior-year loan sales offset by higher wholesale nonaccruals due to client-specific downgrades.
- Firmwide average loans were $1.2T, up 13%, driven by higher loans in CCB and CB, largely from the First Republic acquisition.
- Firmwide average deposits were $2.4T, down 6%, due to continued migration to higher-yielding investments in AWM; declines in CIB and CB from deposit attrition (including CIB actions to reduce certain deposits); and a net decline in CCB from increased customer spending; partially offset by the First Republic impact in CCB and an increase in Corporate related to international consumer initiatives.
- Selected capital and liquidity metrics: CET1 capital $236B; Standardized CET1 ratio 13.8% and Advanced CET1 ratio 13.9%; SLR 5.8%; TBVPS up 15% to $79.90. As of June 30, 2023, eligible end-of-period HQLA ~ $792B and unencumbered marketable securities ~ $620B, totaling ~ $1.4T in liquidity sources.
- References provided to Liquidity Risk Management (pp. 54–61), Consolidated Results of Operations (pp. 10–15), Consolidated Balance Sheets Analysis (pp. 16–19), Business Segment Results (p. 24) and Note 28 for First Republic details. Non-GAAP measures noted (pre-provision profit, ROTCE, TCE, TBVPS, NII and NIR excluding Markets, and total net revenue on a managed basis) with reconciliations on pp. 20–21.

nodes.title: Business segment highlights
nodes.heading: Business segment highlights
nodes.start_phrase: Selected business metrics for each of the Firm’s four lines of business ("LOB") are presented below for the second quarter of 2023 .
nodes.summary:
- Overview: JPMorgan Chase’s second-quarter 2023 business segment highlights and first-half 2023 credit and capital provision.
- Consumer & Community Banking (CCB): ROE 38%; average deposits down 2%; client investment assets up 42%; average loans up 19% YoY and 15% QoQ; Card Services net charge-off rate 2.41%; debit/credit card sales volume up 7% (ex-Commercial Card); active mobile customers up 10% (90-day active users; excludes First Republic impact as of June 30, 2023).
- Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB): ROE 15%; #1 in Global Investment Banking fees with 8.4% YTD wallet share; Total Markets revenue $7.0B, down 10% (Fixed Income down 3%, Equities down 20%).
- Commercial Banking (CB): ROE 16%; Gross Investment Banking and Markets revenue $767M, down 3%; average loans up 23% YoY and 14% QoQ; average deposits down 8%.
- Asset & Wealth Management (AWM): ROE 29%; AUM $3.2T, up 16%; average loans up 1% YoY and 4% QoQ; average deposits down 21%.
- Credit provided and capital raised (1H23): $1.2T total (loans and commitments), including $120B to consumers, $17B to U.S. small businesses, $520B to corporations, $535B capital raised for corporate clients and non-U.S. government entities, and $24B for nonprofit and U.S. government entities (states, municipalities, hospitals, universities).
- Reference: Further detail available in Business Segment Results (pages 22–46).

nodes.title: Recent events
nodes.heading: Recent events
nodes.start_phrase: •Basel III Finalization: In July 2023, the Federal Reserve, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the FDIC released a proposal to amend the risk-based capital framework, entitl ed "Regulatory capital rule: Amendments applicable to large banking organizations and to banking organizations with significant trading activity".
nodes.summary:
- Regulatory proposals:
  - Basel III Finalization (July 2023): Fed, OCC, and FDIC proposed replacing the advanced approach with an expanded risk-based approach that generally disallows internal models (except for market risk), applies the stress capital buffer to both expanded and standardized approaches, and significantly revises risk-based capital for banks with $100B+ in assets, including U.S. GSIBs. Proposed effective date: July 1, 2025, with a three-year transition.
  - GSIB Surcharge (July 2023): Fed proposed revising the GSIB surcharge to use annual averages of quarterly calculations (with daily averaging for certain measures), reduce surcharge increments from 50 bps to 10 bps, and make technical changes to Method 2. Would take effect two calendar quarters after finalization and impact risk-based capital for U.S. GSIBs.

- Outlook and disclosures:
  - Forward-looking statements caution under the PSLRA; outcomes subject to economic, market, geopolitical, competitive, client activity, and regulatory factors. References to Risk Factors and no obligation to update.

- FDIC special assessment:
  - May 2023 proposal to recover DIF losses tied to the March 12, 2023 systemic risk determination: 12.5 bps annual rate on estimated uninsured deposits as of Dec 31, 2022. If finalized as proposed, JPMorgan Chase expects to record an estimated ~$3B pre-tax expense in the quarter of finalization (anticipated 2H 2023).

- 2023 guidance:
  - Net interest income (NII) and NII excluding Markets: approximately $87B, market dependent.
  - Adjusted expense: approximately $84.5B, market dependent and excluding any FDIC special assessment.
  - Card Services net charge-off rate: approximately 2.6%.
  - Notes: NII excluding Markets and adjusted expense are non-GAAP; reconciliations referenced.

nodes.title: Outlook
nodes.heading: Outlook
nodes.start_phrase: These current expectations are forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995.
nodes.summary:
- Regulatory updates: In July 2023, U.S. banking regulators proposed Basel III “finalization” changes replacing the advanced approach with an expanded risk-based approach (no internal models except for Market risk) and applying the stress capital buffer to both expanded and standardized approaches. The rule would impact banks with assets of $100B+ (including U.S. GSIBs), with a proposed effective date of July 1, 2025 and a three-year transition. Separately, the Federal Reserve proposed revising the GSIB surcharge to an annual assessment based on averaged quarterly calculations (with daily averaging for certain inputs), reducing surcharge increments from 50 bps to 10 bps, and making technical Method 2 amendments, effective two quarters after finalization.

- Outlook and disclosures: The document contains forward-looking statements subject to significant risks and uncertainties, with references to detailed risk factors and forward-looking statements sections. It notes that 2023 performance depends on macroeconomic, market, geopolitical, competitive, client activity, and regulatory developments, and that the firm will adjust operations as conditions evolve.

- FDIC special assessment: The FDIC proposed a special assessment (12.5 bps annual rate) on estimated uninsured deposits as of December 31, 2022, to recover DIF losses tied to March 12, 2023 systemic risk actions. If finalized as proposed, JPMorgan Chase expects to record approximately $3B pre-tax expense in the quarter of finalization, anticipated in 2H 2023.

- 2023 guidance: Management expects full-year net interest income and net interest income excluding Markets to be approximately $87B (market dependent), adjusted expense to be approximately $84.5B (market dependent and excluding any FDIC special assessment), and a Card Services net charge-off rate of about 2.6%. Certain figures are non-GAAP, with references to reconciliation pages.

nodes.title: Business Developments
nodes.heading: Business Developments
nodes.start_phrase: On May 1, 2023, JPMorgan Chase acquired certain assets and assumed certain liabilities of First Republic Bank (the "First Republic acquisition") from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (“FDIC”), as receiver, for $67.9 billion , resulting in an estimated bargain purchase gain of $2.7 billion recorded in other income.
nodes.summary:
- JPMorgan Chase acquired certain assets and assumed certain liabilities of First Republic Bank from the FDIC on May 1, 2023, for $67.9 billion, generating an estimated $2.7 billion bargain purchase gain recorded in other income.
- In connection with the acquisition, the Firm issued a five-year, $50 billion secured Purchase Money Note to the FDIC and entered into shared-loss agreements covering certain acquired loans and assumed lending-related commitments.
- The Firm’s Consolidated Financial Statements for the period ended June 30, 2023 reflect the acquisition’s impact; integration of operations, clients, products, and services is ongoing, and segment allocations (including deposits) may change in future periods.
- The document references risk factors related to current market and economic conditions—such as inflation, higher interest rates, geopolitical tensions (including effects of the war in Ukraine), potential market disruptions, government/monetary policy actions, and supply chain issues—with cross-references to the 2022 Form 10-K and this Form 10-Q.
- Regarding the IBOR transition, U.S. dollar LIBOR ceased June 30, 2023, with certain tenors continuing on a “synthetic” basis through September 30, 2024 for legacy contracts; in Q2 2023 the Firm converted predominantly all cleared derivatives to SOFR, is remediating nearly all remaining USD LIBOR-linked products via contractual fallbacks or the LIBOR Act, and continues client outreach to complete remediation by September 30, 2024.

nodes.title: First Republic acquisition
nodes.heading: First Republic acquisition
nodes.start_phrase: On May 1, 2023, JPMorgan Chase acquired certain assets and assumed certain liabilities of First Republic Bank (the "First Republic acquisition") from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (“FDIC”), as receiver, for $67.9 billion , resulting in an estimated bargain purchase gain of $2.7 billion recorded in other income.
nodes.summary:
- First Republic acquisition: On May 1, 2023, JPMorgan Chase acquired certain assets and assumed certain liabilities of First Republic Bank from the FDIC for $67.9 billion, recognizing an estimated $2.7 billion bargain purchase gain in other income. The Firm issued a five-year, $50 billion secured Purchase Money Note to the FDIC and entered into shared-loss agreements covering certain acquired loans and lending commitments. The acquisition’s effects are reflected in the Firm’s June 30, 2023 financials. Ongoing integration may lead to future changes in reporting classifications and segment allocations. Referenced Note 28 for more details.

- Current market and economic conditions: Points to Risk Factors in the 2022 Form 10-K and this Form 10-Q, highlighting potential impacts from inflation, higher interest rates, geopolitical tensions (including effects of the war in Ukraine), possible market disruptions, government/monetary policy actions, supply chain issues, and other geopolitical risks.

- IBOR transition: U.S. dollar LIBOR’s remaining principal tenors ceased June 30, 2023, with one-, three-, and six-month tenors continuing on a synthetic basis for legacy contracts through September 30, 2024. In Q2 2023, the Firm converted predominantly all cleared derivatives to SOFR via CCP-led conversions. Nearly all other remaining USD LIBOR-linked products will be remediated via contractual fallbacks or the LIBOR Act. Ongoing client outreach aims to complete remediation of contracts referencing synthetic USD LIBOR by September 30, 2024. References prior disclosures in the 2022 Form 10-K.

- The document references ongoing market and economic risks—inflation, higher interest rates, geopolitical tensions (including effects of the war in Ukraine), market disruption, policy actions, supply chain impacts—and points to detailed Risk Factors in the 2022 Form 10-K and this Form 10-Q.
- LIBOR transition: Publication of key USD LIBOR tenors ceased June 30, 2023; one-, three-, and six-month USD LIBOR continue on a synthetic basis for legacy contracts through September 30, 2024.
- In Q2 2023, the Firm converted nearly all cleared USD LIBOR-linked derivatives to SOFR via CCP initiatives; most remaining USD LIBOR-linked products will be remediated via contractual fallbacks or the LIBOR Act.
- Client outreach continues to remediate the limited contracts still referencing synthetic USD LIBOR by the September 30, 2024 deadline; additional background is referenced in the 2022 Form 10-K Business Developments section.

nodes.start_phrase: This section provides a comparative discussion of JPMorgan Chase’s Consolidated Results of Operations on a reported basis for the three and six months ended June 30, 2023 and 2022 , unless otherwise specified.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Comparative discussion of JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated results for the three and six months ended June 30, 2023 vs. 2022, with segment-specific factors referenced elsewhere and notes to critical accounting estimates.

- Headline results:
  - Q2 2023 total net revenue $41.3B vs. $30.7B (+34%); H1 2023 $79.7B vs. $61.4B (+30%).
  - Net interest income (NII): Q2 $21.8B vs. $15.1B (+44%); H1 $42.5B vs. $29.0B (+47%).
  - Noninterest revenue: Q2 $19.5B vs. $15.6B (+25%); H1 $37.2B vs. $32.4B (+15%).

- Noninterest revenue detail and changes (Q2/H1):
  - Investment banking fees: $1.51B/$3.16B (down 5%/12%).
  - Principal transactions: $6.91B/$14.53B (up 38%/44%).
  - Lending- and deposit-related fees: $1.83B/$3.45B (down 2%/7%).
  - Asset management fees: $3.77B/$7.24B (up 7%/1%).
  - Commissions and other fees: $1.74B/$3.43B (flat).
  - Investment securities losses: $(0.90)B/$(1.77)B (larger losses).
  - Mortgage fees and related income: $0.28B/$0.50B (down 26%/40%).
  - Card income: $1.09B/$2.33B (down 3% in Q2; up 10% YTD).
  - Other income: $3.29B/$4.30B (significant increase; includes $2.7B bargain purchase gain from the First Republic acquisition; also operating lease income and losses on tax-oriented investments).

- Quarterly drivers and commentary:
  - Investment banking fees decreased on lower advisory due to fewer announced deals; partly offset by higher equity underwriting (notably convertibles and follow-ons amid lower equity volatility).
  - Principal transactions revenue rose on:
    - Higher Equity Markets (especially Prime Finance).
    - Higher Fixed Income Markets (Securitized Products and Fixed Income Financing), partly offset by lower Rates and Currencies & Emerging Markets.
    - Absence of $337MM prior-year markdowns on held-for-sale (mainly unfunded commitments) in bridge financing in CIB and CB.
    - Credit Adjustments & Other swung to a $36MM gain vs. a $218MM loss.
    - Higher revenue from cash deployment in Treasury and CIO.
    - Partly offset by net losses on certain legacy private equity investments in Corporate vs. prior-year gains.
    - Note: Markets principal transactions often offset with NII; Markets performance assessed on total net revenue. Markets NII declined due to higher funding costs.
  - Lending- and deposit-related fees declined due to lower cash management fees in CIB and CB as higher client earnings credits reduced fees; partly offset by higher lending-related fees tied to the First Republic acquisition in AWM and CCB.
  - Asset management fees increased on strong net inflows in AWM and the impact of the First Republic acquisition (noted in CCB).

- Notable acquisition impact: First Republic acquisition contributed a $2.7B estimated bargain purchase gain (Corporate) and boosted certain lending-related and asset management fees.

- Cross-references: Segment results (CIB, CB, CCB, AWM, Corporate) and Notes 6 and 28 for additional details; operating lease income amounts disclosed.

nodes.title: Revenue
nodes.heading: Revenue

nodes.summary:
- Scope: Comparative discussion of JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated results for the three and six months ended June 30, 2023 vs. 2022; segment-specific drivers addressed in segment sections; references to critical accounting estimates and non-GAAP measures.

- Headline results:
  - Q2 2023: Noninterest revenue $19.5B (+25%); Net interest income (NII) $21.8B (+44%); Total net revenue $41.3B (+34%).
  - H1 2023: Noninterest revenue $37.2B (+15%); NII $42.5B (+47%); Total net revenue $79.7B (+30%).

- Quarterly (Q2 2023 vs. Q2 2022) revenue line drivers:
  - Investment banking fees: Down 5%; lower advisory amid weaker deal activity; largely offset by higher equity underwriting (more convertible and follow-on offerings as volatility eased).
  - Principal transactions: Up 38%; stronger Equity Markets (Prime Finance) and Fixed Income Markets (Securitized Products, Fixed Income Financing); absence of prior-year bridge financing markdowns; Credit Adjustments & Other swung to a gain; higher Treasury & CIO cash deployment revenue; partly offset by weaker Rates and Currencies & Emerging Markets and losses on legacy private equity in Corporate. Markets principal transactions gains were more than offset by lower Markets NII due to higher funding costs; performance is assessed on total net revenue.
  - Lending- and deposit-related fees: Down 2%; lower cash management fees from higher client earnings credits; partly offset by higher lending-related fees tied to the First Republic acquisition in AWM and CCB.
  - Asset management fees: Up 7%; higher management fees on strong AWM net inflows and First Republic impact in CCB.
  - Commissions and other fees: Flat.
  - Investment securities losses: Larger losses from sales of U.S. Treasuries and agency MBS tied to portfolio repositioning in Treasury & CIO.
  - Mortgage fees and related income: Down 26%; lower production volumes and lower net servicing revenue.
  - Card income: Down 3%; higher rewards liability from program term changes reduced net interchange; partly offset by stronger Commercial Card in CIB and CB.
  - Other income: Up sharply (includes a $2.7B estimated bargain purchase gain from the First Republic acquisition); also benefited from absence of prior-year Payments equity investment losses and net investment hedges in Treasury & CIO; partially offset by lower auto operating lease income and absence of a prior-year CB equity-method gain.

- Year-to-date (H1 2023 vs. H1 2022) revenue line drivers:
  - Investment banking fees: Down 12%; lower debt underwriting (weaker acquisition financing) and lower advisory; partly offset by higher equity underwriting (more convertibles and Q2 follow-ons).
  - Principal transactions: Up 44%; stronger Fixed Income (Securitized Products, Fixed Income Financing) and Equity Markets (Prime Finance); improved Credit Adjustments & Other vs. prior-year losses; higher Treasury & CIO cash deployment revenue; Markets principal transactions strength more than offset by lower Markets NII from higher funding costs.
  - Lending- and deposit-related fees: Down 7%; lower cash management fees from higher client earnings credits; partly offset by First Republic-driven lending-related fees in AWM and CCB.
  - Asset management fees: Up 1%; increase driven by First Republic impact in CCB; AWM roughly flat as market declines were offset by fewer money fund fee waivers and net inflows.
  - Commissions and other fees: Flat.
  - Investment securities losses: Higher losses from sales of Treasuries and agency MBS as portfolios were repositioned in both periods in Treasury & CIO.
  - Mortgage fees and related income: Down 40%; lower production volumes and lower servicing revenue (including lower MSR risk management gains).
  - Card income: Up 10%; higher payments-related revenue (Commercial Card growth in CIB and CB); CCB net interchange roughly flat—Q1 partner payments benefit from a tax refund on airline miles offset by higher rewards liability from program changes.
  - Other income: Higher, driven by the $2.7B First Republic bargain purchase gain, net investment hedges in Treasury & CIO, and a $339M gain in AWM from stepping up its CIFM stake; partially offset by lower auto lease income, absence of prior-year insurance settlement and CB equity-method gain, and lower gains on certain Corporate investments.

- Net interest income and balance/yield metrics:
  - NII increased in both periods primarily from higher rates, with additional contributions from the First Republic acquisition (and higher revolving Card balances YTD); partially offset by lower Markets NII and lower average deposits.
  - Average interest-earning assets: $3.3T (Q2 down $42B; H1 down $113B).
  - Yield on interest-earning assets: 5.01% in Q2 (+279 bps); 4.85% YTD (+281 bps).
  - Net yield on these assets (FTE): 2.62% in Q2 (+82 bps); 2.63% YTD (+89 bps).
  - Net yield excluding Markets (non-GAAP): 3.83% in Q2 (+157 bps); 3.82% YTD (+171 bps).

- Notable one-time/transactional items:
  - Estimated $2.7B bargain purchase gain from the First Republic acquisition (recorded in Corporate) materially lifted Other income.
  - Investment securities portfolio repositioning in Treasury & CIO drove elevated realized losses.
  - Markets results show offsets between principal transactions and NII; firm evaluates Markets on total net revenue.

nodes.title: Provision for credit losses
nodes.heading: Provision for credit losses
nodes.start_phrase: The provision for credit losses was $2.9 billion, reflec ting a $1.5 billion net addition to the allowance for credit losses and $1.4 billion of net charge-offs.
nodes.summary:
- Presents a breakdown of provision for credit losses for the three and six months ended June 30, 2023 vs. 2022, by category: consumer excluding credit card, credit card, total consumer, wholesale, investment securities, and total.
- Shows significant year-over-year increases in provisions across categories, with total provision rising to $2.9 billion for Q2 2023 and $5.2 billion year-to-date.
- Quarterly results: $2.9 billion provision comprised of a $1.5 billion net addition to the allowance for credit losses and $1.4 billion in net charge-offs.
- First Republic impact: $1.2 billion established for allowance on acquired loans and lending-related commitments in Q2 2023 ($763 million wholesale, $400 million consumer).
- Additional quarterly allowance changes: $233 million increase in consumer (primarily Card Services) and $79 million in wholesale (driven by $389 million in CB, offset by a $243 million reduction in Corporate).
- Net charge-offs rose by $754 million year-over-year in the quarter, mainly in CCB/Card Services as 30+ day delinquencies returned to pre-pandemic levels; prior-year quarter had a $428 million allowance build and $657 million of net charge-offs.
- Year-to-date: $5.2 billion provision includes a $2.6 billion allowance build and $2.5 billion net charge-offs; allowance build comprises $800 million in wholesale (downgrades, office real estate assumption updates, higher weighting of adverse scenarios) and $649 million in consumer (Card Services loan growth, macro outlook including unemployment peak in Q3 2024, higher adverse scenario weighting, partially offset by reduced borrower uncertainty), plus $1.2 billion for First Republic.
- Year-to-date net charge-offs increased by $1.3 billion, predominantly in CCB/Card Services as delinquencies normalized; prior year included a $1.3 billion allowance build and $1.2 billion in net charge-offs.

nodes.title: Income tax expense

nodes.start_phrase: the impact of the income tax expense associated with the First Republic acquisition that was reflected in the estimated bargain purchase gain, which resulted in a reduction in the Firm’s effective tax rate.
nodes.summary: Summary of income tax expense and effective tax rate for Q2 and first half ended June 30, 2023 versus 2022. Pre-tax income rose 62% in Q2 ($17.6B vs $10.9B) and 60% year-to-date ($33.6B vs $20.9B). Income tax expense increased 41% in Q2 ($3.1B vs $2.2B) and 62% year-to-date ($6.5B vs $4.0B). The Q2 effective tax rate fell to 17.7% from 20.4%, mainly due to the First Republic acquisition’s tax effect embedded in the estimated bargain purchase gain, which lowered the rate by 3.4 percentage points, partially offset by higher pre-tax income and shifts in the tax mix across federal, state, and local jurisdictions. Year-to-date, the effective tax rate was relatively flat at 19.3% versus 19.1%, as higher pre-tax income, mix changes, and lower benefits from stock-based award vesting were largely offset by the First Republic acquisition’s impact on the rate.

nodes.start_phrase: The following is a discussion of the significant changes between J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 3, and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 2.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Analysis of significant changes in the consolidated balance sheet between June 30, 2023 and December 31, 2022; total assets up 6% to $3.87T, total liabilities up 5% to $3.56T, and stockholders’ equity up 7% to $312.5B. Major drivers include the First Republic acquisition, client-driven Markets activity, portfolio repositioning, and the higher-rate environment.

Assets
- Cash and due from banks and deposits with banks: Declined due to First Republic-related repayments and FDIC payments, and CIB Markets activity; balances reflect excess cash placed with central banks.
- Federal funds sold and securities purchased under resale agreements: Increased on a lower level of netting in Markets.
- Securities borrowed: Decreased on lower client-driven activity and demand to cover shorts.
- Trading assets: Rose 40% on higher debt and equity instruments to support client market-making and a rebound from seasonally low year-end levels.
- Investment securities (AFS and HTM): Net decline driven by paydowns, maturities, and net sales, and transfers between HTM and AFS; partially offset by $25.8B of securities from the First Republic acquisition.
- Loans: Increased (gross +14%; net +15%), primarily from ~$150B of First Republic loans (in CCB, CB, AWM), Card revolving growth normalizing toward pre-pandemic levels, and higher CB revolver use and originations; partially offset by lower AWM securities-based lending.
- Allowance for loan losses: Increased due to $1.8B net additions (wholesale downgrades and office CRE assumptions; higher weighting of adverse scenarios; consumer additions tied to Card growth and a macro outlook with U.S. unemployment peaking in 3Q24), plus $1.1B for First Republic loans; partially offset by a $587M reduction from adoption of new TDR guidance. Allowance for lending-related commitments had a $196M net reduction, including a $97M addition for First Republic.
- Accrued interest and accounts receivable: Decreased on lower Markets client receivables.
- Premises and equipment: Increased from First Republic lease right-of-use assets and headquarters construction-in-process.
- Goodwill, MSRs, and other intangibles: Increased due to acquiring the remaining 51% of CIFM and core deposit intangibles from First Republic.
- Other assets: Decreased on lower cash collateral posted to CCPs.

Liabilities
- Deposits: Up 3% driven by CIB client inflows and structured note issuances, $68B of deposits from First Republic in CCB, and Corporate growth from international consumer initiatives; partially offset by AWM migration to higher-yielding investments and CB attrition (largely offset by 1Q23 inflows amid market disruptions).
- Federal funds purchased and securities loaned or sold under repurchase agreements: Up 31% on higher secured financing of trading assets and lower netting in Markets.
- Short-term borrowings: Down 7% due to lower Markets financing needs, partially offset by short-term FHLB advances tied to the First Republic acquisition.
- Trading liabilities: Flat.
- Accounts payable and other liabilities: Down 4% on lower Markets client payables.
- Beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs: Up 56% due to higher third-party holdings of multi-seller conduit commercial paper and increased conduit loans in CIB.
- Long-term debt: Up 23% reflecting the First Republic-related Purchase Money Note issued to the FDIC and $25B of FHLB advances, partially offset by maturities and redemptions.

nodes.title: BUSINESS SEGMENT RESULTS
nodes.heading: BUSINESS SEGMENT RESULTS
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm is managed on an LOB basis.
nodes.summary:
- The firm manages and reports results by lines of business (LOBs): Consumer & Community Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, Commercial Banking, and Asset & Wealth Management, plus a Corporate segment.
- Segment results are presented on a managed (non-GAAP) basis consistent with how the Operating Committee evaluates performance; each segment is portrayed as if a stand‑alone business.
- Methodology includes allocating certain income and expenses to LOBs; assumptions, methodologies, and classifications are periodically reassessed and may change over time. Capital requirements for each LOB are evaluated at least annually.
- Revenue sharing: when multiple LOBs collaborate on client transactions, revenue is recognized in the segment owning the product/service with allocations to participating segments.
- Funds transfer pricing (FTP): allocates interest income/expense to LOBs and transfers primary interest rate and liquidity risks to Treasury and CIO; FTP reflects the risk/liquidity characteristics of assets, liabilities, and off‑balance sheet items and may be updated periodically, affecting segment net interest income.
- Foreign exchange risk: certain FX exposures are transferred from LOBs to Treasury and CIO, which centrally manage and report the impact of FX movements.
- Capital allocation: equity is assigned to each segment and reassessed at least annually; allocations were updated as of June 30, 2023 to reflect the First Republic acquisition. nodes.title: Quarterly results
nodes.heading: Quarterly results
nodes.start_phrase: Net income was $5.3 billion , up 71% .
nodes.summary:
- Overview: Strong growth in earnings and revenue, driven primarily by higher net interest income on rising rates and increased card revolving balances, with expense and credit costs higher; First Republic acquisition boosted asset management fees and required allowance builds.

- Quarterly results:
  - Net income: $5.3B, up 71%.
  - Net revenue: $17.2B, up 37%.
  - Net interest income (NII): $13.7B, up 57%, driven by deposit margin expansion in Banking & Wealth Management (BWM) and higher NII in Card Services from increased revolving balances.
  - Noninterest revenue: $3.5B, down 8%, due to lower auto operating lease income and lower card income from increased rewards liability tied to changes in reward program terms; partially offset by higher BWM asset management fees from the First Republic acquisition.
  - Noninterest expense: $8.3B, up 9%, on higher compensation (wage inflation, headcount), marketing, and technology; partially offset by lower auto lease depreciation.
  - Provision for credit losses: $1.9B, including $1.3B net charge-offs (up $640MM, mainly Card Services as delinquencies normalize) and a $611MM net allowance build, which includes $408MM to establish allowance for First Republic loans/commitments and $203MM for Card Services (loan growth and macro outlook with U.S. unemployment peaking in 3Q24, largely offset by reduced borrower uncertainty). Prior year included a $150MM Card addition.
  - References: Notes on card income, asset management fees, MSR asset/hedges, and credit/allowance discussions.

- Year-to-date results:
  - Net income: $10.5B, up 75%.
  - Net revenue: $33.7B, up 36%.
  - NII: $26.5B, up 56%, driven by deposit margin expansion (partially offset by lower average BWM deposits) and higher Card Services NII; partially offset by lower PPP loan forgiveness in BWM.
  - Noninterest revenue: $7.2B, down 7%, due to lower auto lease income and lower Home Lending production and MSR-related net gains; partially offset by higher travel-related card commissions and higher BWM asset management fees from First Republic.
  - Card income: roughly flat; 1Q23 higher net interchange from reduced rewards costs/partner payments tied to a periodic tax refund on airline miles was offset by a 2Q23 increase to the rewards liability from reward program term changes.
  - Noninterest expense: $16.4B, up 7%, on higher compensation, marketing, and technology; partially offset by lower auto lease depreciation.
  - Provision for credit losses: $3.3B, including $2.3B net charge-offs (up $1.1B, mainly Card Services), a $553MM net allowance build (Card Services loan growth, macro outlook including unemployment peaking in 3Q24, and added weight on adverse scenarios in 1Q23; partially offset by reduced borrower uncertainty), and a $408MM addition to establish allowance for First Republic loans/commitments in 2Q23. Prior year included a $275MM addition in Card Services and Home Lending.

nodes.title: Year-to-date results
nodes.heading: Year-to-date results
nodes.start_phrase: Net income was $10.5 billion , up 75% .
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Quarterly and year-to-date financial performance, revenue/expense drivers, credit costs, balance sheet and credit quality trends, and operating/business metrics, with multiple references to notes and clear impacts from the First Republic acquisition.

- Quarterly results:
  - Net income $5.3B, up 71%; net revenue $17.2B, up 37%.
  - Net interest income (NII) $13.7B, up 57%, driven by deposit margin expansion in Banking & Wealth Management (BWM) on higher rates and higher NII in Card Services from increased revolving balances.
  - Noninterest revenue $3.5B, down 8%, on lower auto operating lease income and reduced card income (higher rewards liability from program term adjustments), partially offset by higher asset management fees in BWM from the First Republic acquisition.
  - Noninterest expense $8.3B, up 9%, on higher compensation (wage inflation, headcount), marketing, and technology, partially offset by lower auto lease depreciation.
  - Provision for credit losses $1.9B: net charge-offs $1.3B (up $640M, mainly Card as delinquencies normalize to pre-pandemic levels) and a $611M net allowance addition, including $408M to establish the First Republic loan/commitment allowance and $203M for Card (loan growth and macro outlook with U.S. unemployment peaking in 3Q24), largely offset by reduced borrower uncertainty.

- Year-to-date results:
  - Net income $10.5B, up 75%; net revenue $33.7B, up 36%.
  - NII $26.5B, up 56% (deposit margin expansion and higher Card revolving balances), partially offset by lower PPP loan forgiveness.
  - Noninterest revenue $7.2B, down 7% (lower auto lease income; Home Lending production and lower net MSR risk management gains), partially offset by higher travel-related card commissions and higher BWM asset management fees from First Republic.
  - Card income roughly flat: Q1 benefit from reduced rewards costs and partner payments tied to a tax refund on airline miles redeemed offset by Q2 increase to the rewards liability from program term changes.
  - Noninterest expense $16.4B, up 7%, on compensation, marketing, and technology; partially offset by lower auto lease depreciation.
  - Provision $3.3B: net charge-offs $2.3B (up $1.1B, mainly Card), $553M net allowance addition (loan growth, macro, heavier adverse-scenario weighting in Q1 2023, partly offset by reduced borrower uncertainty), plus $408M allowance established for First Republic in Q2.

- Balance sheet and credit quality (selected metrics):
  - Period-end: total assets $620B (+24%), total loans $558B (+26%; strong growth in Home Lending +48%, Card +16%, Auto +8%), deposits $1.174T (flat), equity $55.5B (+11%).
  - Average deposits down 2–3%; headcount up 5%.
  - Nonaccrual loans $3.8B (−9% YoY).
  - Net charge-offs rose to $1.25B for the quarter (rate 0.98%); Card charge-offs and 30+/90+ day delinquencies increased (30+ day to 1.70% vs 1.05%).
  - Home Lending 30+ day delinquency improved (0.58% vs 0.85%).
  - Total allowance for loan losses $13.8B (+10%), including $377M tied to First Republic; adoption of updated TDR guidance on Jan 1, 2023 reduced the allowance by $591M.

- Operating and business metrics:
  - Branches 4,874 (+1%); active digital customers 65.6M (+8%); active mobile 52.0M (+10%).
  - Debit/credit card sales volume $424B (+7%); total payments volume $1.5T (flat YoY for the quarter).
  - BWM: average deposits modestly lower; deposit margin expanded to ~2.8%; client investment assets $892.9B (+42%), including ~$151B from First Republic; client advisors up 5%.
  - Home Lending: mortgage originations down sharply YoY (Q2 $11.2B, −49%); third-party servicing up; MSR carrying value up 11%.
  - Card Services: sales volume up 8–10%; net revenue rate ~9.1%; net yield on average loans ~9.3%.
  - Auto: originations up 71% in Q2; average operating lease assets down ~26–28%.

- Notable items and references:
  - Significant impacts from the First Republic acquisition across deposits, loans, client assets, and allowances.
  - Multiple references to Notes (e.g., Note 6 for card/asset management fees; Note 15 for MSR and hedges; Note 1 for TDR guidance) and to Credit/Allowance discussions for deeper detail.

nodes.title: Selected income statement data
nodes.heading: 7.7.1 Selected income statement data
nodes.start_phrase: (a)Include s the impact of the First Republic acquisition.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: JPMorgan Chase Asset & Wealth Management (AWM) performance, with references to the 2022 Form 10-K for business profile and to credit risk and allowance sections for further detail.
- Selected financials (Q2 2023 vs Q2 2022): net income $1.2B (+22%), total net revenue $4.9B (+15%), net interest income $1.6B (+30%), noninterest revenue $3.4B (+9%), provision for credit losses $145M (higher, tied to First Republic), total noninterest expense $3.2B (+8%).
- Year-to-date (1H 2023 vs 1H 2022): net income $2.6B (+29%), total net revenue $9.7B (+13%), net interest income $3.0B (+32%), noninterest revenue $6.7B (+6%).
- Revenue by line of business (Q2 2023): Asset Management $2.1B (flat); Global Private Bank $2.8B (+30%).
- Asset Management drivers: lower net interest income from higher funding costs, largely offset by higher management fees on strong net inflows.
- Global Private Bank drivers: deposit margin expansion from higher rates on lower average deposits; higher lending-related fees and average loans, significantly influenced by the First Republic acquisition.
- Expense dynamics: higher compensation (growth in private banking advisor teams and revenue-related comp) and costs tied to acquisitions (Global Shares and J.P. Morgan Asset Management China).
- Credit provision: $145M in Q2, primarily to establish the allowance for First Republic loans and lending-related commitments.
- Financial ratios (Q2 2023): ROE 29% (vs 23% prior year); overhead ratio 64 (vs 68); pre-tax margins—Asset Management 27% (vs 29%), Global Private Bank 37% (vs 33%), AWM total 33% (vs 31%).
- Notable one-time item (1H 2023): $339M gain on the original minority interest in CIFM upon acquiring the remaining 51% stake.
- References: Business profile (2022 10-K pp. 76–78, metrics pp. 207–208); credit and allowance discussions (pp. 62–83 and 80–82).

nodes.title: Quarterly results
nodes.heading: 7.7.2 Quarterly results
nodes.start_phrase: Net income was $1.2 billion , up 22% .
nodes.summary:
- Focus: JPMorgan Chase Asset & Wealth Management (AWM) performance for Q2 2023 and first half 2023, with references to related 10-K sections and metrics pages.
- Financial snapshot (Q2 and YTD vs. prior year):
  - Net revenue up 15% in Q2 and 13% YTD, driven by strong net interest income growth (up ~30%+).
  - Noninterest revenue up mid-to-high single digits.
  - Noninterest expense up 8% on higher compensation, advisor team growth, and impacts from acquisitions (Global Shares, J.P. Morgan Asset Management China).
  - Provision for credit losses reflects allowance build tied to the First Republic acquisition.
  - Net income up 22% in Q2 and 29% YTD.
- Business mix:
  - Asset Management revenue flat in Q2; YTD up slightly, aided by a $339 million gain on remeasuring the prior minority interest in CIFM upon acquiring the remaining stake.
  - Global Private Bank revenue up 30% in Q2, benefiting from deposit margin expansion (higher rates on lower average balances) and higher lending-related fees/average loans linked to First Republic.
- Ratios and profitability:
  - Return on equity improved (high 20s%).
  - Overhead ratio improved.
  - Pre-tax margin ratios strong across Asset Management, Global Private Bank, and consolidated AWM, with year-over-year improvement.
- Acquisitions and one-time items:
  - First Republic acquisition impacted NII, Global Private Bank revenue, and credit loss allowance.
  - Consolidation of CIFM generated a notable gain; Global Shares and JPMAM China acquisitions contributed to expense growth.
- Guidance and references:
  - Notes direct readers to Credit and Investment Risk Management and Allowance for Credit Losses sections for deeper discussion of credit portfolios and allowances.

nodes.title: Year-to-date results
nodes.heading: 7.7.3 Year-to-date results
nodes.start_phrase: Net income was $2.6 billion , up 29% .
nodes.summary:
- Focuses on JPMorgan Chase’s Asset & Wealth Management (AWM) segment performance for Q2 2023 and year-to-date (YTD) 2023 versus 2022, with references to related disclosures in the 2022 Form 10-K and Line of Business metrics.
- Presents selected income statement data showing strong growth: total net revenue up 15% in Q2 and 13% YTD; net interest income up 30% in Q2 and 32% YTD; noninterest revenue up 9% in Q2 and 6% YTD; net income up 22% in Q2 and 29% YTD.
- Breaks down revenue by line of business:
  - Asset Management: flat in Q2; up 2% YTD, driven by a $339 million gain on consolidating CIFM, offset by lower NII from higher funding costs, lower performance fees, and lower asset management fees tied to market levels, partially offset by prior-year removal of most money market fee waivers and net inflows.
  - Global Private Bank: up 30% in Q2 and 24% YTD, driven by deposit margin expansion from higher rates on lower average deposits and higher lending-related fees and average loans from the First Republic acquisition; partially offset by an investment valuation loss in Q1 2023.
- Highlights operating expense trends: noninterest expense up 8% in Q2 and YTD, mainly from higher compensation (including advisor team growth), higher revenue-related compensation, and the impact of the Global Shares and J.P. Morgan Asset Management China acquisitions.
- Details credit costs: provision for credit losses of $145 million in Q2 and $173 million YTD, primarily reflecting a $146 million allowance established for First Republic loans and lending-related commitments; prior-year provision was $198 million.
- Notes key profitability and efficiency metrics: return on equity improved to 29% in Q2 and 31% YTD; overhead ratio improved to 64; pre-tax margins at 33% for AWM overall (AM: 27% Q2/32% YTD; GPB: 37% Q2/35% YTD).
- Provides selected balance sheet data: period-end assets up 5%; loans up 2% (including First Republic); deposits down 22% year-over-year; average deposits also lower; equity stable.
- Shows continued business growth and investments: headcount up 12% year-over-year to 26,931; Global Private Bank client advisors up 12% to 3,214.
- Summarizes fund quality and performance metrics: 69% of mutual fund assets rated 4- or 5-star; top-half quartile rankings of 59% (1-year), 66% (3-year), and 80% (5-year).
- Outlines credit quality statistics: very low net charge-offs, stable nonaccrual loans, and a higher allowance for credit losses (up 21%), including the First Republic-related allowance; credit ratios remain strong.
- Emphasizes the impact of the First Republic acquisition across NII, lending-related fees, average loans, and credit allowances.
- Points to related sections for more detail on credit and allowance methodologies and on the transaction impacts.

nodes.title: Selected metrics
nodes.heading: 7.7.4 Selected metrics
nodes.start_phrase: (a)Represents the Morningstar Rating for all domiciled funds except for Japan domiciled funds which use Nomura.
nodes.summary:
- Business performance overview for the period ended June 30, 2023 vs. 2022, highlighting revenue, expenses, credit provisions, and key metrics for the Global Private Bank within Asset & Wealth Management.
- Revenue drivers: Global Private Bank revenue of $5.2B, up 24%, driven by deposit margin expansion from higher rates on lower average deposits, and higher lending fees/average loans tied to the First Republic acquisition; partially offset by a Q1 2023 investment valuation loss.
- Offsetting factors in Asset Management: lower net interest income from higher funding costs, lower performance fees, and lower asset management fees due to weaker markets, largely offset by the prior-year removal of most money market fund fee waivers and net inflows.
- Expenses: Noninterest expense of $6.3B, up 8%, due to higher compensation (including private bank advisor growth), higher revenue-related compensation, and impacts from the Global Shares and J.P. Morgan Asset Management China acquisitions.
- Credit costs: Provision for credit losses of $173M, driven mainly by a $146M allowance established for First Republic loans and commitments; prior year provision was $198M.
- Mutual fund performance: 69% of JPM mutual fund assets rated 4- or 5-star; 1/3/5-year quartile rankings show mixed near-term and strong long-term relative performance.
- Balance sheet trends (period-end): Total assets up 5% to $247.1B; loans up 2% to $222.5B (including First Republic); deposits down 22% to $199.8B; equity flat at $17.0B. Averages show similar trends with deposits down ~21% and modest asset/loan growth.
- Headcount: Up 12% to 26,931; Global Private Bank client advisors up 12% to 3,214.
- Credit quality: Net charge-offs minimal; nonaccrual loans stable at $615M; allowance for loan losses up 19% to $649M; total allowance up 21% to $688M, including $146M tied to First Republic. Ratios indicate stable credit metrics (nonaccrual loans at 0.28% of loans; allowance to loans at 0.29%).

nodes.title: Client assets

- Client segments (AUM, YoY): Private Banking $881B (+24%), Global Institutional $1,423B (+10%), Global Funds $884B (+20%).
- Client segments (Total client assets, YoY): Private Banking $2,170B (+27%), Global Institutional $1,497B (+12%), Global Funds $891B (+20%). Private Banking reflects impact of the Global Shares acquisition.

  - 1H 2023: Beg. $2,766B; net flows +$261B; market/performance/other +$161B; End $3,188B (vs. $2,743B in 1H 2022).

nodes.title: CORPORATE
nodes.heading: 7.8 CORPORATE
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to pages 79-80 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 Form 10-K for a discussion of Corporate.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: JPMorgan Chase Corporate segment quarterly and year-to-date results (Q2 and H1 2023 vs 2022), including Treasury and CIO and Other Corporate.
- Profitability: Q2 net income of $2.6B vs a net loss of $174M in prior year; H1 net income of $2.9B vs a loss of $1.0B.
- Revenue: Q2 total net revenue of $3.7B vs $80M, primarily from higher net interest income driven by higher rates, partly offset by lower firmwide average deposit balances available for deployment in Treasury and CIO.
- Noninterest revenue: Improved to $2.0B from a loss of $244M, mainly due to:
  - A $2.7B estimated bargain purchase gain from the First Republic acquisition.
  - Higher revenue from cash deployment transactions in Treasury and CIO.
  - Lapping higher prior-year losses tied to foreign exchange rate movements.
  - Partly offset by higher net investment securities losses from repositioning U.S. Treasuries and agency MBS, and net losses on certain legacy private equity investments (vs gains in prior year).
- Expenses: Q2 noninterest expense rose to $1.2B, up $946M, driven by $562M of expenses tied to the First Republic acquisition, higher legal expense, and a smaller FX-related benefit versus the prior year.
- Credit costs: Q2 provision for credit losses was a net release of $243M vs an expense of $28M in the prior year; H1 provision increased to $127M from $57M.
- Segment contributions:
  - Treasury and CIO: Q2 net revenue $1.3B (vs $82M) and net income $1.1B (vs $88M).
  - Other Corporate: Q2 net revenue $2.5B (vs approximately flat) and net income $1.6B (vs a $262M loss), including First Republic impacts.
- Balance sheet and other metrics (period-end YoY): Corporate total assets down 13% to $1.26T; loans slightly down to $2.2B; deposits up 60% to $21.1B (largely from international consumer initiatives); headcount up 12% to 45,235.
- Notables/footnotes: Results include the impacts of the First Republic acquisition; related income taxes are reflected in the bargain purchase gain. Tax-equivalent adjustments recognized due to tax-exempt municipal bond income.

nodes.title: Quarterly results
nodes.heading: 7.8.2 Quarterly results
nodes.start_phrase: Net income was $2.6 billion , compared with a net loss of $174 million in the prior year.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Corporate segment of JPMorgan Chase, including Treasury and CIO and Other Corporate; references to 2022 Form 10-K and various Notes for detail.
- Headline quarterly results (Q2 2023 vs Q2 2022):
  - Net income of $2.6B vs a $174M loss.
  - Total net revenue of $3.7B vs $80M, driven by higher net interest income from higher rates, partially offset by lower Firmwide average deposits available to Treasury and CIO.
  - Noninterest revenue of $2.0B vs a $244M loss, primarily:
    - Positive: $2.7B estimated bargain purchase gain from the First Republic acquisition; higher cash deployment revenue in Treasury and CIO; prior-year FX-related losses not repeating.
    - Negative: higher net investment securities losses from sales of U.S. Treasuries and agency MBS as the portfolio was repositioned; net losses on certain legacy private equity investments vs prior-year gains.
  - Noninterest expense of $1.2B, up $946M, mainly from $562M of First Republic-related expense, higher legal expense, and a larger prior-year FX benefit that did not recur.
  - Provision for credit losses: $243M net benefit from reducing the allowance tied to the Q1 2023 deposit placed with First Republic Bank.
  - Tax: expense benefited from acquisition-related tax effects embedded in the bargain purchase gain, partially offset by changes in mix of taxable income and related reserves.
- Year-to-date (1H 2023 vs 1H 2022):
  - Net income of $2.9B vs a $1.0B loss.
  - Total net revenue of $4.7B vs a $801M loss, on higher net interest income from higher rates, partly offset by lower deployable deposits in Treasury and CIO.
  - Noninterest revenue of $1.2B vs a $589M loss, with the same drivers as Q2 plus the absence of prior-year insurance settlement proceeds and lower gains on certain other Corporate investments.
  - Noninterest expense of $1.3B, up $922M, largely from First Republic-related expense, higher legal expense, and less FX-related benefit than prior year.
  - FX movements tied to risk transferred to Treasury and CIO were not material to net income.
  - Tax: benefit from acquisition-related tax effects largely offset by changes in level/mix of taxable income and related reserves.
- Segment contribution:
  - Treasury and CIO: Q2 net revenue $1.26B and net income $1.06B; 1H net revenue $2.37B and net income $1.68B.
  - Other Corporate: Q2 net revenue $2.46B and net income $1.58B; 1H net revenue $2.34B and net income $1.20B.
- Balance sheet and operational metrics (period-end vs prior year):
  - Total assets $1.264T, down 13%.
  - Loans $2.2B, roughly flat.
  - Deposits $21.1B, up 60% (predominantly from international consumer initiatives).
  - Headcount 45,235, up 12%.
- International consumer initiatives within Other Corporate: Chase U.K. (digital retail bank), Nutmeg (U.K. digital wealth manager), and 40% stake in C6 Bank (Brazil).
- Treasury and CIO investment securities portfolio:
  - Average credit rating AA+.
  - Significant investment securities losses: $900M in Q2 and $1.77B YTD, vs $153M and $547M prior-year, respectively, reflecting portfolio repositioning (sales of U.S. Treasuries and U.S. GSE/agency MBS).
  - Portfolio size (average): $609B in Q2 (down 9% YoY); period-end net $610B (down 8% YoY).
  - AFS securities period-end $201B (includes $25.8B from First Republic); HTM period-end $409B.
  - Allowance for credit losses on investment securities: $74M vs $47M prior year.
  - Accounting changes: adopted new hedge accounting guidance on Jan 1, 2023, transferring $7.1B from HTM to AFS; in 2022, $78.3B transferred from AFS to HTM for capital management.
- Notable acquisition impacts:
  - First Republic drove a $2.7B estimated bargain purchase gain, $562M of associated expenses, inclusion of AFS securities, and tax effects recorded within the bargain purchase gain.

nodes.title: Basel III Overview
nodes.heading: 8.3.1 Basel III Overview
nodes.start_phrase: The capital rules under Basel III establish minimum capital ratios and overall capital adequacy standards for large and internationally active U.S. Bank Holding Companies (“BHCs” ) and banks, including the Firm and its insured depository institution (“IDI”) subsidiaries, including JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
nodes.summary:
- Defines capital risk as the possibility that the Firm’s capital level or composition is insufficient to support activities and risks in both normal and stressed conditions, with references to the 2022 Form 10-K (pp. 86–96), this Form 10-Q Note 23, and Pillar 3 disclosures.
- Provides a Basel III overview: regulatory capital is based on risk-weighted assets (RWA) using two approaches—Standardized and Advanced—with capital adequacy assessed against the lower of the two; the Firm’s Standardized risk-based ratios are currently more binding. Notes an SLR requirement for Advanced Approaches firms and points to an SLR section for more detail.
- Details key regulatory developments:
  - CECL regulatory capital transition: the $2.9 billion COVID-related CECL capital benefit is being phased out 25% per year starting January 1, 2022; as of June 30, 2023, $1.4 billion remained in CET1. Effective January 1, 2023, 50% of other CECL transition provisions affecting Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, total leverage exposure, and RWA were phased out.
  - Risk-based capital targets: the Firm’s Basel III Standardized CET1 target for 1Q24 remains 13.5%, with actual quarterly ratios subject to market conditions, based on currently effective rules.
  - Basel III finalization proposal (July 2023): replaces the Advanced Approach with an expanded risk-based approach (no internal models except for market risk), applies the stress capital buffer to both expanded and standardized approaches, and significantly revises requirements for banks with assets ≥$100 billion, including U.S. GSIBs; proposed effective date July 1, 2025, with a three-year transition for the expanded approach.
  - GSIB surcharge proposal (July 2023): shifts to an annual assessment using the average of quarterly calculations (with daily averaging for certain measures), reduces surcharge increments from 50 bp to 10 bp, and includes technical Method 2 changes; would take effect two calendar quarters after the final rule.

- Outlines July 2023 GSIB surcharge proposal: annual assessment using averages of quarterly calculations (with daily averaging for certain measures); reduces surcharge step size from 50 bps to 10 bps; includes technical Method 2 changes; would adjust risk-based capital requirements for U.S. GSIBs and take effect two calendar quarters after final rule adoption.

- Key regulatory developments:
  - CECL regulatory capital transition: The $2.9 billion pandemic-related CET1 benefit is being phased out 25% per year over three years starting January 1, 2022; $1.4 billion remained in CET1 as of June 30, 2023. Effective January 1, 2023, 50% of other CECL transition elements (affecting Tier 2, adjusted average assets, total leverage exposure, and RWA) were phased out. Reported metrics reflect CECL transition provisions.
  - Risk-based capital target: The Firm’s Basel III Standardized CET1 ratio target for 1Q24 remains 13.5%, with quarterly outcomes varying by market conditions.

Proposed effective date July 1, 2025, with a three-year transition.
  - GSIB surcharge proposal (July 2023): Would shift to annual assessment using the average of quarterly calculations (with daily averaging for certain inputs), reduce surcharge increments from 50 bps to 10 bps, and include other technical changes; effective two calendar quarters after final rule adoption.

- First Republic Bank acquisition: First Republic was not subject to the Advanced approach; for certain acquired exposures, Advanced RWA and related total capital impacts are calculated under the Standardized approach per U.S. capital rule transition provisions.

- RWA rollforward:
  - Presents beginning (Dec 31, 2022) and ending (June 30, 2023) RWA under both Basel III Standardized and Advanced frameworks, with changes attributed to model & data changes and movement in portfolio levels.
  - Standardized approach:
    - Total RWA rose from $1,653.5 billion to $1,706.9 billion (+$53.4 billion).
    - Model & data changes reduced RWA by $9.6 billion; portfolio movements increased RWA by $63.0 billion.
    - Components: Credit risk RWA increased by $64.2 billion; Market risk RWA decreased by $10.8 billion.
  - Advanced approach:
    - Total RWA rose from $1,609.8 billion to $1,694.7 billion (+$84.9 billion).
    - Model & data changes reduced RWA by $7.4 billion; portfolio movements increased RWA by $92.3 billion.
    - Components: Credit risk RWA increased by $99.0 billion; Market risk RWA decreased by $11.1 billion; Operational risk RWA decreased by $3.0 billion.
  - Key drivers noted:
    - Portfolio movements include First Republic acquisition impacts (including FDIC shared-loss benefits), changes in book size and composition/credit quality, home lending portfolio roll-offs, market movements, deductions for excess eligible credit reserves, market risk position/multiplier changes (Regulatory VaR backtesting exceptions), and updates to operational risk loss/macro inputs.
    - Off-balance sheet RWA: Standardized $221.2B (vs. $210.1B at 12/31/22); Advanced $199.0B (vs. $180.8B).
    - Approx. $57.1B of credit risk RWA calculated under the Standardized approach for certain First Republic assets per U.S. capital rule transition provisions.
  - References to Pillar 3 reports for additional detail on Credit, Market, and Operational risk RWA.
- Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR):
  - Tier 1 capital: $262.6B (vs. $245.6B at 12/31/22).
  - Total adjusted average assets: $3,796.6B (vs. $3,703.9B).
  - Off-balance sheet exposures: $696.2B (vs. $663.2B).
  - Total leverage exposure: $4,492.8B (vs. $4,367.1B).
  - SLR: 5.8% (vs. 5.6%).
  - Notes on regulatory capital adjustments and methodology; references to Pillar 3 and 2022 Form 10-K (page 93) for more information.
- Line of business equity (allocated capital):
  - Allocation updated to reflect the First Republic acquisition.
  - As of June 30, 2023 (in billions): Consumer & Community Banking $55.5; Corporate & Investment Bank $108.0; Commercial Banking $30.0; Asset & Wealth Management $17.0; Corporate $74.6; Total common stockholders’ equity $285.1.
  - Comparatives provided for March 31, 2023 and December 31, 2022; reference to 2022 Form 10-K (page 93) for methodology.

nodes.title: LIQUIDITY RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: 8.4 LIQUIDITY RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase: Liquidity risk is the risk that the Firm will be unable to meet its contractual and contingent financial obligations as they arise or that it does not have the appropriate amount, composition and tenor of funding and liquidity to support its assets and liabilities.
nodes.summary:
- Defines liquidity risk as the inability to meet obligations or maintain appropriate funding and liquidity profile; points to JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 Form 10-K and U.S. LCR Disclosure reports for more detail.
- Explains the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) rule: requires the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. to hold sufficient High-Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA) to cover 30 days of stressed net cash outflows; minimum LCR of 100% for both.
- Notes that excess HQLA held at JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. that is not transferable to non-bank affiliates is excluded from the Firm’s reported HQLA.
- Summarizes average LCR and liquidity metrics for the three months ended June 30, 2023, March 31, 2023, and June 30, 2022:
  - JPMorgan Chase & Co.: LCR of 112%, 114%, and 110%; total average HQLA of $768.1B, $731.5B, and $742.0B; net cash outflows of $683.4B, $642.7B, and $676.2B; net excess eligible HQLA of $84.7B, $88.9B, and $65.7B. End-of-period HQLA: $791.5B, $758.9B, $721.1B.
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.: LCR of 129%, 140%, and 169%; net excess eligible HQLA of $211.2B, $278.7B, and $487.9B.
- Details HQLA composition: eligible cash (primarily central bank deposits) and eligible securities (predominantly U.S. Treasuries, U.S. GSE/agency MBS, and sovereign bonds), with securities potentially reported across multiple balance sheet line items.
- Describes quarter-over-quarter Firm LCR decrease (2Q23 vs 1Q23) driven by long-term debt maturities, share repurchases, and dividends, largely offset by a dividend from the bank to the parent; year-over-year Firm LCR increase (2Q23 vs 2Q22) driven by bank dividends to the parent, partially offset by capital returns.
- Explains JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.’s LCR decreases:
  - 2Q23 vs 1Q23: roughly 50% reduction tied to the First Republic acquisition (lower HQLA, higher net cash outflows), plus lower cash from higher average loans, a dividend to the parent, and a decline in average deposits.
  - 2Q23 vs 2Q22: lower HQLA due to deposit declines, loan growth, lower market values of HQLA-eligible securities, and the First Republic acquisition.
- Notes Federal Reserve actions affected depositor behavior and reduced system-wide deposits; LCRs may fluctuate with changes in HQLA, net cash outflows, business activity, and policy impacts.
- Outlines internal liquidity stress testing across adverse scenarios (including resolution and recovery planning), with results informing the funding plan and liquidity assessment.
- States the Firm maintains liquidity at the Parent Company, IHC, and operating subsidiaries to meet liquidity risk tolerances and minimum requirements; references additional details in the 2022 Form 10-K and Notes on investment securities and the First Republic acquisition.
