nodes.title: LCR and HQLA
nodes.heading: 8.4.1 LCR and HQLA
nodes.start_phrase: The LCR rule requires that the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. maintain an amount of eligible HQLA that is sufficient to meet their respective estimated total net cash outflows over a prospective 30 calendar-day period of significant stress.
nodes.summary:
- Defines liquidity risk as the Firm’s potential inability to meet obligations or maintain appropriate funding and liquidity profile; points to JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 Form 10-K (pp. 97–104) and U.S. LCR Disclosure reports for more detail.
- Outlines LCR and HQLA requirements: both the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. must maintain a minimum 100% LCR, holding sufficient eligible HQLA to cover 30 days of stressed net cash outflows. Excess HQLA at the bank that is not transferable to non-bank affiliates is excluded from the Firm’s reported HQLA.
- Provides average LCR metrics for the three months ended June 30, 2023, March 31, 2023, and June 30, 2022:
  - JPMorgan Chase & Co.: LCR 112% (Q2’23), 114% (Q1’23), 110% (Q2’22); average HQLA $768.1B (cash $440.3B; securities $327.8B); net cash outflows $683.4B; net excess eligible HQLA $84.7B. End-of-period HQLA: $791.5B (Q2’23), $758.9B (Q1’23), $721.1B (Q2’22).
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.: LCR 129% (Q2’23), 140% (Q1’23), 169% (Q2’22); net excess eligible HQLA $211.2B (Q2’23), $278.7B (Q1’23), $487.9B (Q2’22).
- Describes HQLA composition and reporting: eligible cash primarily central bank deposits; eligible securities predominantly U.S. Treasuries, U.S. GSE/agency MBS, and sovereign bonds (net of LCR haircuts); eligible HQLA securities may appear in securities financing, trading assets, or investment securities lines.
- Explains drivers of LCR changes:
  - Firm QoQ (Q2’23 vs Q1’23): lower LCR due to long-term debt maturities and capital returns (buybacks/dividends), largely offset by a dividend from the bank to the Parent Company.
  - Firm YoY (Q2’23 vs Q2’22): higher LCR driven by bank dividends to Parent, partially offset by capital returns.
  - Bank QoQ: lower LCR primarily from the First Republic acquisition (reduced HQLA and higher net cash outflows), plus lower cash due to higher average loans, a dividend to Parent, and lower average deposits.
  - Bank YoY: lower LCR due to reduced cash from deposit declines and loan growth, lower market values of HQLA-eligible securities, and the First Republic acquisition.
- Notes external influences: Federal Reserve actions have affected depositor behavior and reduced system-wide deposits, contributing to variability in LCR through changes in HQLA and estimated net cash outflows.
- Highlights internal liquidity stress testing: regular and ad hoc stress scenarios (including resolution/recovery planning) inform the funding plan and liquidity assessment; the Firm maintains adequate liquidity at the Parent Company, Intermediate Holding Company, and operating subsidiaries to meet risk tolerances and minimum requirements.
- References: additional details on HQLA and net cash outflows (2022 Form 10-K p. 98; U.S. LCR Disclosure reports) and on investment securities and the First Republic acquisition (Notes 10 and 28).

nodes.title: Internal stress testing
nodes.heading: 8.4.2 Internal stress testing
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm conducts internal liquidity stress testing that is intended to ensure that the Firm and its material legal entities have sufficient liquidity under a variety of adverse scenarios, including scenarios analyzed as part of the Firm’s resolution and recovery planning.
nodes.summary:
- Defines liquidity risk and points to the firm’s 2022 Form 10-K and U.S. LCR disclosures for fuller discussion.
- Explains the LCR and HQLA framework:
  - Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. must each maintain eligible HQLA sufficient to cover 30-day stressed net cash outflows; minimum LCR is 100%.
  - Excess HQLA at the bank that is not transferable to non-bank affiliates is excluded from the Firm’s reported HQLA.
  - HQLA composition: eligible cash at central banks and eligible securities (primarily U.S. Treasuries, GSE/agency MBS, and sovereign bonds), which may be reported in multiple balance sheet line items.
- Provides average LCR metrics for Q2 2023, Q1 2023, and Q2 2022:
  - JPMorgan Chase & Co.: Total HQLA $768.1B, net cash outflows $683.4B, LCR 112% in Q2 2023; net excess eligible HQLA $84.7B. End-of-period HQLA: $791.5B (6/30/23), $758.9B (3/31/23), $721.1B (6/30/22).
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.: LCR 129% in Q2 2023; net excess eligible HQLA $211.2B.
- Discusses drivers of LCR changes:
  - Firm: Q2 2023 LCR decreased vs. Q1 2023 due to long-term debt maturities, stock repurchases, and dividends, mostly offset by a dividend from the bank to the parent; increased vs. Q2 2022 primarily due to bank dividends to the parent, partially offset by buybacks/dividends.
  - Bank, N.A.: Q2 2023 LCR decreased vs. Q1 2023, including an approximate 50% decline tied to the First Republic acquisition (lower HQLA, higher net cash outflows); further pressured by higher average loans, a dividend to the parent, and lower average deposits. Decrease vs. Q2 2022 reflects lower cash from deposit declines and loan growth, lower market values of HQLA-eligible securities, and the First Republic impact.
- Notes external factors: Federal Reserve actions influenced depositor behavior and reduced system-wide deposits; LCRs may fluctuate with changes in HQLA, net cash outflows, and Fed actions.
- Describes internal liquidity stress testing:
  - Regular adverse-scenario testing, including resolution/recovery planning; results inform funding plans and liquidity positioning.
  - Liquidity is maintained at the Parent, IHC, and operating subsidiaries to meet risk tolerances and minimum requirements and to manage through stress.
- Outlines other liquidity sources:
  - Unencumbered marketable securities of about $620B at 6/30/23 (down from $694B at 12/31/22), with the decrease driven by lower excess eligible HQLA at the bank, partly offset by higher CIB trading assets and AFS securities associated with the First Republic acquisition. Liquidity realizable depends on market conditions.
  - Available borrowing capacity at FHLBs and the Federal Reserve discount window of about $332B at 6/30/23 (vs. $323B at 12/31/22), excluding HQLA and other currently pledged unencumbered securities; not viewed as a primary liquidity source.
- Confirms NSFR compliance:
  - The Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. meet the 100% minimum NSFR as of 6/30/23.
  - By end of August 2023, the Firm will begin semiannual public disclosure of its quarterly average NSFR.

nodes.title: Other liquidity sources
nodes.heading: 8.4.3 Other liquidity sources
nodes.start_phrase: In addition to the assets reported in the Firm’s eligible HQLA discussed above, the Firm had unencumbered marketable securities, such as equity and debt securities, that the Firm believes would be available to raise liquidity.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on managing liquidity through stress periods when normal funding may be disrupted, highlighting alternative liquidity sources beyond eligible HQLA.
- Unencumbered marketable securities totaled approximately $620 billion as of June 30, 2023 (down from $694 billion at December 31, 2022); includes excess eligible HQLA at JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. that is not transferable to non-bank affiliates; actual liquidity raised would depend on market conditions.
- Year-to-date decrease driven by lower excess eligible HQLA at JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., largely offset by increases in CIB trading assets and AFS securities related to the First Republic acquisition.
- Available borrowing capacity at FHLBs and the Federal Reserve discount window, supported by pledged collateral, was about $332 billion as of June 30, 2023 (versus $323 billion at December 31, 2022); excludes cash/securities already counted in eligible HQLA or other unencumbered securities pledged at central banks.
- The firm does not view discount window and other central bank facilities as primary liquidity sources.
- NSFR: Both the firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. were compliant with the 100% minimum requirement as of June 30, 2023; the firm will begin semiannual public disclosure of quarterly average NSFR by the end of August 2023.

nodes.title: NSFR
nodes.heading: 8.4.4 NSFR
nodes.start_phrase: The net stable funding ratio (“NSFR”) is a liquidity requirement for large banking organizations that is intended to measure the adequacy of “available” stable funding that is sufficient to meet their “required” amounts of stable funding over a one-year horizon.
nodes.summary:
- The firm outlines additional liquidity resources to manage stress when normal funding is disrupted.
- Unencumbered marketable securities available for liquidity were approximately $620 billion at June 30, 2023, down from $694 billion at December 31, 2022; liquidity realizable depends on market conditions.
- The decline was mainly due to reduced excess eligible HQLA at JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., partially offset by increases in CIB trading assets and AFS securities tied to the First Republic acquisition.
- Available borrowing capacity at FHLBs and the Federal Reserve discount window, supported by pledged collateral, was about $332 billion at June 30, 2023 and $323 billion at December 31, 2022; this excludes HQLA and other pledged securities, and the firm does not consider the discount window/other central banks a primary liquidity source.
- The NSFR is described as a measure of available stable funding relative to required stable funding over one year.
- As of June 30, 2023, both the firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. met the 100% minimum NSFR requirement.
- By the end of August 2023, the firm will begin semiannual public disclosure of its quarterly average NSFR.

nodes.title: Funding
nodes.heading: 8.4.5 Funding
nodes.start_phrase: Management believes that the Firm’s unsecured and secured funding capacity is sufficient to meet its on- and off-balance sheet obligations, which includes both short- and long-term cash requirements.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Firm’s funding strategy, capacity, and deposit trends.
- Funding capacity: Management believes unsecured and secured capacity is sufficient to meet on- and off-balance sheet obligations, for both short- and long-term needs.
- Funding sources and structure:
  - Diversified mix of stable deposits, secured and unsecured capital markets funding, and stockholders’ equity.
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. is primarily funded by deposits; it can also use short-/long-term secured borrowings, issue unsecured long-term debt, or borrow from the IHC.
  - Non-bank subsidiaries are mainly funded through long-term unsecured borrowings and short-term secured borrowings (repos/securities loaned).
  - Treasury and CIO invest excess funding in the investment securities portfolio or short-term liquid instruments based on interest-rate and liquidity characteristics.
  - Reference made to Note 24 for off-balance sheet obligations.
- Deposits overview:
  - Table presents period-end deposits by line of business and Corporate as of June 30, 2023 and December 31, 2022, and average deposits for the three and six months ended June 30, 2023 and 2022.
  - Total Firm deposits: period-end $2.40T (6/30/23) vs. $2.34T (12/31/22); average Q2 2023 $2.39T vs. Q2 2022 $2.53T; average 1H 2023 $2.35T vs. 1H 2022 $2.52T.
  - Deposits (especially consumer and wholesale operating deposits tied to operating service relationships) are viewed as a stable funding source that reduces reliance on wholesale markets.
  - Average balances are considered more indicative of trends than period-end balances, though market disruptions can affect them.
- Drivers of year-over-year declines in average deposits (Q2 and 1H 2023 vs. 2022):
  - Asset & Wealth Management: continued migration to higher-yielding investments amid rising rates.
  - Corporate & Investment Bank: continued deposit attrition, including deliberate reductions; partially offset by net structured note issuances driven by client demand.
  - Commercial Banking: continued attrition; partially offset by inflows related to market disruptions in Q1 2023.
  - Consumer & Community Banking: net decline from increased customer spending; largely offset by the impact of the First Republic acquisition.
  - Partially offset overall by higher Corporate balances from international consumer initiatives.

nodes.title: Deposits
nodes.heading: 8.4.6 Deposits
nodes.start_phrase: The table below summarizes, by LOB and Corporate, the period-end deposit balances as of J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 3, and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2022 , and the average deposit balances for the three and six months ended June 30, 2023 and 2022 , respectively.
nodes.summary:
- Funding overview: The Firm asserts ample unsecured and secured funding capacity to meet on- and off-balance sheet obligations. It funds the global balance sheet through diversified sources: consumer and wholesale deposits, secured and unsecured capital markets, and stockholders’ equity. JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. relies primarily on deposits, with access to secured/unsecured borrowings and IHC funding; non-bank subsidiaries use long-term unsecured and short-term secured borrowings (repos/securities loaned). Excess liquidity is managed by Treasury and CIO in investment securities and short-term instruments.

- Deposits profile and trends:
  - Period-end deposits rose to ~$2.4T at June 30, 2023 from ~$2.34T at Dec 31, 2022; deposits comprised 67% of total liabilities.
  - Average deposits declined year-over-year for both the three- and six-month periods ended June 30, 2023, driven by:
    - Migration in AWM to higher-yielding investments amid rising rates.
    - Ongoing deposit attrition in CIB and CB (partly offset by structured note issuances and Q1 2023 market-disruption inflows).
    - Net decline in CCB from higher customer spending, partly offset by deposits from the First Republic acquisition.
    - Partially offset by growth in Corporate tied to international consumer initiatives.
  - Period-end increases were led by: CIB client-driven inflows and structured notes, ~$68B of CCB deposits from First Republic, and Corporate growth; partially offset by AWM migration and CB attrition.
  - Deposits are viewed as a stable funding source, particularly consumer and wholesale operating deposits; average balances considered more representative than period-end, though market disruptions can alter trends.

- Uninsured deposits and time deposits:
  - Estimated uninsured deposits were ~$1.38T at June 30, 2023 (up from ~$1.35T), largely wholesale operating deposits.
  - Uninsured time deposits increased, with schedules provided by U.S./non-U.S. and maturity buckets; prior-period figures were refined.

- Loans and deposit ratios:
  - Loans increased to ~$1.3T; loans-to-deposits ratio rose to 54% (from 49%).
  - Deposits as a share of total liabilities declined to 67% (from 69%).

- Deposit mix and pricing:
  - Detailed average balances and rates by U.S./non-U.S., noninterest-bearing vs interest-bearing, and by product (demand, savings, time).
  - Notable rise in deposit costs in 2023 vs 2022, with higher rates across demand, savings, and especially time deposits; shift toward time deposits and reduced noninterest-bearing balances.

- Non-deposit funding (sources of funds excluding deposits):
  - Short-term unsecured funding (commercial paper, other borrowed funds, fed funds purchased) declined vs prior periods due to liquidity management (lower CP issuance) and lower overdrafts/structured note maturities.
  - Short-term secured funding (repos and securities loaned) increased, primarily from higher secured financing of trading assets and lower netting on client-driven market-making.
  - Long-term unsecured funding (senior notes, subordinated debt, structured notes) was modestly lower overall.
  - Long-term secured funding rose significantly, driven by higher FHLB advances and a Purchase Money Note related to the First Republic acquisition; credit card securitizations decreased.
  - Capital: preferred stock steady; common equity increased.

- Short-term funding dynamics:
  - Repo balances fluctuate with client activity, financing needs, liability mix management, and market factors.
  - Narrative explains repo increase and decline in commercial paper and other unsecured borrowings.

- Cross-references:
  - Pointers to other sections/notes for off-balance sheet obligations, deposit/structured note details, capital disclosures, and First Republic acquisition impacts.

- Short-term secured funding:
  - Primarily securities loaned or sold under agreements to repurchase, secured by high-quality collateral (government and agency/GSE MBS).

- Short-term unsecured funding:
  - Comprised mainly of wholesale commercial paper and other borrowed funds.
  - Decrease in commercial paper outstanding at June 30, 2023 vs. year-end and lower average balances year-over-year due to short-term liquidity management (lower net issuance).
  - Lower average “other borrowed funds” vs. prior-year periods due to fewer overdrafts and net maturities of structured notes classified as other borrowed funds in CIB.
  - Totals: $21.0B vs. $22.7B; commercial paper $11.7B vs. $12.6B.

  - Preferred stock steady at $27.4B.

  - Commercial paper and unsecured other borrowed funds averages fell vs. 2022 due to liquidity management, lower overdrafts, and structured note maturities.
- Notable footnotes/disclosures:
  - Repo and securities lending classified as short-term secured; certain items are beneficial interests of consolidated VIEs.
  - TLAC-eligible long-term unsecured debt included within structured notes.

nodes.title: Long-term funding and issuance
nodes.heading: 8.4.8 Long-term funding and issuance
nodes.start_phrase: Long-term funding provides an additional source of stable funding and liquidity for the Firm.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: The firm’s long-term funding and issuance strategy, activity, and composition for the three and six months ended June 30, 2023 versus 2022.
- Strategy and objectives: Long-term funding is used to provide stable liquidity, guided by expected client activity, liquidity needs, and regulatory requirements (including TLAC). Objectives include diversification, maximizing market access, and optimizing funding costs across markets, tenors, and currencies.
- Funding structure: The Parent Company issues the significant majority of long-term unsecured funding, advancing substantially all net proceeds to its intermediate holding company (IHC). The IHC does not issue debt to external counterparties.
- Unsecured funding activity:
  - Parent Company issuance: Q2 2023 senior notes of $2.5B in the U.S. (vs $13.0B in Q2 2022); no non‑U.S. senior notes in 2023; structured notes of $563M in Q2 2023 ($1.444B YTD) vs $918M ($2.074B) in 2022.
  - Subsidiaries issuance: Structured notes of $7.947B in Q2 2023 ($15.665B YTD) vs $11.230B ($19.679B) in 2022.
  - Parent Company maturities/redemptions: $8.686B in Q2 2023 ($16.231B YTD), including $2.027B of subordinated debt.
  - Subsidiaries maturities/redemptions: $6.481B in Q2 2023 ($14.048B YTD).
  - Certain Parent Company unsecured debt is TLAC‑eligible.
- Secured long-term funding sources and activity:
  - Sources: Credit card securitizations, FHLB advances, and a Purchase Money Note associated with the First Republic acquisition.
  - Q2 2023 issuance: $76.366B total, driven by a $50.0B Purchase Money Note and $25.775B of FHLB advances; $660M of maturities/redemptions.
  - YTD 2023 issuance: $76.517B; credit card securitization issuance of $1.0B YTD; other secured structured notes are included in “Other long-term secured funding.”
- Exclusions: Client-driven securitizations in wholesale businesses are not a funding source for the firm and are excluded from the tables.
- References: Additional details in Note 18 (IHC and long-term debt), Liquidity Risk Management (2022 Form 10-K, pages 97–104), Note 28 (First Republic acquisition), and Note 14 (client-driven securitizations).

nodes.title: Credit ratings
nodes.heading: 8.4.9 Credit ratings
nodes.start_phrase: The cost and availability of financing are influenced by credit ratings.
nodes.summary:

- States that downgrade impacts vary by contractual and behavioral factors and are incorporated into the Firm’s liquidity risk management and stress testing; the Firm believes it holds sufficient liquidity to withstand funding capacity declines from downgrades.

  - Fitch: Parent AA‑/F1+ Stable; Bank AA/F1+ Stable; Securities AA/F1+ Stable

- Portfolio snapshot (June 30, 2023 vs. December 31, 2022):

  - Total credit-related assets: $1.407T vs. $1.256T; nonperforming: $7.56B vs. $7.02B.

  - Lending-related commitments: $1.473T vs. $1.327T; nonperforming: $332M vs. $455M.
  - Total credit portfolio: $2.880T vs. $2.583T; nonperforming: $8.17B vs. $7.70B.

  - Liquid securities and other cash collateral held against derivatives: $(23.3)B vs. $(23.0)B.
- Impact of the First Republic acquisition: included $104.6B of Consumer and $98.2B of Wholesale credit exposure in the total credit portfolio.
- Nonaccrual metrics: firmwide nonaccrual loans/total loans at 0.56% (vs. 0.59%).
- Credit performance:

- Scope and composition: Describes JPMorgan Chase’s retained consumer credit portfolio, focused on the prime segment, spanning residential real estate, credit card, scored auto, and business banking loans and commitments. - Portfolio size and mix (June 30, 2023 vs. Dec 31, 2022):
  - Consumer excluding credit card: $408.2B in loans (retained, HFS, and at fair value) and $50.8B in lending-related commitments; total exposure $459.1B (up from $344.9B).
  - Credit card: $191.3B in loans and $881.5B in lending-related commitments; total exposure $1.073T (up from $1.006T).
  - Total consumer credit portfolio exposure: $1.532T (up from $1.351T).
  - Nonaccrual loans (consumer excluding credit card): $4.27B (slightly down from $4.33B).
  - Credit-related notes used in credit portfolio management: $985M notional protection outstanding.

- Performance and credit costs:
  - Q2 2023 net charge-offs (NCOs) and rates (vs. Q2 2022):
    - Consumer excluding credit card: $122M; 0.14% (up from $27M; 0.04%).
      - Residential real estate: net recoveries of $25M; -0.03% (vs. -$67M; -0.12%).
      - Auto and other: $147M; 0.89% (up from $94M; 0.56%).
    - Credit card: $1,124M; 2.41% (up from $580M; 1.47%).
    - Total consumer retained: $1,246M; 0.91% (up from $607M; 0.53%).
  - 1H 2023 vs. 1H 2022 shows similar trends: higher NCOs and rates, particularly in credit card (2.25% vs. 1.42%) and auto (0.93% vs. 0.61%), while residential real estate remains in net recoveries.

- Maturities and interest rate sensitivity (June 30, 2023):
  - Consumer excluding credit card loans: $408.2B by maturity—$36.6B within 1 year, $73.4B in 1–5 years, $114.2B in 5–15 years, $183.9B after 15 years (majority in residential real estate).
  - Credit card loans: $191.3B, largely due within 1 year (revolving).
  - Rate mix for loans due after one year:
    - Residential real estate: substantial mix of both fixed and variable rate balances across 1–5, 5–15, and >15-year buckets.
    - Auto and other: predominantly fixed rate.
  - Tables also break out fixed vs. variable allocations and identify amounts included in HFS and fair value categories.

- First Republic acquisition impact:
  - Adds $104.6B of consumer exposure excluding credit card ($101.5B residential real estate; $3.1B auto/other).
  - Detailed breakout across maturity buckets and fixed/variable rate categories.

- Key policy and data notes:
  - Nonaccrual excludes U.S. government-insured mortgages and SBA-guaranteed PPP loans; credit card loans are generally not placed on nonaccrual per regulatory guidance.
  - Commitments represent total available lines; the firm can reduce/cancel certain lines.
  - Operating lease assets are excluded from auto balances and reported in other assets.
  - Credit card loans include billed interest and fees; commercial card commitments are included in credit card commitments.
  - Average loans used in NCO rate calculations exclude HFS and fair value loans.

nodes.title: Consumer, excluding credit card Portfolio analysis
nodes.heading: 8.5.2.2 Consumer, excluding credit card Portfolio analysis
nodes.start_phrase: Loans increased compared to D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 2 driven by residential real estate loans associated with the First Republic acquis ition and higher auto loans.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Consumer lending (excluding credit cards); portfolio analysis through June 30, 2023 versus December 31, 2022.
- Portfolio growth drivers: Overall loans rose, led by residential real estate from the First Republic acquisition and higher auto loans.
- Residential real estate:
  - Composition: Predominantly prime mortgages and HELOCs; includes loans held-for-sale and at fair value.
  - Retained loans increased due to First Republic; retained nonaccrual loans declined.
  - Net recoveries fell year over year on lower prepayments amid higher interest rates.
  - Loans at fair value decreased overall (CIB sales > purchases), partly offset by higher Home Lending originations; nonaccrual at fair value was flat.
- Interest-only mortgages: Carrying value jumped to $90.0B from $36.3B, driven by First Republic; interest-only period followed by amortizing; skew to higher-balance, higher-income borrowers; performance in line with prime; no charge-offs from the acquisition.
- HELOCs: $16.9B outstanding (incl. $2.6B from First Republic); includes $4.6B recast/modified and $4.7B interest-only balloon HELOCs (mainly maturing after 2030). Risk managed by reducing/closing lines on credit deterioration.
- Government-insured/guaranteed mortgages: Total $941M at 6/30/23 (down from $1,097M), with declines across delinquency buckets.
- Geographic concentration/LTVs: 70% ($229.8B) of retained residential real estate concentrated in CA, NY, FL, TX, MA (up from 62%/$147.8B); LTV details referenced in Note 12.
- Loan modifications and accounting:
  - 2Q23/1H23 FDMs: $35M/$75M; additional trial mods: $33M/$48M; Chapter 7 loans: $3M/$5M.
  - TDR guidance changes removed certain criteria; trial mods and Chapter 7 loans considered TDRs but not FDMs.
  - Prior-year TDRs: $115M (2Q22) and $233M (1H22).
- Auto and other loans: Portfolio increased (scored Auto originations and unsecured FVO loans from First Republic, partly offset by paydowns). Net charge-offs rose as delinquencies normalized and vehicle values fell; scored Auto NCO rates: 0.41% (2Q23) vs 0.12% (2Q22); 0.43% (1H23) vs 0.15% (1H22).
- Nonperforming assets: Slight decline to $4.43B from $4.48B. Nonaccrual loans: residential $4.12B; auto/other $143M. Assets acquired in satisfaction: $162M. Excludes certain government-insured and PPP loans.
- Nonaccrual loan activity (1H23 vs 1H22): Ending balance $4.27B vs $4.67B; additions $1.29B; reductions $1.35B (payments, charge-offs, cures, liquidations). Net small decrease in 2023 vs larger decrease in 2022.
- References: Additional details in Notes 1 and 12 (credit quality, delinquencies, LTVs, modifications, foreclosure status).

nodes.title: WHOLESALE CREDIT PORTFOLIO
nodes.heading: 8.5.3 WHOLESALE CREDIT PORTFOLIO
nodes.start_phrase: In its wholesale businesses, the Firm is exposed to credit risk primarily through its underwriting, lending, market- making, and hedging activities with and for clients and counterparties, as well as through various operating services (such as cash m anagement and clearing activities), securities financing activities and cash placed with banks.
nodes.summary:
- Describes the Firm’s wholesale credit risk sources across underwriting, lending, market-making, hedging, operating services (cash management, clearing), securities financing, and cash placed with banks. Notes that a portion of originated loans is retained while a significant share is syndicated to manage concentration and credit risk, with active portfolio management via client/structure reviews and concentration monitoring.
- Defines portfolio scope: exposures in CIB, CB, AWM and Corporate, plus risk-rated BWM and auto dealer exposures in CCB that use the wholesale methodology for the allowance.
- Highlights ongoing integration of the First Republic acquisition, which is influencing portfolio size and may change reporting classifications and internal risk ratings going forward.
- Performance as of June 30, 2023: rise in nonperforming exposure driven by client-specific downgrades in CB and AWM, partly offset by lower lending-related commitments; wholesale charge-offs remained low for the first half of 2023, with Q2 increases concentrated in Office real estate.
- Growth drivers and activity: retained loans up $64.5B and lending-related commitments up $69.1B, both predominantly due to the First Republic acquisition; additional net portfolio activity in CIB and CB, including more held-for-sale positions in the bridge financing portfolio.
- Key balances and credit quality snapshot (Jun 30, 2023 vs Dec 31, 2022): 
  - Total wholesale credit portfolio $1.35T vs $1.23T, including $98.2B from First Republic.
  - Wholesale credit-related assets $807.5B vs $759.2B.
  - Lending-related commitments $541.1B vs $472.0B.
  - Nonperforming exposure $3.74B vs $3.22B.
  - Components: loans retained $668.1B (nonperforming $2.59B), loans at fair value $27.3B (nonperforming $0.37B), loans held-for-sale $5.0B (nonperforming $0.05B), derivative receivables $64.2B (nonperforming $0.29B), receivables from customers (margin loans) $42.7B. Assets acquired in loan satisfactions include $117M of real estate owned.
- Risk mitigation and collateral: net notional protection of $31.1B via credit derivatives and credit-related notes used in credit portfolio management (not hedge-accounted under U.S. GAAP); $23.3B of liquid securities and cash collateral held against derivatives.
- Cross-references to further discussions on industry concentrations, credit derivatives, and business developments.

Key balances (Jun 30, 2023 vs Dec 31, 2022): loans $700.5b vs $639.1b (nonperforming $3.0b vs $2.4b); derivative receivables $64.2b vs $70.9b; receivables from customers $42.7b vs $49.3b; total wholesale credit‑related assets $807.5b vs $759.2b (nonperforming $3.294b vs $2.691b); lending‑related commitments $541.1b vs $472.0b (nonperforming $332m vs $455m); total wholesale credit portfolio $1,348.6b vs $1,231.2b (nonperforming $3.743b vs $3.220b). nodes.title: Wholesale credit exposure – maturity and ratings profile
nodes.heading: 8.5.3.1 Wholesale credit exposure – maturity and ratings profile
nodes.start_phrase: The following tables present the maturity and internal risk rating profiles of the wholesale credit portfolio as of J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 3, and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 2.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Presents JPMorgan Chase’s wholesale credit exposure by contractual maturity and internal risk ratings as of June 30, 2023 and December 31, 2022. Investment grade is defined as internal ratings equivalent to BBB-/Baa3 or higher, with collateral and structural support considered.
- Components covered: Loans retained; derivative receivables net of liquid securities and other cash collateral; lending-related commitments; subtotal of these exposures; plus loans held-for-sale/at fair value and receivables from customers to derive total exposure. Also shows credit derivatives and credit-related notes used in credit portfolio management (CPM).
- June 30, 2023 key figures:
  - Loans retained: $668.1B; IG 68%; maturity: $225.6B ≤1yr, $265.9B 1–5yrs, $176.7B >5yrs.
  - Derivative receivables (net of collateral): $40.9B; IG 80%; maturity: $12.2B ≤1yr, $11.1B 1–5yrs, $17.6B >5yrs.
  - Lending-related commitments: $541.1B; IG 65%; maturity: $141.4B ≤1yr, $375.3B 1–5yrs, $24.4B >5yrs.
  - Subtotal exposure: $1,250.2B; IG 67%; maturity: $379.2B ≤1yr, $652.2B 1–5yrs, $218.8B >5yrs.
  - Loans held-for-sale/at fair value: $32.4B; receivables from customers: $42.7B.
  - Total exposure net of derivative collateral: $1,325.3B.
  - CPM credit derivatives and credit-related notes (notional, net by reference entity): ($31.1B); IG 86%; maturity: ($6.6B) ≤1yr, ($22.5B) 1–5yrs, ($2.0B) >5yrs.
- December 31, 2022 key figures:
  - Loans retained: $603.7B; IG 70%.
  - Derivative receivables (net): $47.9B; IG 76%.
  - Lending-related commitments: $472.0B; IG 69%.
  - Subtotal exposure: $1,123.5B; IG 70%.
  - Loans held-for-sale/at fair value: $35.4B; receivables from customers: $49.3B.
  - Total exposure net: $1,208.2B.
  - CPM credit derivatives and credit-related notes: ($18.1B); IG 83%.
- Notable trends from 12/31/22 to 6/30/23: Total wholesale exposure increased to $1.33T (from $1.21T), driven by higher loans retained and lending commitments; net derivative receivables declined; IG mix edged down in loans and commitments but rose in derivatives; CPM protection increased and remains predominantly IG.
- Methodology and footnotes: Internal ratings per Note 12 of the 2022 Form 10-K; derivative receivables shown net of liquid securities and cash collateral; maturity profiles based on remaining contractual maturity, noting receivable derivatives can become payable earlier; loans held-for-sale primarily syndicated or transferred loans; CPM derivatives do not qualify for hedge accounting; notional amounts shown net by reference entity; protection largely purchased from IG counterparties, with some protection via credit-related notes.

nodes.title: Wholesale credit exposure – industry exposures
nodes.heading: 8.5.3.2 Wholesale credit exposure – industry exposures
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm focuses on the management and diversification of its industry exposures, and pays particular attention to industries with actual or potential credit concerns.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: The firm’s management, diversification, and monitoring of wholesale credit exposure by industry, with heightened attention to sectors showing actual or potential credit concerns.
- Criticized exposure: Aligns with U.S. regulatory categories (special mention, substandard, doubtful). Excluding loans held-for-sale and at fair value, criticized exposure was $35.0B (2.8% of total wholesale credit exposure) at June 30, 2023, up from $31.3B (2.7%) at December 31, 2022. The increase was driven by client-specific downgrades in Real Estate, Consumer & Retail, Technology, Media & Telecommunications, and Healthcare, plus exposures from the First Republic acquisition, partially offset by upgrades. About half of criticized exposure was undrawn, and $31.8B was performing.
- Industry exposure tables: Detailed breakdowns as of June 30, 2023 and December 31, 2022 show, by industry, credit exposure, investment-grade vs noninvestment-grade, criticized (performing and nonperforming), 30+ days past due and accruing loans, net charge-offs/(recoveries), credit derivative hedges/credit-related notes, and liquid securities/cash collateral held against derivative receivables.
  - June 30, 2023 subtotal credit exposure across industries: $1,273.5B; plus loans held-for-sale and at fair value $32.4B; receivables from customers $42.7B; total $1,348.6B.
  - December 31, 2022 subtotal: $1,146.5B; plus loans held-for-sale and at fair value $35.4B; receivables from customers $49.3B; total $1,231.2B.
  - At June 30, 2023, criticized performing totaled $31.8B and criticized nonperforming $3.2B.
  - Largest industry exposures (June 30, 2023) include Real Estate ($206.9B), Individuals & Individual Entities ($141.2B), Asset Managers ($138.1B), and Consumer & Retail ($125.9B).
- First Republic acquisition: $98.2B of credit exposure added, predominantly in Asset Managers, Real Estate, and Individuals & Individual Entities; Real Estate includes $33.2B related to this acquisition.
- Real Estate detail:
  - Total exposure rose to $206.9B at June 30, 2023 (from $170.9B at December 31, 2022).
  - Criticized exposure increased by $1.3B to $5.3B due to client-specific downgrades (partly offset by upgrades).
  - Composition (June 30, 2023): Multifamily $119.9B (largely in California), Other Income Producing $18.8B, Industrial $18.0B, Office $17.6B, Services/Non-Income Producing $15.7B, Retail $12.9B, Lodging $3.9B.
  - Investment-grade share 73% (vs 76% at year-end 2022); drawn 80% (vs 77%); approximately 82% secured; unsecured exposure ~76% investment-grade.
- Methodology and footnotes highlights:
  - Industry of risk is based on the counterparty’s primary business.
  - Credit exposure is net of risk participations and excludes the benefit of credit derivatives/credit-related notes and liquid securities/cash collateral held against derivative receivables; includes held-for-sale and fair value option lending-related commitments.
  - Cash and other deposits placed with banks are excluded ($485.4B at June 30, 2023; $556.6B at December 31, 2022).
  - Additional state and municipal government exposures are held in trading, AFS, and HTM securities.
  - “All other” primarily includes SPEs; “Individuals & Individual Entities” largely reflects private banking and wealth management clients.
  - Credit derivative hedges and credit-related notes are used for credit portfolio management and do not qualify for hedge accounting; the “All other” category includes purchased credit protection on certain credit indices.
  - Industry rankings for December 31, 2022 are presented based on June 30, 2023 rankings.

nodes.title: Lending-related commitments
nodes.heading: 8.5.3.5 Lending-related commitments
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm uses lending-related financial instruments, such as commitments (including revolving credit facilities) and guarantees, to address the financing needs of its clients.
nodes.summary:
- Lending-related commitments: The Firm provides commitments (including revolving credit facilities) and guarantees to meet client financing needs. Contractual amounts represent maximum potential credit risk if drawn or if guarantees are honored and clients default, but historically many are refinanced, extended, canceled, or expire undrawn; thus, contractual totals are not indicative of expected future exposure or funding needs. Refer to Note 24.
- Receivables from customers: Held-for-investment margin loans to brokerage clients in CIB, CCB, and AWM, collateralized by cash and liquid securities in client accounts. Due to strong collateralization, no allowance for credit losses is generally held. The Firm manages risk via margin requirements, ongoing monitoring, and collateral calls or position reductions. Reported in accrued interest and accounts receivable on the Consolidated balance sheets.
- Derivative contracts: Used to help clients manage market and credit risks and by the Firm to manage risks from market-making and its own exposures. Credit risk varies by counterparty and settlement type (OTC vs. exchange-traded vs. OTC-cleared), including exposure to CCPs. Risk is mitigated through legally enforceable master netting and collateral agreements.
- Collateralization levels: Approximately 88% (June 30, 2023) and 87% (December 31, 2022) of OTC derivatives (excluding FX spot and daily-settled centrally cleared trades) are subject to collateral agreements. See Note 5.
- Derivative receivables: Fair value of derivative receivables was $64.2 billion at June 30, 2023, down from $70.9 billion at December 31, 2022, primarily due to market movements in CIB Markets. Balances reflect effects of enforceable netting and related cash collateral.
- Collateral held: The Firm holds liquid securities and cash collateral consistent with HQLA under the LCR rule, plus other collateral that may not qualify as HQLA. These are subject to enforceable netting and limited to the net receivable per counterparty.
- Additional collateral: The Firm also holds collateral posted at trade initiation, for non-daily margining, and collateral agreed to be returned but unsettled; this does not reduce reported receivable balances but provides security against potential future exposure. Refer to Note 5 for further details on collateral and derivatives.

nodes.title: Receivables from customers
nodes.heading: 8.5.3.6 Receivables from customers
nodes.start_phrase: Receivables from customers reflect held-for-investment margin loans to brokerage clients in CIB, CCB and AWM that are collateralized by assets maintained in the clients’ brokerage accounts (e.g., cash on deposit, and liquid and readily marketable debt or equity securities).
nodes.summary:
- Overview of lending-related commitments: The firm extends commitments (including revolving credit facilities) and guarantees to meet client financing needs. Contractual amounts represent maximum potential credit risk if drawn or if guarantees are called and clients default, but historically most are refinanced, extended, canceled, or expire undrawn, so totals are not indicative of expected future exposure or funding needs. Referenced Note 24 for details.
- Receivables from customers (margin loans): Held-for-investment margin loans to brokerage clients in CIB, CCB, and AWM are collateralized by clients’ brokerage assets (cash and liquid marketable securities). Due to strong collateralization, no allowance for credit losses is generally recorded. Risk is managed via margin requirements, continuous monitoring, and margin calls or position reductions as needed. These receivables are reported within accrued interest and accounts receivable on the Consolidated balance sheets.
- Derivative contracts and credit risk management: Derivatives are used by clients and the firm to manage credit, interest rate, FX, equity, and commodities risks. The firm makes markets in derivatives, manages risks from market-making (including counterparty credit risk), and uses derivatives to manage its own credit and market risks. Credit risk varies by counterparty type and settlement mechanism: OTC derivatives expose the firm to counterparty risk; ETD and OTC-cleared derivatives can expose it to CCP risk. Risk mitigation includes legally enforceable master netting and collateral agreements.
- Collateralization levels: Approximately 88% of OTC derivative transactions (excluding FX spot and centrally cleared trades settled daily) were subject to collateral agreements at June 30, 2023, versus 87% at December 31, 2022. Referenced Note 5 for more on collateral and derivative arrangements.
- Derivative receivables: Fair value of derivative receivables was $64.2 billion at June 30, 2023, down from $70.9 billion at December 31, 2022, primarily due to market movements in CIB Markets. Balances are presented net of legally enforceable master netting and related cash collateral.
- Collateral held: In addition to cash, the firm holds liquid securities consistent with HQLA under the LCR rule and considers other non-HQLA collateral (subject to enforceable netting and limited to net receivables) in assessing current credit risk. The firm also holds additional collateral (e.g., cash, G7 government securities, other liquid government/agency/guaranteed securities, and corporate debt/equity) posted at trade initiation, for non-daily call frequencies, and amounts pending return; these do not reduce reported balances but serve as security if exposures increase. Referenced Note 5 for further information.

nodes.title: ALLOWANCE FOR CREDIT LOSSES
nodes.heading: 8.5.4 ALLOWANCE FOR CREDIT LOSSES
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm’s allowance for credit losses represents management's estimate of expected credit losses over the remaining expected life of the Firm's financial asset s measured at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet lending-related commitments.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Describes the Firm’s allowance for credit losses (ACL) as management’s estimate of expected losses over the remaining life of financial assets measured at amortized cost and certain off–balance sheet lending-related commitments.
- Components of ACL:
  - Allowance for loan losses (retained scored and risk-rated loan portfolios).
  - Allowance for lending-related commitments (recorded in accounts payable and other liabilities).
  - Allowance for credit losses on investment securities (recorded in investment securities).
- Level and change: ACL was $24.3 billion at June 30, 2023, a net increase of $2.7 billion from December 31, 2022.
- Drivers of change:
  - $1.5 billion net addition:
    - $819 million in wholesale due to net downgrades, updated office real estate assumptions in Commercial Banking in Q2 2023, and higher weighting of adverse scenarios initiated in Q1 2023.
    - $649 million in consumer, largely Card Services, reflecting loan growth and macro outlook changes (including a higher projected unemployment peak in Q3 2024), and increased adverse-scenario weights, partly offset by reduced borrower uncertainty.
  - $1.2 billion established for First Republic loans and lending-related commitments in Q2 2023.
  - $587 million reduction from adoption of updated TDR accounting guidance on January 1, 2023.
- Scenario methodology and outlook:
  - ACL estimated using a weighted average of five internally developed macroeconomic scenarios.
  - Maintains elevated weighting on adverse scenarios reflecting higher probability of a moderate recession due to tightening financial conditions.
  - Adverse scenarios imply a weighted average U.S. unemployment peak of 5.8% in Q3 2024 and U.S. real GDP 1.5% lower by Q4 2024 versus the central case.
- Central case macro assumptions:
  - As of June 30, 2023: U.S. unemployment 4.2% (Q4’23), 4.9% (Q2’24), 5.0% (Q4’24); YoY real GDP growth 0.5% (Q4’23), 0.0% (Q2’24), 1.0% (Q4’24).
  - As of December 31, 2022: U.S. unemployment 3.8% (Q2’23), 4.3% (Q4’23), 5.0% (Q2’24); YoY real GDP growth 1.5% (Q2’23), 0.4% (Q4’23), 0.0% (Q2’24).
- Notes:
  - Future changes in forecasts will flow through provision for credit losses.
  - References provided to 2022 Form 10-K Notes and sections on consumer and wholesale credit portfolios and critical accounting estimates for methodologies and judgments.

nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s allowance for credit losses (ACL) estimates expected losses over the remaining life of financial assets at amortized cost and certain off‑balance sheet lending commitments, comprising the allowance for loan losses (retained scored and risk‑rated portfolios), allowance for lending‑related commitments (in accounts payable and other liabilities), and allowance on investment securities (in investment securities). As of June 30, 2023, ACL was $24.3 billion, a net $2.7 billion increase from December 31, 2022, driven by $1.5 billion higher reserves—$819 million wholesale (downgrades, updated office real estate assumptions in CB, and added adverse‑scenario weighting in 1Q23) and $649 million consumer (Card Services loan growth and macro outlook, including unemployment peaking in 3Q24, with partial offset from reduced borrower uncertainty)—plus $1.2 billion to establish reserves for First Republic loans and lending‑related commitments, partly offset by a $587 million reduction from adopting changes to TDR accounting on January 1, 2023. The Firm uses a weighted average of five internally developed macroeconomic scenarios and maintained increased weighting on a relative adverse scenario reflecting tighter financial conditions and a higher probability of a moderate recession; adverse scenarios imply a weighted‑average U.S. unemployment peak of 5.8% in 3Q24 and U.S. real GDP 1.5% lower exiting 4Q24 versus the central case. Central case assumptions at June 30, 2023: unemployment 4.2% (4Q23), 4.9% (2Q24), 5.0% (4Q24); YoY real GDP growth 0.5% (4Q23), 0.0% (2Q24), 1.0% (4Q24); at December 31, 2022: unemployment 3.8% (2Q23), 4.3% (4Q23), 5.0% (2Q24); GDP 1.5% (2Q23), 0.4% (4Q23), 0.0% (2Q24). Subsequent forecast changes will be reflected in future provision for credit losses; references are provided to the 2022 Form 10‑K notes and portfolio sections for policies, methodologies, and judgments.

nodes.title: INVESTMENT PORTFOLIO RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: 8.5.5 INVESTMENT PORTFOLIO RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase: Investment portfolio risk is the risk associated with the loss of principal or a reduction in expected returns on investments arising from the investment securities portfolio or from principal investments.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines JPMorgan Chase’s investment portfolio risk management, defining portfolio risk as potential loss of principal or reduced returns from investment securities and principal investments. It distinguishes two main risk areas: investment securities risk—primarily default risk mitigated by a high-quality Treasury and CIO portfolio totaling $610.2 billion at June 30, 2023, with an average AA+ rating—and principal investment risk—privately held ownership/junior capital positions, including tax-oriented investments and strategic investments managed by LOBs and Corporate. The Firm emphasizes long-term holding with no expectation of short-term gains. As of June 30, 2023, principal investments carried $38.9 billion (up from $37.0 billion at year-end 2022), comprising $27.5 billion in tax-oriented assets (alternative energy and affordable housing, including ~$1.2 billion tied to the First Republic acquisition) and $11.4 billion in private equity, various debt/equity, and real assets, including a 40% stake in C6 Bank and 49% in Viva Wallet. The text references related sections on liquidity and market risk, corporate segment results, and the 2022 Form 10-K (page 130) for governance and oversight, and notes the Firm’s commitment to supporting underserved communities and minority-owned businesses through its investment strategy.

- Points to JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 Form 10-K for detailed discussion of the Market Risk Management organization, measurement, monitoring, control, and business activities that generate market risk.
- Acknowledges inherent limitations and imprecision of risk models, especially under sudden or severe market shifts; refers to model risk governance in the 10-K.
- Describes ongoing review and calibration of market risk measures to enhance effectiveness over time.
- Explains the Firm’s single value-at-risk (VaR) framework supporting both Risk Management VaR and Regulatory VaR.
- Details Risk Management VaR: one-day holding period, expected tail-loss methodology approximating a 95% confidence level, aligned to daily risk management decisions.
- Describes Regulatory VaR: daily aggregated VaR calculated per regulatory rules and used to determine Basel III VaR-based capital requirements.
- Notes that model updates due to portfolio composition, market conditions, and modeling improvements can affect historical VaR comparisons; references model review and approval processes.
- Directs readers to the 10-K and Basel III Pillar 3 disclosures for inherent VaR limitations, differences between Risk Management VaR and Regulatory VaR, stressed VaR, backtesting, and other market risk regulatory capital components.
- Mentions additional nonstatistical market risk measures used by the Firm, with further detail in the 10-K.

nodes.title: Value-at-risk
nodes.heading: 8.6.1 Value-at-risk
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase utilizes value-at-risk (“VaR”), a statistical risk measure , to estimate the potential loss from adverse market moves in the current market environment.
nodes.summary:
- Defines market risk as exposure to changes in interest rates, FX rates, equity/commodity prices, credit spreads, and implied volatilities, affecting assets and liabilities over short and long horizons.
- Points to JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 Form 10-K for detailed discussion of the Market Risk Management organization, measurement, monitoring/controls, and businesses that generate market risk.
- Acknowledges model imprecision, especially under sudden/severe market shifts, and references Estimations and Model Risk Management (10-K, p. 148) for model uncertainty.
- Describes the Firm’s single value-at-risk (VaR) framework used for both Risk Management VaR and Regulatory VaR.
- Risk Management VaR: one-day holding period; expected tail-loss methodology approximating a 95% confidence level; intended to align with daily risk management decisions.
- Regulatory VaR: separately calculated under regulatory rules and used for Basel III market risk capital; references Basel III Pillar 3 disclosures for details (VaR, stressed VaR, backtesting).
- Notes ongoing VaR model evaluation/enhancement as portfolios and markets evolve; changes can affect historical comparability; references model review/approval governance (10-K, p. 148).
- Mentions other nonstatistical market risk measures (10-K, pp. 136–138) and key differences/limitations of Risk Management VaR vs. Regulatory VaR (10-K, p. 133).
- Presents a table of Risk Management VaR (95% confidence) showing:
  - Total VaR averages: $47mm (Q2 2023), $47mm (Q1 2023), $54mm (Q2 2022), with associated minimum/maximum values.
  - Breakdown for CIB trading by risk type (fixed income, FX, equities, commodities), Credit Portfolio VaR, CCB VaR, Corporate/other LOB VaR.
  - Diversification benefits reducing aggregate VaR, highlighting the non-additive nature of VaR.
- Footnotes highlight:
  - Diversification benefit is not meaningful for max/min due to timing differences.
  - Credit Portfolio VaR excludes certain counterparties’ CVA credit risk (and related hedges) since Q1 2022 due to spread widening; exposure now reflected in sensitivity-based measures.
  - Corporate/other includes a legacy publicly traded private equity position.
  - CCB VaR increase driven by interest rate volatility affecting Home Lending warehouse loans, MSR, and hedges.
  - Elevated maximum Credit Portfolio VaR in 2022 linked to nickel market volatility.
- Commentary:
  - Quarter over quarter (Q2 2023 vs. Q1 2023): average total VaR flat; higher fixed income risk offset by commodity volatility rolling out of the one-year look-back window.
  - Year over year (Q2 2023 vs. Q2 2022): average total VaR down $7mm, mainly from risk reductions in Credit Portfolio VaR and fixed income.
- Includes a chart of daily Risk Management VaR over the last five quarters.

nodes.title: Total VaR
nodes.heading: 8.6.2 Total VaR
nodes.start_phrase: The table below shows the results of the Firm’s Risk Management VaR measure using a 95% confidence level.
nodes.summary:
- Presents the Firm’s Risk Management Value-at-Risk (VaR) at a 95% confidence level, noting VaR can change with positions, market volatility, and diversification effects.
- Provides a table of Total VaR for the three months ended June 30, 2023; March 31, 2023; and June 30, 2022, with average, minimum, and maximum values.
- Breaks down CIB trading VaR by risk type (fixed income, foreign exchange, equities, commodities and other), shows associated diversification benefits, and reports resulting CIB trading VaR.
- Includes Credit Portfolio VaR (covering derivative CVA, associated hedges, and hedges of the retained loan portfolio reported in principal transactions revenue), and shows diversification benefits to derive overall CIB VaR.
- Reports other lines of business VaR:
  - CCB VaR (increase driven by interest rate volatility affecting Home Lending warehouse loans, MSR, and related hedges).
  - Corporate and other LOB VaR (includes a publicly traded legacy private equity position).
  - Diversification benefits and resulting “Other VaR.”
- Shows diversification benefit between CIB and Other to arrive at Total VaR; notes “NM” (not meaningful) for diversification on min/max because component extremes occur on different days.
- Key figures:
  - Average Total VaR: $47 million in Q2 2023 (flat vs. Q1 2023), $54 million in Q2 2022.
  - Average CIB trading VaR: $41 million in Q2 2023.
  - Average Credit Portfolio VaR: $14 million in Q2 2023.
  - Average CCB VaR: $9 million in Q2 2023.
  - Average Corporate and other LOB VaR: $13 million in Q2 2023.
- Methodology and model notes:
  - Diversification benefit reflects non-additivity due to imperfect correlations across LOBs, Corporate, and risk types.
  - In Q1 2022, the credit risk component of CVA for certain counterparties and related hedges were removed from Credit Portfolio VaR due to elevated credit spreads; these exposures are now captured via other sensitivity-based measures.
  - Elevated maximum Credit Portfolio VaR in the period ended June 30, 2022 was linked to nickel price spikes and volatility in early 2022.
- Trend commentary:
  - Quarter-over-quarter: Average Total VaR flat in Q2 2023 versus Q1 2023; higher fixed income VaR offset by commodities volatility rolling out of the one-year historical look-back period.
  - Year-over-year: Average Total VaR decreased by $7 million versus Q2 2022, driven by risk reductions affecting Credit Portfolio VaR and fixed income.
- References a chart of daily Risk Management VaR over the last five quarters.

nodes.title: VaR backtesting
nodes.heading: 8.6.3 VaR backtesting
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm performs daily VaR model backtesting , which compares the daily Risk Management VaR results with the daily gains and losses that are utilized for VaR backtesting purposes.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Daily Value-at-Risk (VaR) backtesting of the Firm’s Risk Management VaR.
- Method: Compares daily Risk Management VaR to daily backtesting gains/losses; these gains/losses exclude components of total net revenue (e.g., intraday new transactions, fees, commissions, certain valuation adjustments, and net interest income). Definition aligns with Basel III backtesting requirements.
- Exception definition: A backtesting exception occurs when the daily backtesting loss exceeds the prior day’s Risk Management VaR.
- Expected frequency: Assuming market changes mirror the historical simulation window, about 5 exceptions per 100 trading days on average; deviations can occur if current volatility differs from the 12-month historical period used in VaR.
- Results:
  - 12 months ended June 30, 2023: backtesting gains on 134 of 259 days; 15 exceptions.
  - Three months ended June 30, 2023: backtesting gains on 34 of 65 days; 2 exceptions.
- Chart described: Shows distribution of daily backtesting gains and losses over trailing 12 months and three months ended June 30, 2023. Losses are expressed as a percentage of corresponding daily Risk Management VaR, aggregated in 50-percentage-point intervals; exceptions appear in intervals >100%.
- Note on disclosure differences: These results differ from those in the Market Risk section of the Firm’s Basel III Pillar 3 Regulatory Capital Disclosures, which use Regulatory VaR for covered positions.

nodes.title: Structural interest rate risk management
nodes.heading: 8.6.4 Structural interest rate risk management
nodes.start_phrase: The effect of interest rate exposure on the Firm’s reported net income is important as interest rate risk represents one of the Firm’s significant market risks.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: How the firm manages structural interest rate risk, a key market risk affecting reported net income, arising from both trading and traditional banking activities (loans, deposits, debt issuance, investment securities).
- Primary measure: Earnings-at-risk (EaR), which estimates 12‑month sensitivity of a baseline (net interest income plus certain interest-sensitive fees) under specified interest rate scenarios for U.S. dollar and non‑U.S. dollar exposures. Simulations include retained loans, deposits, deposits with banks, investment securities, long-term debt, related hedges, and funds transfer pricing positions.
- Scenario design: Parallel shifts (+/−100 bps), steeper yield curve (hold short-term rates, move long-term), and flatter curve (move short-term, hold long-term; or hold short-term, move long-term). EaR considers instantaneous shocks, forecasted balance sheet dynamics, modeled prepayment/reinvestment, and deposit behavior; it excludes management and customer actions in response to rate shocks. EaR is a risk sensitivity, not a forecast.
- Key assumptions and uncertainties:
  - Mortgage prepayment modeling based on rate differentials, seasonality, and historical behavior.
  - Deposit forecasts influenced by uncertain monetary policy dynamics (e.g., QE reversal, use of the Federal Reserve’s Reverse Repurchase Facility), industry loan levels, and competition.
  - Deposit betas and repricing dynamics: Model updated in Q2 2023 to incorporate repricing lags for consumer and wholesale deposits based on observed behavior in rising and falling rate environments; actual deposit pricing may differ due to customer behavior and competition.
  - Models and scenarios are periodically enhanced to reflect balance sheet mix, market conditions, and methodology improvements.
- U.S. dollar EaR sensitivities (in billions):
  - As of June 30, 2023: Parallel +100 bps: +$2.5; Parallel −100 bps: −$2.2; Steeper (+100 bps long-term): +$0.6; Steeper (−100 bps short-term): −$1.6; Flatter (+100 bps short-term): +$1.8; Flatter (−100 bps long-term): −$0.6.
  - As of December 31, 2022: Parallel +100 bps: −$2.0; Parallel −100 bps: +$2.4; Steeper (+100 bps long-term): +$0.8; Steeper (−100 bps short-term): +$3.2; Flatter (+100 bps short-term): −$2.8; Flatter (−100 bps long-term): −$0.9.
  - Q2 2023 model update note: Prior periods not revised. Without the repricing lag update, June 30, 2023 sensitivities would have been lower by $4.2 for +100 bps short-term and parallel scenarios and higher by $4.4 for −100 bps short-term and parallel scenarios.
  - Changes vs year-end 2022 reflect balance sheet shifts, including the First Republic acquisition. As of June 30, 2023, parallel shift sensitivity is driven primarily by assets repricing more than liabilities.
  - Ongoing integration of First Republic operations and product allocations (including deposits) may affect future EaR results.
- Non‑U.S. dollar EaR sensitivities (in billions):
  - As of June 30, 2023: Parallel +100 bps: +$0.8; Parallel −100 bps: −$0.8; Steeper (−100 bps short-term): −$0.7; Flatter (+100 bps short-term): +$0.8.
  - As of December 31, 2022: Parallel +100 bps: +$0.7; Parallel −100 bps: −$0.6; Steeper (−100 bps short-term): −$0.6; Flatter (+100 bps short-term): +$0.6.
  - Steeper/flatter scenarios moving only long-term rates ±100 bps with short-term rates unchanged were not material at both dates.
- Additional measure: Economic Value Sensitivity (EVS), which stress-tests the longer-term economic value of equity for the current balance sheet (loans, deposits, debt, securities, and hedges) under rate scenarios; limits are set as a percentage of tangible common equity (TCE). References are made to related VaR and sensitivity measures and to additional disclosures in the firm’s Form 10‑K.

nodes.title: Other sensitivity-based measures
nodes.heading: 8.6.5 Other sensitivity-based measures
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm quantifies the market risk of certain debt and equity and credit and funding-related exposures by assessing the potential impact on net revenue, other comprehensive income (“OCI”) and noninterest expense due to changes in relevant market variables.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose: Presents “other sensitivity-based measures” the Firm uses to quantify market risk for certain debt, equity, credit, and funding-related exposures that are not included in VaR or earnings-at-risk, showing potential impacts on net revenue, OCI, and noninterest expense from specified market shocks.
- Scope and methodology: Positions include hedges reported net of the hedged items; sensitivities are based on standardized shocks (e.g., 10% market value decline, 1 bp spread or cross-currency basis move, 10% FX depreciation) and are not predictions or necessarily representative of realized results; maturity effects can differ.
- Key sensitivity results as of June 30, 2023 (Dec 31, 2022):
  - Debt and equity:
    - Asset Management activities (seed capital, co-investments, deferred compensation and hedges): 10% market value decline → loss of $58m ($56m).
    - Other debt and equity (real estate-related FVO loans, privately held equity and other fair value investments): 10% market value decline → loss of $1,016m ($1,046m).
  - Credit- and funding-related:
    - Non-USD LTD cross-currency basis: 1 bp parallel tightening → loss of $11m ($12m).
    - Non-USD LTD FX hedges: 10% currency depreciation → gain of $4m ($3m).
    - Derivatives funding spread risk (FVA): 1 bp parallel spread increase → loss of $4m ($4m).
    - CVA counterparty credit risk and hedges: 10% credit spread widening → $0m loss ($1m loss).
    - FVO liabilities funding spread risk (DVA): 1 bp parallel spread increase → gain of $45m ($43m).
    - FVO liabilities interest rate sensitivity to own credit spread: 1 bp parallel spread increase → $0m ($0m), including related risk management interest rate sensitivity → $0m ($0m).
- Financial statement impacts: certain items recognized in net revenue, others in OCI or noninterest expense, as indicated.
- Notes:
  - Excludes equity securities without readily determinable fair values measured under the measurement alternative.
  - In 1Q22, the credit risk component of CVA for certain counterparties and related hedges was moved out of Credit Portfolio VaR into these other sensitivity-based measures due to elevated credit spread widening.
  - For business activities giving rise to market risk, refer to the Firm’s 2022 Form 10-K (page 138).

nodes.title: COUNTRY RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: 8.7 COUNTRY RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm, through its LOBs and Corporate, may be exposed to country risk resulting from financial, economic, political or other significant developments which adversely affect the value of the Firm’s exposures related to a particular country or set of countries.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Describes how the Firm’s Country Risk Management group monitors financial, economic, political, and other country-specific risks across portfolios, assesses diversification, and aligns exposures with strategy and risk tolerance.
- Reference: Points to JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 Form 10-K (pp. 139–140) for more detail.
- Risk reporting framework: Presents top 20 non-U.S. country exposures as of June 30, 2023, with comparisons to December 31, 2022, noting selections are based on internal methodology and are not judgments about adverse credit conditions; exposures fluctuate with client activity and market flows.
- Key period changes: Higher exposures to Germany and the United Kingdom driven by increased cash placed with their central banks due to client-driven activity and interest rate changes; lower exposure to Australia due to reduced central bank cash placements for similar reasons.
- Geopolitical monitoring: Ongoing monitoring of impacts from the war in Ukraine; Russia exposure approximately $430 million as of June 30, 2023, excluding certain client deposits at the Depository Insurance Agency of Russia.
- Quantitative highlights: Germany ($112.3B) and the United Kingdom ($89.0B) are the largest non-U.S. country exposures; Japan totals $43.4B; other notable exposures include Brazil, Canada, Australia, Switzerland, France, China, and more; the top 20 countries account for 88% of total firmwide non-U.S. exposure.
- Exposure composition categories:
  - Deposits with banks: Predominantly cash placed with central banks.
  - Lending: Loans and accrued interest, lending-related commitments net of eligible collateral and allowances; excludes intra-day/operating exposures.
  - Trading and investing: Market-making inventory, investment securities, and counterparty exposure on derivatives and securities financing, net of eligible collateral and hedging; includes exposures via single-name and index transactions referencing listed countries.
  - Other: Physical commodities inventory and clearing house guarantee funds.
- Methodological notes: Country attribution follows the Firm’s internal country risk management approach; December 31, 2022 comparatives are aligned to the June 30, 2023 country ranking order.

nodes.title: CRITICAL ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES USED BY THE FIRM
nodes.heading: 8.8 CRITICAL ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES USED BY THE FIRM
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase ’s accounting policies and use of estimates are integral to understanding its reported results.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of JPMorgan Chase’s critical accounting estimates, emphasizing the importance of management judgment in determining carrying values of assets and liabilities.
- Description of governance around estimates: established policies, controls, independent reviews, consistency across periods, and controlled methodology changes.
- Focus on the allowance for credit losses (ACL), covering:
  - Allowance for loan losses on retained loan portfolios.
  - Allowance for lending-related commitments (recorded in liabilities).
  - Allowance for credit losses on investment securities (recorded within investment securities).
- Key judgments in ACL estimation: macroeconomic forecasts and their weighting, historical loss experience, portfolio risk characteristics and ratings, collateral valuation, and remaining expected life.
- Use of an eight-quarter macroeconomic forecast incorporating hundreds of MEVs; modeled losses primarily driven by fewer than twenty variables.
  - Consumer key MEVs: regional U.S. unemployment, home price index (HPI).
  - Wholesale key MEVs: U.S. unemployment, real GDP, equity prices, interest rates, corporate credit spreads, oil prices, commercial real estate prices, and HPI.
- Statement that changes in assumptions and economic forecasts can materially impact ACL estimates and drive period-to-period variability.
- Impact of the First Republic acquisition:
  - ACL recorded for acquired loans and assumed commitments as of May 1, 2023.
  - Due to differing risk rating methodologies and ongoing integration, wholesale ACL measured by analogy to similar JPM facilities rather than modeled estimates; excluded from sensitivity analysis.
  - Consumer portfolio (predominantly residential real estate) measured using modeled approach and included in sensitivity analysis.
- Acknowledgment of the difficulty in isolating the effect of any single factor on ACL due to interacting and potentially offsetting inputs across geographies and products.
- Sensitivity analysis framework: comparison of modeled credit losses under the Firm’s central and relative adverse macroeconomic scenarios (two of five scenarios used), which differ in the paths and extremity of MEVs over the eight-quarter horizon.

nodes.title: Allowance for credit losses
nodes.heading: 8.8.1 Allowance for credit losses
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm’s allowance for credit losses represents management’s estimate of expected credit losses over the remaining expected life of the Firm’s financial assets measured at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet lending-related commitments.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines JPMorgan Chase’s critical accounting estimates, emphasizing governance over estimation methods and consistent application across periods. It focuses on the allowance for credit losses, which covers loan losses, lending-related commitments, and investment securities, and relies on significant judgments including macroeconomic forecasts, historical loss experience, risk ratings, collateral values, and remaining expected life. Expected losses are modeled over an eight-quarter forecast using hundreds of macroeconomic variables, with a smaller subset driving results: for consumer portfolios, key variables include regional U.S. unemployment and home price index (HPI); for wholesale, unemployment, real GDP, equity prices, interest rates, credit spreads, oil prices, commercial real estate prices, and HPI. The First Republic acquisition led to allowances for acquired loans and commitments; due to differing risk rating methodologies and ongoing integration, wholesale allowances were benchmarked to similar JPMorgan facilities (and excluded from modeled sensitivity), while the predominantly residential consumer portfolio used the Firm’s modeled approach (and is included in sensitivity). A scenario sensitivity comparing a relative adverse scenario to the central scenario (with unemployment averaging 1.6% higher and peaking 2.2% higher in Q1 2024, real GDP about 3.1% lower at the end of the horizon with a 3.4% peak difference in Q3 2024, and HPI peaking 10.5% lower in Q1 2025) indicates modeled increases of approximately $750 million for residential real estate loans and related commitments (including First Republic), $2.4 billion for credit card loans, and $3.8 billion for wholesale loans and commitments (excluding First Republic). The Firm cautions that these modeled sensitivities are not predictions of allowance changes due to scenario weighting, nonlinear and interrelated macro variable effects, and potential portfolio and behavior shifts, and asserts its estimates were reasonable as of June 30, 2023. The excerpt also summarizes fair value measurements: many assets and liabilities are measured at fair value on a recurring basis (e.g., derivatives, structured products, securities financing), while certain loans are measured on a nonrecurring basis using collateral fair value. As of June 30, 2023, total assets measured at fair value were about $1.281 trillion, of which $27.9 billion were Level 3; total Firm assets were $3.868 trillion, with Level 3 assets equal to 0.7% of total assets and 2.2% of assets at fair value. Level 3 balances are concentrated in derivative receivables (~$10.7 billion), mortgage servicing rights (~$8.2 billion), loans (~$3.8 billion), and trading instruments (~$3.3 billion), with a note that Level 3 derivative figures are shown before netting benefits.

nodes.title: Valuation
nodes.heading: 8.8.3 Valuation
nodes.start_phrase: Estimating fair value requires the application of judgment.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on the judgment required to estimate fair value, which increases as market observability decreases, especially for Level 3 instruments in the fair value hierarchy.
- For Level 3 valuations, management selects appropriate models/techniques and derives significant unobservable inputs from empirical data (e.g., transaction details, yield curves, interest rates, prepayment speeds, default rates, volatilities, correlations, prices, comparable valuations, FX rates, credit curves). Referenced Note 2 for details.
- For Levels 2 and 3, management applies valuation adjustments for counterparty and own credit, market funding rates, liquidity, unobservable parameters, and portfolio-size considerations; these judgments are influenced by product terms, market liquidity, and volatility. Referenced Note 2 for further discussion.
- Acknowledgment that imprecision in unobservable inputs can impact recorded gains/losses and that methods/assumptions may vary across businesses; different methodologies could yield different fair values. Note 2 covers the valuation process, hierarchy, and instrument-level determinations.
- Credit card rewards liability totaled $12.2 billion at June 30, 2023, up from $11.3 billion at December 31, 2022, recorded in accounts payable and other liabilities; increase driven by higher spend and promotional accruals outpacing redemptions, plus program term adjustments in Q2 2023. References to 2022 Form 10-K (pp. 151–152) for assumptions and sensitivities.
- Income taxes: points to 2022 Form 10-K (p. 152) for key assumptions, judgments, and interpretations.
- Goodwill impairment: significant valuation judgment required; references to 2022 Form 10-K (p. 151) and Note 15 for the assessment as of June 30, 2023.
- Litigation reserves: references to Note 26 of this Form 10-Q and Note 30 of the 2022 Form 10-K for significant estimates and judgments.

nodes.title: Credit card rewards liability
nodes.heading: 8.8.4 Credit card rewards liability
nodes.start_phrase: The credit card rewards liability was $12.2 billion and $11.3 billion at J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 3 and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 2, respectively, and is recorded in accounts payable and other liabilities on the Consolidated balance sheets.
nodes.summary:
- Valuation: The Firm emphasizes that estimating fair value involves significant judgment that increases with less observable market data, especially for Level 3 instruments. Management selects valuation models and derives unobservable inputs (e.g., yield curves, interest rates, prepayment speeds, default rates, volatilities, correlations, commodity/equity/debt prices, comparable valuations, FX rates, credit curves) from empirical data. For Levels 2 and 3, additional valuation adjustments reflect counterparty credit, the Firm’s own credit, market funding rates, liquidity, unobservable parameters, and, where applicable, portfolio net open risk size. Market volatility widens reasonable estimate ranges, particularly for less-liquid positions. Imprecision in inputs can affect reported gains/losses, and differing methodologies could yield different fair values. Further detail is referenced to Note 2.

- Credit card rewards liability: Reported at $12.2 billion as of June 30, 2023, up from $11.3 billion at December 31, 2022, recorded in accounts payable and other liabilities. The increase was mainly due to higher spend and promotional offers driving points earned outpacing redemptions throughout 2023, plus certain program term adjustments in Q2 2023. Significant assumptions and sensitivities are referenced to the 2022 Form 10-K (pp. 151–152).

- Income taxes: Significant assumptions, judgments, and interpretations in tax accounting are referenced to the 2022 Form 10-K (p. 152).

- Goodwill impairment: Testing involves significant valuation judgment; additional details and the June 30, 2023 assessment are referenced to the 2022 Form 10-K (p. 151) and Note 15.

- Litigation reserves: Significant estimates and judgments in establishing reserves are referenced to Note 26 of this Form 10-Q and Note 30 of the 2022 Form 10-K.
