nodes.title: Financial Accounting Standards Board (“FASB”) Standards Adopted since January 1, 2021
nodes.heading: 9.1 Financial Accounting Standards Board (“FASB”) Standards Adopted since January 1, 2021
nodes.start_phrase: •Provides optional expedients and exceptions to current accounting guidance when financial instruments, hedge accounting relationships, and other transactions are amended due to reference rate reform.
nodes.summary:
- The section summarizes recent Accounting and Reporting Developments, focusing on FASB standards adopted and those issued but not yet adopted, and how they affect the firm’s financial statements and disclosures.

- Standards adopted since January 1, 2021:
  - Reference Rate Reform (issued March 2020; updates in Jan 2021 and Dec 2022): Provides optional expedients and exceptions for contracts, financial instruments, and hedge accounting modified due to benchmark rate reform; effective upon issuance. Further details referenced to the firm’s 2022 Form 10-K.

- Standards adopted since January 1, 2023:
  - Derivatives and Hedging: Fair Value Hedging – Portfolio Layer Method (issued March 2022): Expands portfolio hedging to include more prepayable assets and also non-prepayable assets in the same portfolio; clarifies eligible derivatives, balance sheet presentation, and disclosures; permits a one-time HTM-to-AFS reclassification. Adopted prospectively effective January 1, 2023; see Note 1.
  - Financial Instruments – Credit Losses: Troubled Debt Restructurings and Vintage Disclosures (issued March 2022): Eliminates TDR accounting and related disclosures; requires disclosures for certain loan modifications for borrowers in financial difficulty and charge-offs by origination year; adoption permitted prospectively or via modified retrospective method. Adopted using the modified retrospective method effective January 1, 2023; see Note 1.

- Standards issued but not yet adopted:
  - Investments—Equity Method and Joint Ventures: Accounting for Investments in Tax Credit Structures Using the Proportional Amortization Method (issued March 2023): Expands proportional amortization election beyond low-income housing tax credits to other tax-oriented investment programs; allows full or modified retrospective adoption. Effective January 1, 2024, with early adoption permitted. The firm is evaluating the impact on its Consolidated Financial Statements.

nodes.title: FASB Standards Adopted since January 1, 2023
nodes.heading: 9.2 FASB Standards Adopted since January 1, 2023
nodes.start_phrase: •Expands the current ability to hedge a portfolio of prepayable assets to allow more of the portfolio to be hedged.
nodes.summary:
- The document summarizes recent FASB accounting standards, their guidance, adoption status, effective dates, and expected or actual effects on the firm’s financial statements.
- Standards adopted since January 1, 2021:
  - Reference Rate Reform: Provides optional expedients and exceptions for contracts and hedging relationships modified due to reference rate changes; effective beginning March 2020 with updates in 2021 and 2022; additional details referenced to prior filings.
- Standards adopted since January 1, 2023:
  - Derivatives and Hedging – Fair Value Hedging: Portfolio Layer Method: Expands hedging of portfolios (including prepayable and non-prepayable assets), clarifies permissible derivatives and presentation/disclosure, and permits a one-time HTM-to-AFS reclassification; adopted prospectively on January 1, 2023.
  - Financial Instruments – Credit Losses: Troubled Debt Restructurings and Vintage Disclosures: Eliminates TDR accounting and certain disclosures, introduces required disclosures for specified loan modifications to borrowers in financial difficulty, and requires charge-off disclosures by origination year; adopted using a modified retrospective approach on January 1, 2023.
- Standards issued but not yet adopted:
  - Investments—Equity Method and Joint Ventures: Proportional Amortization Method for Tax Credit Structures: Expands proportional amortization election beyond low-income housing tax credits to other tax-oriented investments on a program-by-program basis; effective January 1, 2024 (early adoption permitted), with choice of full or modified retrospective adoption; the firm is evaluating the impact.

nodes.heading: 9.3 FASB Standards Issued but not yet Adopted
nodes.start_phrase: •Expands the ability to elect proportional amortization for more types of tax-oriented investments (beyond low income housing tax credit investments) on a program-by-program basis.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of recent Accounting and Reporting Developments focused on FASB guidance affecting JPMorgan Chase.
- Standards adopted since Jan 1, 2021: Reference Rate Reform providing optional expedients for contracts and hedges affected by benchmark transitions; effective upon issuance with updates in 2021 and 2022; further details referenced to the 2022 Form 10-K.
- Standards adopted since Jan 1, 2023:
  - Derivatives and Hedging—Fair Value Hedging: Portfolio Layer Method (Mar 2022): expands portfolio hedging to include prepayable and non‑prepayable assets, clarifies eligible derivatives and presentation/disclosure, and permits a one-time HTM-to-AFS reclassification; adopted prospectively on Jan 1, 2023; see Note 1.
  - Credit Losses—Troubled Debt Restructurings and Vintage Disclosures (Mar 2022): eliminates TDR accounting/disclosure, adds required disclosures for certain loan modifications to borrowers in financial difficulty, and requires charge-offs disclosed by origination year; adopted via modified retrospective method on Jan 1, 2023; see Note 1.
- Standards issued but not yet adopted:
  - Investments—Equity Method and Joint Ventures: Proportional Amortization Method for tax credit structures (Mar 2023): expands eligibility beyond LIHTC on a program-by-program basis; effective Jan 1, 2024 with early adoption permitted; firm is evaluating impact.
- Document highlights effective dates, adoption methods (prospective vs. modified retrospective), permitted reclassifications, and new disclosure requirements.

nodes.summary:
- Forward-looking statements disclaimer:
  - Explains that certain statements are not historical facts and can be identified by terms like anticipate, expect, estimate, intend, plan, goal, believe, etc.
  - Notes such statements reflect current expectations and are subject to risks and uncertainties beyond the Firm’s control, which may cause actual results to differ materially.
  - Outlines key risk factors, including: macroeconomic and geopolitical conditions (e.g., Ukraine war); regulatory and policy changes (capital/liquidity, trade, monetary, fiscal, taxes, FDIC assessments); market liquidity and volatility; investor/consumer behavior; capital and liquidity management; credit ratings; reputation; ESG and sustainability considerations; economic slowdowns and interest rate environment; technology changes; effectiveness of controls; product development/discontinuation and potential legacy liabilities; market acceptance and competition; talent attraction/retention; expense control; client/counterparty credit quality; risk management, disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting; legal/regulatory proceedings; valuation challenges; disasters, pandemics, climate effects and geopolitical instability; operational resilience and third-party dependencies; cybersecurity threats.
  - References additional risks in Part I, Item 1A of the 2022 Form 10-K.
  - States no obligation to update forward-looking statements and directs readers to future SEC filings for updates.

- Consolidated statements of income (unaudited) summary for JPMorgan Chase & Co.:
  - Periods presented: Three and six months ended June 30, 2023 and 2022.
  - Q2 2023 vs Q2 2022:

    - Net income: $14.5B vs $8.6B; diluted EPS: $4.75 vs $2.76.
  - First half 2023 vs first half 2022:
    - Total net revenue: $79.7B vs $61.4B; net interest income: $42.5B vs $29.0B; noninterest revenue: $37.2B vs $32.4B.
    - Provision for credit losses: $5.2B vs $2.6B.
    - Total noninterest expense: $40.9B vs $37.9B.

nodes.title: Level 3 valuations
nodes.heading: Level 3 valuations
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 2 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 Form 10-K for further information on the Firm’s valuation process and a detailed discussion of the determination of fair value for individual financial instruments.
nodes.summary:
- Explains presentation and netting conventions:
  - Long positions are reduced by identical short positions when presenting balances.
  - Certain investments valued using the NAV practical expedient (hedge funds, private equity, real estate and other funds) are excluded from the fair value hierarchy; totals were $956 million at June 30, 2023 and $950 million at December 31, 2022, comprising trading assets of $40 million/$43 million and other assets of $916 million/$907 million, respectively.
  - Loans include $9.3 billion/$9.7 billion of residential first-lien mortgages and $6.8 billion of commercial first-lien mortgages at June 30, 2023/December 31, 2022; residential loans intended for sale to U.S. GSEs and agencies were $3.3 billion/$2.4 billion.
  - Under U.S. GAAP, derivative receivables/payables and related cash collateral are presented on a net basis when subject to legally enforceable master netting agreements; applying netting would reduce reported Level 3 balances.

- Describes Level 3 valuation framework:
  - References the firm’s valuation process (2022 Form 10-K, Note 2) and details how fair value for individual instruments is determined.
  - Level 3 instruments can include both observable and unobservable inputs; observable risks are hedged with Level 1/2 positions.
  - The table provides key Level 3 instruments, valuation techniques, significant unobservable inputs, with input ranges and weighted/arithmetic averages; ranges/averages reflect instrument characteristics, not input uncertainty, and vary period to period.

- Summarizes primary Level 3 instruments and key inputs as of June 30, 2023:
  - Residential MBS and loans ($1,641 million): discounted cash flows; key inputs include yield, prepayment speed, conditional default rate, loss severity.
  - Commercial MBS and loans ($2,318 million): market comparables; price as key input.
  - Corporate debt ($789 million), other loans ($1,671 million), and non-U.S. government debt ($199 million): market comparables; price as key input.
  - Net interest rate derivatives (-$1,105 million): option pricing; interest rate volatilities, Bermudan switch value, rate and IR-FX correlations; also discounted cash flows with prepayment speed.
  - Net credit derivatives ($673 million): discounted cash flows; credit correlation, credit spread, recovery rate; small market-comparable positions.
  - Net foreign exchange derivatives ($461 million): option pricing with IR-FX correlation; some discounted cash flow items with prepayment speed and interest rate curve.
  - Net equity derivatives (-$1,881 million): option pricing; forward equity price, equity volatility, equity/equity-FX/equity-IR correlations.
  - Net commodity derivatives (-$353 million): option pricing; oil and natural gas forwards, commodity volatility and correlation.
  - Mortgage servicing rights (MSRs) ($8,229 million): discounted cash flows (further details in Note 15).
  - Long-term debt, short-term borrowings, and deposits ($27,806 million via option pricing; $1,376 million via discounted cash flows): include structured notes with embedded derivatives; key inputs include interest rate and equity volatilities, Bermudan switch value, and cross-asset correlations.
  - Other Level 3 assets and liabilities, net: $1,056 million.

- Footnote clarifications:
  - Product categories may differ from balance sheet classifications; not all listed inputs apply to every instrument within a technique.
  - RMBS composition: $706 million U.S. GSE/agency, $5 million nonagency, and $930 million non-trading loans.
  - CMBS/loans composition: $6 million nonagency securities, $72 million trading loans, $2.2 billion non-trading loans.
  - Loans composition: $1.0 billion trading, $638 million non-trading.
  - Structured notes’ fair values include embedded derivative features; unobservable inputs align with those for derivative receivables.
  - Includes $843 million of equity securities (of which $213 million in Other assets) without quoted prices, valued using internal methods (e.g., EBITDA multiples, comparables).
  - Price inputs assume par of $100; forward equity price expressed as a percent of current price.
  - Averages are weighted by fair value, except derivative-related inputs which use arithmetic averages.

- Rollforward disclosures: Detailed Level 3 rollforwards for assets and liabilities for:
  - Three months ended June 30, 2023 and 2022
  - Six months ended June 30, 2023 and 2022
  These tables show beginning balances, realized/unrealized gains and losses, transfers into/out of Level 3, purchases, sales, issuances, settlements, and ending balances, plus unrealized gains/losses on instruments held at period-end.
- Covered categories:
  - Assets: Trading assets (debt instruments such as MBS, US states/munis, non-US sovereigns, corporates, loans, ABS; equity securities; physical commodities; other), net derivative receivables (interest rate, credit, FX, equity, commodity), available-for-sale securities, loans, mortgage servicing rights, and other assets.
  - Liabilities: Deposits, short-term borrowings, trading liabilities, accounts payable and other liabilities, and long-term debt.
- Key quantitative context:
  - Level 3 assets were 2% of total firm assets at fair value, and Level 3 liabilities were 8% of total firm liabilities at fair value at both June 30, 2023 and December 31, 2022.
  - Level 3 assets increased to approximately $26.8 billion at June 30, 2023, up about $3.0 billion from March 31, 2023 and $3.2 billion from December 31, 2022, driven predominantly by non-trading loans (about $2.3–$2.4 billion), including roughly $1.9 billion of CIB loans from the First Republic acquisition.
- Transfers between levels (drivers and direction):
  - 2023 Q2: Significant transfers into Level 3 included about $1.2 billion of gross interest rate derivative payables due to the transition to term SOFR and about $760 million of non-trading loans due to decreased observability; no significant transfers out.
  - 2023 YTD: Transfers into Level 3 included ~$1.6 billion of IR derivative payables (term SOFR), ~$901 million of equity derivative receivables, and ~$917 million of non-trading loans (decreased observability). Transfers out included ~$1.3 billion of equity derivative receivables and ~$827 million of equity derivative payables (increased observability and reduced significance of unobservable inputs).
  - 2022 Q2: No significant transfers into Level 3; transfers out included ~$930 million of interest rate derivative receivables (increased observability).
  - 2022 YTD: Transfers into Level 3 included ~$1.6 billion of total debt/equity instruments (notably ~$959 million of equity securities due to restricted market access and decreased observability) and ~$1.3 billion of equity derivative payables. Transfers out included ~$965 million of interest rate derivative receivables and ~$920 million of equity derivative receivables and ~$1.4 billion of payables (increased observability).
- Important interpretive notes:
  - Level 3 instruments often contain observable components; gains/losses in tables therefore reflect both observable and unobservable drivers.
  - The firm hedges observable components with Level 1/2 instruments not shown in the Level 3 rollforwards; reported gains/losses do not reflect these hedges.
  - Presentation and accounting:
    - Level 3 derivatives presented net by counterparty.
    - Most P&L effects recorded in principal transactions; mortgage-related items (certain loans/commitments and MSRs) in mortgage fees and related income.
    - AFS realized results in investment securities gains/losses; unrealized in OCI.
    - DVA impacts on fair value option liabilities were not material to earnings; related unrealized amounts are in OCI.
    - “Settlements” encompass maturities, repayments, modifications, VIE deconsolidations, and other items.

nodes.title: Equity securities without readily determinable fair values
nodes.heading: Equity securities without readily determinable fair values

nodes.summary:
- The firm measures equity securities without readily determinable fair values using the measurement alternative: cost less impairment, adjusted for observable price changes in identical or similar securities of the same issuer, with changes recognized in other income. Observed prices may be adjusted to reflect differing rights/obligations and to align with the firm’s private equity valuation techniques.
- These securities are included in nonrecurring fair value disclosures when observable price changes occur.
- Carrying values and changes:
  - Carrying value in other assets: $4.673 billion at June 30, 2023 vs. $4.196 billion at June 30, 2022; $4.1 billion at December 31, 2022.
  - Three months ended June 30: upward changes of $5 million (2023) vs. $76 million (2022); downward changes/impairments of $(37) million (2023) vs. $(463) million (2022).
  - Six months ended June 30: upward changes of $40 million (2023) vs. $445 million (2022); downward changes/impairments of $(133) million (2023) vs. $(474) million (2022).
  - Cumulative since January 1, 2018: upward changes $1.5 billion; downward changes/impairments $(1.0) billion.
- Visa Class B shares:
  - The firm holds ~37 million Visa Class B shares within other assets. These are restricted and convertible into Visa Class A shares at a litigation-dependent conversion rate.
  - On June 28, 2023, the conversion rate decreased from 1.5991 to 1.5902 per Visa’s June 29, 2023 Form 8-K; further adjustments may occur based on litigation outcomes.
  - Due to ongoing uncertainty about timing of restriction removal, final conversion rate, and differing voting rights, Visa B shares are not viewed as similar to Visa A and are carried at nominal value.
- Derivative arrangements related to prior sales of Visa B shares:
  - The firm retains conversion-rate risk via derivatives with purchasers, requiring/payable amounts based on conversion-rate changes and periodic interest payments, continuing while restrictions persist.
  - These derivatives are measured at fair value using a discounted cash flow approach based on the firm’s expectations of litigation resolution timing and magnitude, recorded in trading liabilities, with changes recognized in other income.
  - As of June 30, 2023, derivatives relate to approximately 23 million Visa B shares previously sold.

nodes.title: Additional disclosures about the fair value of financial instruments that are not carried on the Consolidated balance sheets at fair value

- Purpose and scope: Provides additional fair value disclosures for financial instruments not carried at fair value on the Consolidated balance sheets, showing carrying amounts and estimated fair values by fair value hierarchy (Levels 1–3) as of June 30, 2023 and December 31, 2022.
- Assets covered: Cash and due from banks; deposits with banks; accrued interest and accounts receivable; federal funds sold and securities purchased under resale agreements; securities borrowed; investment securities held-to-maturity; loans (net of allowance); and other assets.
- Liabilities covered: Deposits; federal funds purchased and securities loaned or sold under repurchase agreements; short‑term borrowings; accounts payable and other liabilities; beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs; and long‑term debt.
- Fair value hierarchy observations: 
  - Many loan fair values are classified as Level 3, reflecting unobservable inputs.
  - Deposits’ estimated fair values are largely Level 2.
  - Held‑to‑maturity securities’ fair values are primarily Levels 1 and 2 and are below carrying values.
  - Long‑term debt includes both Level 2 and Level 3 elements.
  - Other liabilities include Level 3 components.
- Valuation methodology highlights:
  - Loans are valued mainly using discounted cash flow models incorporating expected lifetime credit losses, rates, prepayments, and market spreads; some loans use collateral valuations.

- Specific items noted:

  - A Purchase Money Note from the First Republic acquisition is included in Level 3 of long‑term debt.

  - Consumer off‑balance sheet lending commitments are not fair‑valued; many can be reduced or canceled by the firm.
- Fair value option (FVO) policy:
  - The firm elects fair value for certain instruments to align accounting with risk management, reduce income statement volatility, and reflect fair value management.
  - Instruments under FVO include: specific loans (e.g., securitization warehousing or managed on a fair value basis), certain securities financing agreements, owned beneficial interests with embedded credit derivatives, structured notes and other hybrids issued in client activities, and certain long‑term beneficial interests of consolidated securitization trusts when underlying assets are at fair value.
- FVO results in earnings:

  - Categories include federal funds/reverse repos, securities borrowed, trading assets and liabilities, loans (with instrument‑specific credit risk disclosed separately), deposits, repos, short‑term borrowings, other assets/liabilities, beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs, and long‑term debt.
  - Related risk management hedges (which are also at fair value) are excluded from these FVO change tables.

nodes.title: Fair value option
nodes.heading: Note 3 – Fair value option
nodes.start_phrase: The fair value option provides an option to elect fair value for selected financial assets, financial liabilities, unrecognized firm commitments, and written loan commitments.
nodes.summary:
- Explains the Firm’s use of the fair value option (FVO), which allows certain financial assets, liabilities, unrecognized firm commitments, and written loan commitments to be measured at fair value.
- States the rationale for electing FVO: to reduce income statement volatility from mixed measurement bases versus related risk management arrangements carried at fair value, and to better reflect instruments managed on a fair value basis.
- Lists the categories of instruments under FVO:
  - Loans tied to securitization warehousing, subject to bifurcation accounting, or otherwise managed on a fair value basis, including lending-related commitments.
  - Certain securities financing agreements.
  - Owned beneficial interests in securitized financial assets with embedded credit derivatives (that would otherwise require separate derivative accounting).
  - Structured notes and other hybrid instruments with embedded derivatives issued or transacted for client-driven activities.
  - Certain long-term beneficial interests issued by CIB’s consolidated securitization trusts where the underlying assets are carried at fair value.
- Presents how changes in fair value for FVO-elected items are reported in the Consolidated statements of income, split between “Principal transactions” and “All other income,” for the three- and six-month periods ended June 30, 2023 and 2022.
- Notes that the profit and loss table includes only the FVO-elected instruments and excludes related risk management instruments that are required to be at fair value.
- Shows line-item detail for the three months ended June 30 (2023 vs. 2022) across categories such as:
  - Federal funds sold and securities purchased under resale agreements.
  - Securities borrowed.
  - Trading assets (debt and equity instruments, excluding loans).
  - Loans reported as trading assets (separating instrument-specific credit risk from other fair value changes).
  - Loans carried under FVO (separating instrument-specific credit risk from other fair value changes).
  - Other assets.
  - Deposits, federal funds purchased and securities loaned or sold under repurchase agreements, short-term borrowings, trading liabilities.
  - Beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs.
  - Other liabilities and long-term debt.
- Highlights that for loans, the disclosure distinguishes changes attributable to instrument-specific credit risk from other fair value movements.

nodes.title: Fair value option - Introduction

Key figures and trends:
- Loans:
  - Total loans: Contractual principal $52.9B vs fair value $46.9B at 6/30/23 (fair value $6.1B under principal); $54.0B vs $48.6B at 12/31/22 (under by $5.4B).
  - Nonaccrual loans: $3.65B principal vs $1.29B FV at 6/30/23 (under by $2.36B); $3.48B vs $1.20B (under by $2.29B) at 12/31/22.
  - 90+ days past due and government guaranteed: $82M principal vs $76M FV (under by $6M) at 6/30/23; $124M vs $115M (under by $9M) at 12/31/22.
  - Other performing loans: $49.21B principal vs $45.51B FV (under by $3.70B) at 6/30/23; $50.41B vs $47.27B (under by $3.14B) at 12/31/22.

  - Total long-term debt fair value: $78.61B at 6/30/23; $72.28B at 12/31/22.
- Long-term beneficial interests:

- Off-balance sheet lending-related commitments (fair value option):

Explanatory notes:

nodes.title: Credit risk concentrations
nodes.heading: Note 4 – Credit risk concentrations
nodes.start_phrase: Concentrations of credit risk arise when a number of clients, counterparties or customers are engaged in similar business activities or activities in the same geographic region,
nodes.summary:
- Note 4 – Credit risk concentrations:
  - Defines credit risk concentrations and explains JPMorgan Chase’s ongoing monitoring across portfolios, active senior management involvement in approvals/reviews, and adjustments to align with risk appetite.
  - Consumer portfolio: concentrations managed primarily by product and U.S. geography; portfolio-level trends guide changes to underwriting policies and guidelines. Geographic composition referenced in Note 12.
  - Wholesale portfolio: concentrations evaluated primarily by industry and monitored at both aggregate and single obligor levels; risk mitigated via syndications/participations, loan sales, securitizations, credit derivatives, master netting, collateral, and other techniques. Additional loan details referenced in Note 12.
  - The Firm states no single loan product or industry results in a significant concentration of credit risk; loan terms and collateral are considered in underwriting and in the allowance for loan losses.
  - Credit exposure table (June 30, 2023 vs. December 31, 2022) presents on-balance-sheet and off-balance-sheet consumer and wholesale exposures:
    - Total credit exposure: $2.88T (6/30/23) vs. $2.58T (12/31/22).
    - Consumer exposure: $1.53T (incl. $1.07T credit card) vs. $1.35T prior period.
    - Wholesale exposure: $1.35T vs. $1.23T, detailed by industry (e.g., Real Estate, Asset Managers, Consumer & Retail, Industrials, TMT, Healthcare, Banks & Finance, State & Municipal Govt, Utilities, Oil & Gas, Automotive, etc.).
    - Also shown: loans held-for-sale/at fair value and receivables from customers (collateralized margin loans with generally no allowance; managed via margin requirements).
  - Key footnotes/qualifiers:
    - Excludes cash placed with banks ($485.4B at 6/30/23; $556.6B at 12/31/22).
    - Credit exposure is net of risk participations and excludes benefits of credit derivatives and collateral against derivative receivables.
    - First Republic acquisition included: ~$104.6B in Consumer (ex-credit card) and ~$98.2B in Wholesale (primarily Asset Managers, Real Estate, Individuals and Individual Entities).
    - Additional holdings in U.S. state and municipal securities noted outside credit exposure totals; “All other” wholesale largely SPEs; methodology notes on industry rankings and lending-related off-balance-sheet instruments.

- Note 5 – Derivative instruments:
  - JPMorgan Chase makes markets in derivatives for clients and uses derivatives to hedge/manage its own risks; disclosures follow accounting treatment and purpose.
  - Hedge-designated derivatives:
    - Fair value hedges: interest rate (fixed-rate assets/liabilities), foreign exchange (FX-denominated A/L), commodity (inventory).
    - Cash flow hedges: interest rate (floating-rate assets/liabilities), foreign exchange (forecasted revenue/expense).
    - Net investment hedges: FX exposure of investments in non-USD functional currency entities.
  - Derivatives not designated as hedges (specified risk management):
    - Interest rate: mortgage commitments, warehouse loans, MSRs (CCB).
    - Credit: wholesale lending exposures (CIB).
    - Interest rate and FX: other specified assets/liabilities (Corporate).
  - Market-making and other derivatives: used in client market-making and related risk management across CIB, AWM, and Corporate.

  - Fair value hedges: interest rate hedges of fixed-rate assets and liabilities; foreign exchange hedges of FX-denominated assets and liabilities; commodity hedges of inventory (segments: Corporate; CIB, AWM).

nodes.title: Fair value hedge gains and losses

nodes.start_phrase: The following tables present derivative instruments, by contract type, used in fair value hedge accounting relationships, as well as pre-tax gains/(losses) recorded on such derivatives and the related hedged items for the three and six months ended June 30, 2023 and 2022 , respectively.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Presents the impact of derivatives on the Consolidated statements of income, focusing on fair value hedge accounting.
- Periods covered: Detailed results for the three and six months ended June 30, 2023 and 2022.
- Content of tables: Pre-tax gains and losses by contract type (interest rate, foreign exchange, commodity) for both the hedging derivatives and related hedged items; the Firm records derivative gains/losses in the same income statement line as the hedged item.
- Income statement and OCI effects: Breakout of (i) gains/losses recorded in income, (ii) the income statement impact of excluded hedge components (via amortization and fair value changes), and (iii) related other comprehensive income (OCI) impacts, including amounts tied predominantly to cross-currency basis spreads.
- Contract-type details:
  - Interest rate hedges primarily of benchmark (e.g., SOFR) risk on fixed-rate long-term debt and AFS securities, with effects in net interest income; includes amortization of inception hedge accounting adjustments but excludes swap interest accruals.
  - Foreign exchange hedges of spot FX risk on long-term debt and AFS securities, with impacts primarily in principal transactions revenue and net interest income.
  - Commodity hedges of physical inventory positions (overall fair value hedges), with impacts in principal transactions revenue.
- Hedge effectiveness exclusions: Forward points, time value, and cross-currency basis spreads are excluded from effectiveness testing and recognized either via amortization over the derivative’s life or current-period fair value changes; related OCI reflects changes in excluded amounts under the amortization approach.
- Balance sheet basis adjustments: Discloses cumulative fair value hedge basis adjustments embedded in AFS investment securities and long-term debt at June 30, 2023 and December 31, 2022, split between active and discontinued hedging relationships; notes these amounts will reverse through income as yield adjustments, with sign conventions indicating direction of future net interest income effects.
- Portfolio layer method: Notes adoption effective January 1, 2023, expanding hedging of portfolios of prepayable assets; provides amounts for closed portfolios designated as hedged and the associated cumulative basis adjustments for active and discontinued hedges.
- Exclusions and clarifications: 
  - Physical commodities inventories under fair value hedge accounting are carried at fair value, so unrealized gains/losses are recognized currently with no incremental future net income impact upon exit.
  - Hedged items where only FX risk is designated are excluded from basis adjustments expected to reverse through the income statement; amounts excluded for AFS securities and long-term debt are disclosed.

nodes.start_phrase: The Firm makes markets in derivatives in order to meet the needs of customers and uses derivatives to manage certain risks associated with net open risk positions from its market-making activities, including the counterparty credit risk arising from derivative receivables.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Pre-tax gains and losses on a limited set of derivatives not designated as hedges, used to manage specific risks tied to mortgage commitments, warehouse loans, MSRs, wholesale lending exposures, and foreign currency-denominated assets and liabilities.
- Reporting periods: Three and six months ended June 30, 2023 vs. 2022.

- Results by contract type and where recorded:
  - Interest rate derivatives: losses of $112m (Q2 2023) vs $(309)m (Q2 2022); YTD $(126)m (2023) vs $(538)m (2022). Primarily hedging mortgage-related interest rate risk; gains/losses recorded predominantly in mortgage fees and related income.
  - Credit derivatives: $(67)m (Q2 2023) vs $89m (Q2 2022); YTD $(163)m (2023) vs $122m (2022). Mitigate credit risk on wholesale lending exposures; recorded in principal transactions revenue. Excludes credit derivatives used to offset counterparty credit risk on derivative receivables (those are in market-making category).
  - Foreign exchange derivatives: $41m (Q2 2023) vs $6m (Q2 2022); YTD $43m (2023) vs $(76)m (2022). Mitigate FX risk of specified FX-denominated assets/liabilities; recorded in principal transactions revenue.
  - Total: net losses of $(138)m (Q2 2023) vs $(214)m (Q2 2022); YTD $(246)m (2023) vs $(492)m (2022).

- Market-making and other derivatives: The firm makes markets in derivatives and uses derivatives to manage risks of net open positions, including counterparty credit risk from derivative receivables. All derivatives not in hedge accounting or the specified risk management set fall here. Gains/losses are primarily recorded in principal transactions revenue (see Note 6).

- Ratings and maturity profile for protection sold show concentration in investment-grade references and 1–5 year maturities:

- Other income: Includes operating lease income and losses from tax‑oriented (primarily alternative energy) equity‑method investments in CIB; such losses are more than offset by related tax credits. 2023 items include a $2,712M estimated bargain purchase gain from the First Republic acquisition and a $339M gain related to acquiring the remaining interest in CIFM. - FDIC special assessment: May 2023 proposal to levy a special assessment at 12.5 bps on estimated uninsured deposits as of December 31, 2022, to recoup DIF losses tied to March 12, 2023 systemic risk actions; the Firm expects to be subject to this assessment.
- Interest income and expense (Note 7): Detailed composition and sharp year-over-year increases across categories.

  - Components cover loans; taxable and tax-exempt investment securities; trading assets (debt); federal funds/resale agreements; securities borrowed; deposits with banks; and other interest‑earning assets; and on the expense side, interest-bearing deposits, repos/fed funds purchased, short-term borrowings (incl. commercial paper), trading liabilities/other interest-bearing liabilities (incl. brokerage-related payables), long-term debt, and beneficial interests of consolidated VIEs. nodes.title: Securities financing activities
nodes.heading: Note 11 – Securities financing activities
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 11 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 Form 10-K for a discussion of accounting policies relating to securities financing activities.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Securities financing activities (repos, reverse repos, securities borrowing and lending), with cross-references to accounting policies (2022 Form 10-K Note 11), fair value option (Note 3), and assets pledged/collateral (Note 25).
- Netting and presentation under U.S. GAAP: Balances with the same counterparty are netted on the Consolidated balance sheets when master netting agreement criteria are met and supported by an appropriate legal opinion. Cash/securities collateral exchanged reduces economic exposure but is not eligible for balance sheet netting; such amounts are shown as “Amounts not nettable on the Consolidated balance sheets” and reduce the “Net amounts.” Where no legal opinion is obtained, exposures are shown gross within “Net amounts.”
- Securities-for-securities lending (when JPMorgan Chase is the lender): Securities received that can be pledged or sold are recognized at fair value in other assets, with a corresponding obligation to return them in accounts payable and other liabilities.
- Scale and net exposure (June 30, 2023 vs. December 31, 2022):
  - Assets: Securities purchased under resale agreements (gross: $561.4B vs. $597.9B; net: $5.6B vs. $11.4B). Securities borrowed (gross: $205.6B vs. $228.3B; net: $44.0B vs. $53.8B).
  - Liabilities: Securities sold under repurchase agreements (gross: $496.9B vs. $480.8B; net: $34.3B vs. $31.0B). Securities loaned and other (gross: $50.6B vs. $52.4B; net: $0.1B vs. near zero).
  - Overall, large gross balances with substantially reduced net exposures after netting and collateral.
- Notable footnotes:
  - Includes securities-for-securities lending at fair value where the Firm is lender: $5.0B (6/30/23) and $7.0B (12/31/22).
  - “Amounts not nettable” may be capped at the related net asset/liability with the counterparty.
  - Agreements with collateral rights but lacking legal opinions included in net amounts: at 6/30/23, approx. $4.5B reverse repos, $39.6B securities borrowed, $33.3B repos (comparable amounts at 12/31/22: $6.0B, $49.0B, $29.1B; securities loaned not material).
- Collateral types backing securities financing liabilities (gross): Predominantly U.S. Treasury/GSE/government and non-U.S. government debt for repos; equity securities are the largest component for securities loaned. Other collateral includes agency and nonagency MBS, corporate debt, ABS, and municipal obligations.
- Maturity profile: Activities are concentrated in overnight/continuous and short-dated tenors.
  - 6/30/23: Repos—$268.2B overnight/continuous; $120.6B up to 30 days; $30.1B 30–90 days; $77.9B >90 days. Securities loaned—$49.2B overnight/continuous; small balances in longer buckets.
  - 12/31/22: Similar short-term concentration for both repos and securities loaned.
- Transfers not qualifying for sale accounting: At both dates, $692M of financial assets were transferred but did not meet sale criteria; recognized as collateralized financings. Transferred assets recorded in trading assets and loans; related liabilities predominantly in short-term borrowings.

nodes.title: Loan accounting framework
nodes.heading: Loan accounting framework
nodes.start_phrase: The accounting for a loan depends on management’s strategy for the loan.
nodes.summary:
- Overview: Note 12 outlines JPMorgan Chase’s loan accounting framework, portfolio segmentation, the impact of new credit loss disclosure guidance adopted in 2023, and a snapshot of loan balances as of June 30, 2023 versus December 31, 2022.
- Loan accounting framework: Loans are categorized as (1) originated or purchased loans held-for-investment (retained), (2) loans held-for-sale, and (3) loans at fair value. The note cross-references the 2022 Form 10-K (loan policies), and this Form 10-Q’s Notes 2 (trading assets at fair value) and 3 (fair value option elections).
- New guidance adoption (effective Jan 1, 2023): The Firm adopted Financial Instruments—Credit Losses guidance eliminating Troubled Debt Restructuring (TDR) accounting/disclosures and adding disclosure requirements for FDMs, including current-period gross charge-offs by vintage origination year. Pre-2023 TDR discussion is referenced to the 2022 Form 10-K.
- Portfolio structure: The loan portfolio is grouped into three segments aligned with allowance methodology—Consumer excluding credit card; Credit card; and Wholesale. Classes within segments include residential real estate; auto and other (consumer); credit card loans; and wholesale classes secured by real estate, commercial and industrial, and other. Wholesale classes align with regulatory loan classifications. “Other” includes loans to financial institutions, governments, SPEs, nonprofits, personal investment companies, trusts, and individuals across multiple business lines (CIB, CB, AWM, CCB).
- First Republic acquisition: The portfolio includes $149.8 billion of loans from the acquisition—$91.9 billion retained and $1.9 billion at fair value in Consumer (excluding credit card), and $56.0 billion retained in Wholesale.
- Loan balances:
  - June 30, 2023: Total loans $1,300.1 billion, comprising Retained $1,255.7 billion, Held-for-sale $5.6 billion, and At fair value $38.8 billion. By segment: Consumer excluding credit card $408.2 billion; Credit card $191.3 billion; Wholesale $700.5 billion.
  - December 31, 2022: Total loans $1,135.6 billion, comprising Retained $1,089.6 billion, Held-for-sale $4.0 billion, and At fair value $42.1 billion. By segment: Consumer excluding credit card $311.4 billion; Credit card $185.2 billion; Wholesale $639.1 billion.
- Presentation notes: Accrued interest receivables of $6.0 billion (June 30, 2023) and $5.2 billion (December 31, 2022) are excluded; write-offs of accrued interest were not material. Amounts are presented net of unamortized discounts/premiums and net deferred fees/costs (not material).

nodes.title: Residential real estate
nodes.heading: Residential real estate
nodes.start_phrase: Delinquency is the primary credit quality indicator for retained residential real estate loans.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Credit quality of retained residential real estate loans, using delinquency as the primary indicator. Tables present delinquency and gross charge-offs for the six months ended June 30, 2023, with a comparison to December 31, 2022.
- Portfolio size and status:
  - Total retained loans: $328.0 billion at June 30, 2023 vs. $237.6 billion at December 31, 2022.
  - At June 30, 2023: current $326.2 billion; 30–149 days past due $1.101 billion; 150+ days past due $0.676 billion.
- Delinquency rates (30+ days past due to total):
  - Overall: 0.54% at June 30, 2023 vs. 0.66% at December 31, 2022.
  - By segment (June 30, 2023 examples): Prior to 2019 term loans 1.75%; converted revolving loans 4.23% (higher than revolving within period), reflecting higher fully amortizing payments after conversion; recent vintages (2019–2023) exhibit very low delinquency rates (generally below ~0.25%).
- Product/vintage segmentation:
  - Term loans shown by origination year; revolving loans split between within the revolving period and converted to term loans.
  - Converted revolving loans have higher delinquency than revolving loans still within the revolving period due to payment structure differences.
- Gross charge-offs (six months ended June 30, 2023): $70 million total, concentrated in older vintages and revolving products ($52 million in prior-to-2019 term loans; $14 million in revolving within period; $4 million in converted revolving).
- First Republic acquisition impact:
  - Included across vintages: $5.6b (2023), $26.2b (2022), $22.0b (2021), $15.0b (2020), $7.5b (2019), $12.9b (prior to 2019) in term loans; $2.5b in revolving within the period.
  - $158 million of 30+ days past due loans are associated with the acquisition.
- Methodology/footnotes:
  - Government-insured mortgage loans were not material; 30+ day delinquency ratios exclude such loans due to the guarantee.
  - Loans in COVID-19 deferral programs, performing under modified terms within the deferral period, are generally not considered delinquent.
  - Purchased loans are reported by their original origination year.
  - Approximately 37% of revolving loans are senior liens; lien position is considered in the allowance for credit losses.

- Geographic concentrations highlight largest exposures in California ($128.0 billion), New York ($49.4 billion), Florida ($22.5 billion), Texas ($15.4 billion), and Massachusetts ($14.4 billion), with significant increases tied to First Republic (e.g., +$55.5B CA, +$15.2B NY, +$3.6B FL, +$8.0B MA).
- Footnotes summarize methodology and policies:

nodes.title: Loan modifications
nodes.heading: Loan modifications
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm grants certain modifications of residential real estate loans to borrowers experiencing financial difficulty, which effective January 1, 2023, are reported as FDMs.
nodes.summary:
- Shift in accounting for residential real estate loan modifications effective January 1, 2023: modifications for borrowers experiencing financial difficulty are reported as FDMs, replacing prior TDR accounting. FDMs include proprietary and U.S. GSE programs offering interest rate reductions, term extensions, other-than-insignificant payment delays, and principal forgiveness.
- 2023 activity and effects (three and six months ended June 30, 2023): $35 million and $75 million of FDMs; primarily term extensions and interest rate reductions that extended weighted-average loan life by 15 and 18 years and reduced weighted-average contractual rates from 6.90% to 4.21% and 6.75% to 4.01%, respectively; no additional lending commitments to FDM borrowers. Also reported: $33 million/$48 million of loans in trial modification and $3 million/$5 million of Chapter 7 loans—considered TDRs but not FDMs under revised guidance.
- Pre-2023 (TDR framework): For the three and six months ended June 30, 2022, new TDRs were $115 million and $233 million; no additional lending commitments to TDR borrowers; reference to the firm’s 2022 Form 10-K for more TDR information.
- Nature and extent of 2022 TDR modifications: 1,165/2,691 loans approved for trial modification and 1,289/2,831 permanently modified (three/six months). Concessions on permanent mods (percent of loans; multiple concessions common): interest rate reductions 45%/56%; term/payment extensions 54%/67%; principal/interest deferred 10%/12%; principal forgiveness 1%/1%; other (e.g., variable-to-fixed, qualifying payment delays) 46%/36%.
- Financial effects and redefaults for 2022 TDRs: Weighted-average interest rate reduced from 4.76% to 3.36% (three months) and 4.55% to 3.31% (six months). Remaining contractual term extended from 22 to 38 years and 23 to 39 years. Charge-offs on permanent mods $1 million/$1 million; principal deferred $4 million/$11 million; principal forgiven $0/$1 million. Redefault balances within one year of permanent modification were $27 million/$70 million.

nodes.title: Loan modifications
nodes.heading: Loan modifications
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm grants certain modifications of credit card loans to borrowers experiencing financial difficulty, which effective January 1, 2023, are reported as FDMs.
nodes.summary:
- Overview: The firm modifies credit card loans for borrowers experiencing financial difficulty. Effective January 1, 2023, these are reported as Financial Difficulty Modifications (FDMs), replacing prior TDR accounting.
- Nature of modifications: Customers are placed on fixed payment plans (generally 60 months) with substantial interest rate reductions; credit lines are generally not reinstated. Noncompliance results in continued aging and eventual charge-off under standard policy.
- Volume and terms (2023):
  - Three months ended June 30, 2023: $181 million of FDMs (0.09% of total retained credit card loans); weighted-average contractual interest rate reduced from 23.27% to 3.57%.
  - Six months ended June 30, 2023: $326 million (0.17%); rate reduced from 22.96% to 3.54%.
  - Interest rates are weighted averages at enrollment; term extensions reflect placement on fixed payment plans.
- Trial modifications: $26 million of loans were subject to trial modifications in both the three- and six-month periods; due to changes eliminating certain TDR criteria, trial mods are not considered FDMs.
- Payment status of FDMs (amortized cost basis):

nodes.title: Allowance for credit losses
nodes.heading: Note 13 – Allowance for credit losses
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm's allowance for credit losses represe nts management's estimate of expected credit losses over the remaining expected life of the Firm's financial assets measured at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet lending-related commitments.
nodes.summary:
- Defines the allowance for credit losses as management’s estimate of expected lifetime losses on financial assets measured at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet lending-related commitments.
- Notes adoption on January 1, 2023 of new Troubled Debt Restructurings (TDR) guidance under Financial Instruments—Credit Losses.
- Explains the guidance removes the requirement to use a DCF methodology for TDRs and permits a non-DCF, portfolio-based approach; if DCF is used, the discount rate must be the post-modification effective interest rate.
- States the Firm elected a non-DCF, portfolio-based allowance approach for modified loans to borrowers experiencing financial difficulty across most portfolios, retaining an asset-specific approach only for collateral-dependent loans and nonaccrual risk-rated loans.
- Describes adoption under the modified retrospective method, resulting in a $587 million net decrease to the allowance for credit losses and a $446 million after-tax increase to retained earnings, driven primarily by residential real estate and credit card portfolios.
- Refers readers to Note 13 of the 2022 Form 10-K for further details on allowance policies.

nodes.title: Allowance for credit losses - Introduction
nodes.heading: Note 13 – Allowance for credit losses
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm's allowance for credit losses represe nts management's estimate of expected credit losses over the remaining expected life of the Firm's financial assets measured at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet lending-related commitments.
nodes.summary: Introduces JPMorgan Chase’s allowance for credit losses (ACL) as management’s estimate of expected losses over the remaining life of financial assets at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet lending commitments, and notes adoption on January 1, 2023 of the Financial Instruments – Credit Losses: Troubled Debt Restructurings guidance (see Note 1). The new guidance removes the requirement to use a DCF approach for TDRs, permits a non-DCF portfolio-based method for modified loans to borrowers in financial difficulty, and, if DCF is used, requires the post-modification effective interest rate. The Firm elected a non-DCF, portfolio-based allowance for such modified loans across portfolios, except for collateral-dependent loans and nonaccrual risk-rated loans which remain asset-specific. Adopted via the modified retrospective method, the change decreased the ACL by $587 million and increased retained earnings by $446 million after-tax, largely driven by residential real estate and credit card; see 2022 Form 10-K Note 13 for detailed policies.

nodes.title: Discussion of changes in the allowance
nodes.heading: Discussion of changes in the allowance
nodes.start_phrase: The allowance for credit losses as of J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 3 was $24.3 billion , reflecting a net additio n of $2.7 billion from D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 2.
nodes.summary:
- Allowance for credit losses (ACL) stood at $24.3 billion as of June 30, 2023, a net increase of $2.7 billion from December 31, 2022.
- Drivers of the net addition:
  - $1.5 billion reserve build:
    - $819 million in wholesale, driven by net downgrade activity, revised office real estate assumptions in Commercial Banking in 2Q23, and higher weighting of adverse scenarios initiated in 1Q23.
    - $649 million in consumer, largely in Card Services, reflecting loan growth and macro outlook changes (including weighted-average U.S. unemployment peaking in 3Q24), and higher adverse scenario weighting in 1Q23, partially offset by reduced borrower uncertainty.
  - $1.2 billion established for First Republic loans and lending-related commitments in 2Q23.
  - Partially offset by a $587 million reduction from adopting updated TDR accounting guidance on January 1, 2023.
- Scenario methodology and outlook:
  - ACL estimated using a weighted average of five internal macroeconomic scenarios; the Firm maintained higher weight on adverse scenarios from 1Q23 due to tighter financial conditions and increased recession probability.
  - Adverse scenarios imply a weighted-average U.S. unemployment peak of 5.8% in 3Q24 and U.S. real GDP 1.5% lower by end-4Q24.
  - Central case assumptions at June 30, 2023: U.S. unemployment 4.2% (4Q23), 4.9% (2Q24), 5.0% (4Q24); YoY real GDP growth 0.5%, 0.0%, 1.0%. December 31, 2022 central case for comparison: unemployment 3.8% (2Q23), 4.3% (4Q23), 5.0% (2Q24); GDP 1.5%, 0.4%, 0.0%.
  - Future updates to forecasts will be reflected in provisions for credit losses.
- Cross-references provided to 2022 Form 10-K notes and sections for ACL policies, consumer and wholesale credit portfolios, and critical accounting estimates.
- Variable Interest Entities (Note 14):
  - Defines “Firm-sponsored” VIEs and summarizes significant types by business segment.
  - Key structures:
    - CCB: credit card securitization trusts; mortgage securitization trusts (servicing and securitization of originated/purchased residential mortgages).
    - CIB: mortgage and other securitization trusts (residential, commercial, other consumer loans); multi-seller conduits; municipal bond vehicles.
  - The Firm is the primary beneficiary of the Chase Issuance Trust due to continuing involvement.
  - The Firm may act as servicer and/or retain beneficial interests in mortgage and other securitization trusts.
  - The Firm also invests in and provides financing/services to third-party-sponsored VIEs; references to pages 165–169 for consolidated VIE assets/liabilities and additional details.

- Footnote highlights and accounting treatment:
  - Assets of consolidated VIEs are used to settle those VIEs’ liabilities; intercompany balances are eliminated.
  - Interest-bearing beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs are presented as “Beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs”; holders generally have no recourse to JPMorgan Chase’s general credit.
  - Long-term beneficial interests outstanding were $1.1B at June 30, 2023 and $2.1B at December 31, 2022.

nodes.title: Mortgage servicing rights
nodes.heading: Mortgage servicing right s
nodes.start_phrase: MSRs represent the fair value of expected future cash flows for performing servicing activities for others.
nodes.summary:
- Defines mortgage servicing rights (MSRs) as the fair value of expected future cash flows from servicing loans for others, valued based on estimated fees and ancillary revenue less servicing costs; MSR fair value declines over time as servicing cash flows are realized (effective amortization).
- Explains recognition of MSRs when purchased or when loans are sold/securitized with servicing retained; references additional details in JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 Form 10-K (Notes 2 and 15).
- Summarizes MSR activity for the three and six months ended June 30, 2023 and 2022:
  - Beginning fair value (Q2 2023): $7.755B; ending fair value (6/30/23): $8.229B vs $7.439B (6/30/22).
  - Net additions in Q2 2023: $454MM (originations $78MM, purchases $468MM, dispositions $(92)MM); year-to-date net additions $487MM.
  - Reductions from collection/realization of expected cash flows: $(255)MM in Q2; $(495)MM YTD.
  - Valuation changes driven primarily by market interest rates and other factors: +$283MM in Q2; +$261MM YTD; minor impacts from other inputs/assumptions.
  - Unrealized gains/losses in income mirror valuation changes.
  - Footnotes detail purchase price adjustments for early prepayments, transfers of excess MSRs to agency trusts for SMBS, and definitions of rate-driven vs other prepayment effects.
- Provides servicing and balance metrics:
  - Contractual/ancillary fee income: $388MM in Q2 2023; $776MM YTD.
  - Third-party mortgage loans serviced: $605B at 6/30/23 (vs $576B prior year).
  - Servicer advances net of allowance: $595MM at 6/30/23 (vs $1.166B prior year); advances are generally reimbursable and senior in cash flow priority, with limited credit risk except if advances violate applicable rules/agreements.
- Details mortgage fees and related income (CCB):
  - Production revenue: $102MM in Q2 2023; $177MM YTD.
  - Net mortgage servicing revenue:
    - Operating revenue: loan servicing revenue $402MM less MSR cash flow realization $(255)MM = $147MM in Q2.
    - Risk management: MSR FV changes due to rates/other +$283MM; other model inputs $(8)MM; derivatives and other $(250)MM; net +$25MM in Q2.
    - Total net mortgage servicing revenue: $172MM in Q2; $320MM YTD.
  - Total CCB mortgage fees and related income: $274MM in Q2; $497MM YTD. Firmwide mortgage fees and related income: $278MM in Q2; $499MM YTD.
- Notes on valuation methodology and sensitivities:
  - Changes in assumptions are interrelated and non-linear; sensitivities shown are isolated, holding other inputs constant.
  - Key assumptions and sensitivities:
    - Weighted-average CPR: 6.27% at 6/30/23 (6.12% at 12/31/22); 10%/20% adverse CPR change reduces MSR FV by ~$186MM/~$361MM.
    - Weighted-average option-adjusted spread: 5.77% at both dates; 100bp/200bp adverse OAS change reduces MSR FV by ~$348MM/~$668MM (includes operational risk and regulatory capital).

Net rental expense was $448 million for Q2 2023 ($484 million in Q2 2022) and $935 million for the first half of 2023 ($976 million in the first half of 2022). As lessor, the Firm primarily provides auto operating leases (reported in other assets); operating lease income and related depreciation declined year over year: Q2 2023 income/depreciation were $716 million/$457 million (vs. $945 million/$668 million in Q2 2022), and first half 2023 were $1,471 million/$876 million (vs. $1,993 million/$1,379 million in 2022).

nodes.title: Long-term debt
nodes.heading: Note 18 – Long-term debt
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase issues long-term debt denominated in various currencies, predominantly U.S. dollars, with both fixed and variable interest rates.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 18 details JPMorgan Chase’s long-term debt profile and related practices; Note 19 summarizes outstanding non-cumulative preferred stock, dividend activity, and recent redemptions.

- Long-term debt overview (June 30, 2023 vs. December 31, 2022):
  - Total long-term debt rose to $364.1 billion from $295.9 billion.
  - Parent company subtotal: $215.5 billion (down from $225.8 billion), primarily senior fixed- and variable-rate debt plus subordinated fixed-rate debt.
  - Subsidiaries subtotal: $146.8 billion (up from $68.2 billion), reflecting:
    - Federal Home Loan Bank (FHLB) advances of $36.1 billion, including $25.0 billion tied to the First Republic acquisition.
    - A $48.9 billion fixed-rate Purchase Money Note (3.40%, maturing in 1–5 years) from the First Republic acquisition.
    - Additional senior fixed- and variable-rate borrowings; small amount of subordinated and junior subordinated debt.
  - Junior subordinated debt totaled $1.8 billion.

- Maturities and optional redemption:
  - Debt maturing in the 12-month periods ending June 30: 2024 $41.9B; 2025 $58.5B; 2026 $38.0B; 2027 $29.2B; 2028 $75.2B.
  - $191.7 billion of debt was callable at the Firm’s option as of June 30, 2023.

- Interest rates and hedging:
  - Weighted-average contractual rate (excludes structured notes at fair value): 3.45% at June 30, 2023 (3.26% at Dec. 31, 2022).
  - After derivatives (interest rate and cross-currency swaps) the modified weighted-average rate: 5.02% (4.89% at Dec. 31, 2022).
  - Reported interest rates in tables exclude effects of hedge accounting derivatives and structured notes at fair value.

- Valuation and structure:
  - Certain equity-linked/indexed instruments are carried at fair value with changes in principal transactions revenue; DVA-related unrealized gains/losses in OCI.
  - Long-term debt at fair value: $78.6B (vs. $72.3B).
  - Secured long-term debt: $87.7B secured by $221.2B of assets (vs. $13.8B secured by $208.3B).
  - Zero-coupon notes outstanding: $11.2B (aggregate principal at maturity $45.7B; may exceed principal at next call date).

- Beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs:
  - Long-term beneficial interests totaled $1.1B (down from $2.1B); excludes $18.5B of short-term commercial paper/other short-term interests.

- Guarantees and covenants:
  - JPMorgan Chase & Co. guarantees certain subsidiary long-term debt/structured notes: $34.5B (vs. $28.2B); pari passu with other unsecured, unsubordinated debt.
  - Unsecured debt has no rating-trigger or financial covenant provisions that accelerate payments, change maturities/structure, limit borrowings, or require collateral based on adverse credit events.

- Preferred stock (non-cumulative):
  - Outstanding: 2,740,375 depositary shares representing $27.4B carrying value, across fixed-rate and fixed-to-floating series.
  - Dividends: Quarterly declarations summarized; several series pay fixed coupons until earliest redemption date, then float.
  - Reference rate transition: After June 30, 2023, certain fixed-to-floating series transitioned from USD LIBOR to three-month Term SOFR plus a 0.26% spread adjustment and specified series spreads; one series references five-year CMT plus spread after reset.
  - Series-specific updates:
    - Series Q became floating as of May 1, 2023 (SOFR + 3.25%).
    - Series CC became floating as of Nov. 1, 2022 (SOFR + 2.58%).
  - Liquidation/redemption terms: $10,000 per share plus accrued but unpaid dividends; aggregate liquidation value $27.8B at June 30, 2023.
  - Recent redemptions: Series I ($2.9B) on Oct. 31, 2022; Series V ($2.5B) on Oct. 3, 2022; Series Z ($2.0B) on Feb. 1, 2022.

nodes.title: Preferred stock
nodes.heading: Note 19 - Preferred stock
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 21 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 Form 10-K for a further discussion on preferred stock.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 19 summarizes JPMorgan Chase’s non-cumulative preferred stock outstanding as of June 30, 2023 and December 31, 2022, and the quarterly dividend declarations for the three- and six-month periods ended June 30, 2023 and 2022. It references Note 21 of the 2022 Form 10-K for additional detail.
- Outstanding preferred stock:
  - Total: 2,740,375 depositary shares outstanding; carrying value $27,404 million at both June 30, 2023 and December 31, 2022.
  - Structure: Each series has a $10,000 liquidation and redemption value per share (plus accrued, unpaid dividends); aggregate liquidation value was $27.8 billion at June 30, 2023.
- Series and rate types:
  - Fixed-rate series: DD, EE, GG, JJ, LL, MM with stated fixed coupon rates and earliest optional redemption dates beginning in 2023–2026.
  - Fixed-to-floating series: Q, R, S, U, X, CC, FF, HH, II, KK. These pay fixed coupons until the earliest redemption date, then convert to floating. Floating references include:
    - SOFR-based: three-month Term SOFR plus a 0.26% spread adjustment, plus a series-specific spread (e.g., Q +3.25%, R +3.30%, S +3.78%, U +3.33%, X +3.33%, CC +2.58%, FF +3.38%, HH +3.125%, II +2.745%).
    - CMT-based: Series KK resets to five-year Constant Maturity Treasury plus 2.85%.
- Reference rate transition:
  - Effective after June 30, 2023, CME Term SOFR replaces USD LIBOR for applicable fixed-to-floating preferred stock. Table references to “SOFR” incorporate the 0.26% spread adjustment plus the stated series spread.
- Recent resets:
  - Series Q: Became floating and quarterly-pay starting May 1, 2023 (previously fixed at 5.15% and semiannual). Post–August 1, 2023 dividends reset to three-month Term SOFR + 0.26% + 3.25%.
  - Series CC: Became floating and quarterly-pay starting November 1, 2022 (previously 4.625% and semiannual). Post–August 1, 2023 dividends reset to three-month Term SOFR + 0.26% + 2.58%.
- Dividend declarations: The table presents per-share dividends by series for Q2 and year-to-date periods in 2023 and 2022, reflecting the shift from semiannual fixed to quarterly floating where applicable (e.g., higher Q2 2023 amounts for Series Q and CC following resets).
- Redemptions:
  - Series I: $2.9 billion redeemed on October 31, 2022.
  - Series V: $2.5 billion redeemed on October 3, 2022.
  - Series Z: $2.0 billion redeemed on February 1, 2022.
- Other notes:
  - Fixed-to-floating series convert to floating at the earliest redemption date.
  - All preferred stock series are represented by depositary shares.

nodes.title: Earnings per share
nodes.heading: Note 20 – Earnings per share
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 23 of JPMorgan Chase ’s 2022 Form 10-K for a discussion of the computation of basic and diluted earnings per share (“EPS”).
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 20 – Earnings per share (EPS) for JPMorgan Chase, summarizing the calculation of basic and diluted EPS for the three and six months ended June 30, 2023 and 2022; methodology references Note 23 of the 2022 Form 10-K.
- Key components of EPS calculations:
  - Net income, less preferred stock dividends, to derive net income applicable to common equity.
  - Further reduction for dividends and undistributed earnings allocated to participating securities to arrive at net income applicable to common stockholders.
  - Weighted-average basic shares outstanding.
  - Diluted shares reflect the dilutive impact of unvested PSUs, nondividend-earning RSUs, and SARs.
- Results (in millions, except per share):
  - Q2 2023 vs Q2 2022:
    - Net income: $14,472 vs $8,649; preferred dividends: $373 vs $410.
    - Net income to common stockholders: $14,011 vs $8,195.
    - Basic shares: 2,943.8 vs 2,962.2; Basic EPS: $4.76 vs $2.77.
    - Dilutive impact: 4.5 vs 4.1; Diluted shares: 2,948.3 vs 2,966.3; Diluted EPS: $4.75 vs $2.76.
  - Six months 2023 vs 2022:
    - Net income: $27,094 vs $16,931; preferred dividends: $729 vs $807.
    - Net income to common stockholders: $26,204 vs $16,039.
    - Basic shares: 2,956.1 vs 2,969.6; Basic EPS: $8.86 vs $5.40.
    - Dilutive impact: 4.4 vs 4.1; Diluted shares: 2,960.5 vs 2,973.7; Diluted EPS: $8.85 vs $5.39.
- Highlights:
  - EPS (both basic and diluted) increased significantly year-over-year for both the quarter and year-to-date.
  - Weighted-average share counts declined modestly, and dilution from equity awards added approximately 4–5 million shares.

nodes.title: Accumulated other comprehensive income/(loss)
nodes.heading: Note 21 – Accumulated other comprehensive income/(loss)
nodes.start_phrase: AOCI includes the after-tax change in unrealized gains and losses on investment securities, foreign currency translation adjustments (including the impact of related derivatives), fair value changes of excluded components on fair value hedges, cash flow hedging activities, net gain/(loss) related to the Firm’s defined benefit pension and OPEB plans, and fair value option-elected liabilities arising from changes in the Firm’s own credit risk (DVA).
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 21 summarizes Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income/(Loss) (AOCI), detailing components, period changes, tax effects, and line-item reclassifications to the income statement.
- AOCI components: after-tax unrealized gains/losses on investment securities; foreign currency translation adjustments (including related hedges); fair value changes of excluded components in fair value hedges; cash flow hedging activities; net gains/losses of defined benefit pension and OPEB plans; and DVA on fair value option–elected liabilities (own credit risk).
- Periods covered: three and six months ended June 30, 2023 and 2022, with beginning balances, net changes, and ending balances by component.
- AOCI ending balance: $(14.29)B at June 30, 2023 vs $(14.37)B at June 30, 2022; slight improvement year over year.
- Q2 2023 OCI (after-tax): +$128M vs Q2 2022: $(4.80)B. Key Q2 2023 drivers: +$757M from investment securities; +$70M translation; +$11M fair value hedges; offset by $(497)M cash flow hedges, $(207)M DVA, $(6)M pension/OPEB.
- 1H 2023 OCI (after-tax): +$3.05B vs 1H 2022: $(14.29)B. Key 1H 2023 drivers: +$2.97B investment securities; +$267M translation; +$301M cash flow hedges; partially offset by $(415)M DVA, $(61)M pension/OPEB, $(10)M fair value hedges.
- Component patterns vs 2022: 2022 showed large negative unrealized losses on investment securities and cash flow hedges, partially offset by positive DVA; 2023 shows recovery in securities, smaller translation positives, and DVA losses.
- Detailed pre-tax, tax effect, and after-tax tables provided for each component for both Q2 and 1H of 2023 and 2022.
- Accounting changes/transfers: As of June 30, 2023 includes $(29)M after-tax net unamortized unrealized loss for HTM securities transferred to AFS under hedge accounting guidance adopted Jan 1, 2023. Also includes after-tax net unamortized unrealized losses from AFS-to-HTM transfers of $(1.1)B (2023) and $(1.4)B (2022).
- Reclassification disclosures:
  - Securities realized gains/losses reclassified to Investment securities gains/(losses).
  - Translation and related hedge reclassifications recorded in other income/expense; a small reclassification tied to the CIFM acquisition and net investment hedge loss noted in 1H 2023 (not material).
  - Fair value hedges reflect cross-currency swap basis spreads excluded from effectiveness testing; initial cost recognized in earnings via interest accrual.
  - Cash flow hedge reclassifications primarily affect noninterest revenue, net interest income, and compensation expense.
- Overall: AOCI improved modestly from June 2022 to June 2023, with 2023 OCI gains driven mainly by recovery in unrealized investment securities valuations and modest favorable translation effects, partly offset by DVA and hedge-related movements.

- Note 23 – Regulatory capital:
  - Outlines capital requirements set by the Federal Reserve for the consolidated holding company and the OCC for the principal insured depository institution (IDI), JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
  - States the Firm must meet minimum ratios for CET1, Tier 1, Total capital, Tier 1 leverage, and the Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR); noncompliance could trigger regulatory action. IDI subsidiaries are also subject to these requirements.
  - Presents risk-based ratio requirements and well-capitalized thresholds (as of June 30, 2023 and December 31, 2022):
    - Standardized (BHC): CET1 12.5%, Tier 1 14.0%, Total 16.0; (IDI): 7.0%, 8.5%, 10.5.
    - Advanced (BHC): CET1 11.0%, Tier 1 12.5%, Total 14.5; (IDI): 7.0%, 8.5%, 10.5.
    - Well-capitalized: (BHC) Tier 1 6.0%, Total 10.0; (IDI) CET1 6.5%, Tier 1 8.0%, Total 10.0.
    - Notes BHC requirements include minimums plus a 4.0% GSIB surcharge and a 4.0% stress capital buffer (Standardized) or 2.5% capital conservation buffer (Advanced); IDIs have a 2.5% conservation buffer and no GSIB surcharge. 2022 BHC Standardized requirements were slightly lower (12.0%, 13.5%, 15.5); Advanced 10.5%, 12.0%, 14.0.
  - Leverage-based requirements:
    - Tier 1 leverage: 4.0% (BHC and IDI); well-capitalized IDI threshold 5.0% (no BHC well-capitalized threshold).
    - SLR: 5.0% (BHC), 6.0% (IDI); reflects 3.0% minimum plus supplementary leverage buffers of 2.0% (BHC) and 3.0% (IDI); well-capitalized IDI threshold 6.0% (none for BHC).
  - CECL regulatory capital transition:
    - The $2.9b CECL capital benefit is being phased out 25% per year over three years starting Jan 1, 2022; $1.4b remained in CET1 as of June 30, 2023.

  - References Note 27 of the 2022 Form 10-K for further detail.

nodes.title: Regulatory capital
nodes.heading: Note 23 – Regulatory capital
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 27 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 Form 10-K for a detailed discussion on regulatory capital.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Summary of JPMorgan Chase’s regulatory capital framework and requirements for the consolidated holding company and its insured depository institution (IDI) subsidiaries as of June 30, 2023 and December 31, 2022, plus CECL capital transition details. References Note 27 of the 2022 Form 10-K for more detail.

- Regulators and coverage:
  - Federal Reserve sets capital and leverage requirements for the bank holding company (BHC).
  - OCC sets minimum capital standards for JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (IDI); FDIC rules define IDI “well-capitalized” thresholds.
  - Failure to meet minimums may trigger regulatory action.

- Capital ratios required under risk-based and leverage-based frameworks:
  - The Firm must maintain minimum CET1, Tier 1, Total capital, Tier 1 leverage, and Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR).

- Risk-based capital ratio requirements (as presented):
  - Standardized approach—BHC: CET1 12.5%, Tier 1 14.0%, Total 16.0
  - Standardized approach—IDI: CET1 7.0%, Tier 1 8.5%, Total 10.5
  - Advanced approach—BHC: CET1 11.0%, Tier 1 12.5%, Total 14.5
  - Advanced approach—IDI: CET1 7.0%, Tier 1 8.5%, Total 10.5
  - Well-capitalized thresholds:
    - BHC: Tier 1 6.0%, Total 10.0% (no CET1 threshold shown)
    - IDI: CET1 6.5%, Tier 1 8.0%, Total 10.0

- Leverage-based requirements:
  - Tier 1 leverage minimums: 4.0% for both BHC and IDI; well-capitalized for IDI: 5.0% (no BHC well-capitalized threshold).
  - SLR minimums: 5.0% for BHC, 6.0% for IDI; well-capitalized for IDI: 6.0% (no BHC well-capitalized threshold).
  - SLR components include a 3.0% minimum plus supplementary leverage buffers of 2.0% (BHC) and 3.0% (IDI).

- Buffer and surcharge structure:
  - BHC risk-based requirements include: base minimums + 4.0% GSIB surcharge (Method 2) + a 4.0% Stress Capital Buffer (SCB) for Standardized ratios; for Advanced ratios a fixed 2.5% capital conservation buffer (CCB).
  - IDIs include a fixed 2.5% CCB and are not subject to the GSIB surcharge.
  - Countercyclical buffer set at 0%.

- Prior-year comparator (12/31/2022) for BHC:
  - Standardized: CET1 12.0%, Tier 1 13.5%, Total 15.5
  - Advanced: CET1 10.5%, Tier 1 12.0%, Total 14.0

- CECL regulatory capital transition:
  - $2.9 billion CECL capital benefit (COVID-19 relief) is being phased out over three years starting 1/1/2022 at 25% per year; $1.4 billion remained in CET1 as of 6/30/2023.
  - Effective 1/1/2023, 50% of other CECL transition adjustments were phased out, affecting Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, total leverage exposure, and RWA.

nodes.title: Regulatory capital - Introduction
nodes.heading: Note 23 – Regulatory capital
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 27 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 Form 10-K for a detailed discussion on regulatory capital.
nodes.summary: Overview of JPMorgan Chase’s regulatory capital framework and required ratios as set by the Federal Reserve, OCC, and FDIC for the consolidated holding company and its IDI subsidiary, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., with reference to Note 27 of the 2022 Form 10-K. It outlines minimum risk-based (CET1, Tier 1, Total capital) and leverage-based (Tier 1 leverage, SLR) requirements and notes that failure to meet them may prompt Federal Reserve action. Tables (as of June 30, 2023 and December 31, 2022) present: for the BHC, Basel III Standardized requirements of CET1 12.5%, Tier 1 14.0%, Total 16.0 and Advanced requirements of CET1 11.0%, Tier 1 12.5%, Total 14.5; for IDIs, CET1 7.0%, Tier 1 8.5%, Total 10.5; well-capitalized thresholds of CET1 NA/6.5% (BHC/IDI), Tier 1 6.0%/8.0%, Total 10.0%/10.0%. Leverage requirements: Tier 1 leverage 4.0% (BHC/IDI), SLR 5.0% (BHC) and 6.0% (IDI); well-capitalized thresholds apply to IDIs only (Tier 1 leverage 5.0%, SLR 6.0%). Footnotes specify buffers: Firm requirements include a 4.0% GSIB surcharge (Method 2), a 4.0% SCB for Standardized and a 2.5% capital conservation buffer for Advanced; countercyclical buffer is 0%; IDIs have a 2.5% capital conservation buffer and no GSIB surcharge; SLR includes a 3.0% minimum plus 2.0% (BHC) and 3.0% (IDI) supplementary buffers.

- Overview of U.S. regulatory capital requirements for JPMorgan Chase & Co. (BHC) and its insured depository institution (IDI) subsidiary, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., under Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC rules, with reference to Note 27 of the 2022 Form 10-K for more detail.
- Presentation of risk-based capital ratio minimums and “well-capitalized” thresholds under Basel III Standardized and Advanced approaches:
  - BHC Standardized requirements: CET1 12.5%, Tier 1 14.0%, Total 16.0.
  - BHC Advanced requirements: CET1 11.0%, Tier 1 12.5%, Total 14.5.
  - IDI minimums: CET1 7.0%, Tier 1 8.5%, Total 10.5; IDI well-capitalized: CET1 6.5%, Tier 1 8.0%, Total 10.0.

- Leverage-based capital requirements and well-capitalized thresholds:

- Reported capital metrics as of June 30, 2023 and December 31, 2022 show JPMorgan Chase and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. were well-capitalized and met all requirements.

  - Tables provide CET1, Tier 1 and Total capital, RWA, adjusted average assets, and total leverage exposure for both dates; metrics reflect CECL transition provisions.
  - Note that certain assets from the First Republic acquisition were treated under the Standardized approach within Advanced metrics per U.S. capital rule transition provisions.

nodes.title: Off–balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees, and other commitments
nodes.heading: Note 24 – Off–balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees, and other commitments
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase provides lending-related financial instruments (e.g., commitments and guarantees) to address the financing needs of its customers and clients.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Disclosure of JPMorgan Chase’s off-balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees, and other commitments, including their credit risk implications, accounting treatment, and detailed balances as of June 30, 2023 and December 31, 2022.
- Risk notion: The contractual amount represents the maximum possible credit exposure if clients draw or the Firm must perform under guarantees; historically, many commitments are refinanced, extended, canceled, or expire undrawn, so totals are not indicative of expected future exposure or funding needs.
- Credit loss provisioning: An allowance for expected credit losses is maintained for wholesale and certain consumer lending-related commitments; carrying values for lending-related products include this allowance and guarantee liabilities.
- Product coverage and policy highlights:
  - Consumer commitments: residential real estate (including some correspondent purchase commitments), auto and other, and credit card/commerce card lines (reported as total available credit). The Firm can reduce or cancel certain lines (credit card and scored business banking) with notice or as permitted by law; credit card lines typically closed at 60+ days past due; HELOCs may be reduced/closed upon property value declines or borrower credit deterioration.
  - Wholesale commitments: unfunded commitments to extend credit, standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees, and other letters of credit. Amounts shown net of risk participations (grossed up in Federal Reserve regulatory filings).
