nodes.summary: This section describes JPMorgan Chase’s off–balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees, and other commitments, noting that contractual amounts reflect maximum possible credit risk but are typically not fully utilized; an allowance for credit losses on lending-related commitments is maintained (see Notes 13 and 28). It presents a maturity-dated table of contractual amounts and carrying values as of June 30, 2023 and December 31, 2022 covering consumer (credit card $881.5bn; residential real estate $34.0bn; auto/other $16.8bn; total consumer $932.3bn), wholesale (other unfunded commitments $509.3bn; standby letters of credit/financial guarantees $28.4bn; other letters of credit $3.4bn; total wholesale $541.1bn), and totals (total lending-related $1.473tn; carrying value $5.054bn vs $1.327tn and $2.817bn in 2022). Other guarantees/commitments include securities lending indemnification agreements $296.5bn (collateral held $312.6bn), derivatives qualifying as guarantees $56.9bn, unsettled resale/borrowed $109.1bn, unsettled repo/loaned $93.4bn, exchange and clearing house guarantees $140.1bn, loans sold with recourse $768m (carrying $27m), mortgage repurchase liability (carrying $76m), and other guarantees $11.2bn. Key practices and qualifiers include: most amounts are U.S.-based; amounts for certain items are shown net of risk participations; carrying value reflects allowances/guarantee liabilities or fair value; the Firm can reduce/cancel credit card and certain business banking lines (typically closes cards at 60+ days past due) and may reduce/close HELOCs on property value or credit deterioration; and June 30, 2023 figures include fair value adjustments from the First Republic acquisition ($576m residential RE, $236m auto/other, $1.6bn other unfunded commitments) and bridge financing markdowns.

- Standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees: Conditional lending commitments guaranteeing client performance to third parties for uses such as CP backstops, bond and acquisition financings, trade financings, etc.

- Credit quality reference: Investment-grade and noninvestment-grade classifications are based on the Firm’s internal risk ratings (referenced Note 12).

- Quantitative summary (June 30, 2023 vs. December 31, 2022):

    - Standby LCs and other financial guarantees: $28,406mm (vs. $27,439mm)
    - Other letters of credit: $3,361mm (vs. $4,134mm)
    - By rating (6/30/23): Investment-grade $19,574mm + $2,385mm; Noninvestment-grade $8,832mm + $976mm
  - Loss protection and carrying values:
    - Allowance for lending-related commitments: $146mm (vs. $82mm); Other LCs $23mm (vs. $6mm)
    - Guarantee liability: $371mm (vs. $326mm)
    - Total carrying value: $517mm and $23mm (vs. $408mm and $6mm)
  - Commitments with collateral: $16,414mm and $549mm (vs. $15,296mm and $795mm)

- Derivatives qualifying as guarantees (referenced Note 28):

    - Maximum exposure on stable value contracts: $1,442mm (vs. $2,063mm)
  - Fair value derivative payables: $181mm (vs. $649mm)
  - Note: The Firm is both a purchaser and seller of credit protection in the credit derivatives market (referenced Note 5).

- Merchant charge-backs: As a merchant acquirer, the Firm retains contingent liability for disputed card transactions. If unrecoverable from the merchant, the Firm bears the loss. nodes.title: Interchange Litigation
nodes.heading: Interchange Litigation
nodes.start_phrase: Groups of merchants and retail associations filed a series of class action complaints alleging that Visa and Mastercard, as well as certain banks, conspired to set the price of credit and debit card interchange fees and enacted related rules in violation of antitrust laws.
nodes.summary:
- Foreign exchange (FX) matters: Only remaining governmental inquiry is before the South Africa Competition Commission. In the U.S., a consolidated class action settlement was approved in 2018; opt-out claims were resolved in December 2022. Certification of a separate putative class was denied and summary judgment entered for defendants in March 2023; plaintiffs appealed. Similar actions have been filed outside the U.S. (U.K., Israel, Netherlands, Brazil, Australia). A U.K. action was settled in December 2022; in July 2023, the U.K. Court of Appeal reinstated an opt-out class certification request. In Israel, a settlement in principle awaits court approval.
- Interchange litigation: Merchants alleged Visa/Mastercard and certain banks fixed credit/debit interchange fees. After an initial settlement was reversed, the case was split into monetary and injunctive classes. An amended monetary settlement added $900 million to $5.3 billion and was approved in 2019; the Second Circuit affirmed in March 2023, with rehearing petitions pending. Due to opt-outs, $700 million was returned to defendants. The injunctive class was certified in part in 2021. Some opt-out merchants filed individual suits; settlements cover about 65% of combined Visa/Mastercard sales volume.
- Jeffrey Epstein litigation: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. was sued in SDNY by an alleged victim class and by the U.S. Virgin Islands, alleging the bank facilitated Epstein’s misconduct. In March 2023, parts of both cases were allowed to proceed; JPMorgan impleaded former employee James Edward Staley, and his motion to dismiss was denied in May 2023. In June 2023, the court certified the victim class and preliminarily approved a $290 million settlement for survivors. The USVI action and claims against Staley continue.
- LIBOR/EURIBOR investigations: Ongoing responses to global inquiries concerning LIBOR and EURIBOR. The Swiss Competition Commission’s EURIBOR investigation continues. The European Commission issued a 2016 decision finding EURIBOR-related antitrust infringements against the firm and others; the firm’s appeal to the European General Court remains pending.

nodes.title: Business segments

nodes.start_phrase: The Firm is managed on an LOB basis.
nodes.summary:

The firm has four reportable business segments—Consumer & Community Banking (CCB), Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB), Commercial Banking (CB), and Asset & Wealth Management (AWM)—plus a Corporate segment. Segments are defined by products/services or customer type and align with how the Operating Committee reviews results.
- Reporting basis: Segment results are presented on a managed (FTE) basis, which adjusts revenue for the tax-equivalent impact of tax-advantaged investments to be comparable with taxable items. nodes.heading: Note 28 – Business combinations
nodes.start_phrase: On M a y 1 , 2 0 2 3, JPMorgan Chase acquired certain assets and assumed certain liabilities of First Republic Bank (the "First Republic acquisition") from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (“FDIC”), as receiver, fo r $67.9 billion , resulting in an estimated bargain purchase gain of $2.7 billion recorded in other income.
nodes.summary:
- JPMorgan Chase’s Note 28 details its May 1, 2023 acquisition of certain assets and liabilities of First Republic Bank from the FDIC, accounted for as a U.S. GAAP business combination measured at estimated fair value on the acquisition date.
- Total purchase price consideration was $67.9 billion, including $13.6 billion paid/due to the FDIC (net of cash acquired), a five-year $50 billion secured Purchase Money Note at 3.4%, settlement of JPMorgan’s prior $5 billion deposit and related party items ($5.447 billion), and $15 million contingent consideration for shared-loss agreements.
- Fair value of assets acquired totaled $192.3 billion (notably $152.3 billion of loans, $30.3 billion of securities, $1.462 billion of core deposit and customer relationship intangibles, $675 million indemnification assets, and $7.6 billion other assets). Liabilities assumed totaled $121.7 billion (including $87.5 billion deposits, $27.9 billion FHLB advances, $2.4 billion lending-related commitments, $3.0 billion other liabilities, and $856 million deferred taxes).
- The fair value of net assets acquired was $70.6 billion, resulting in an estimated after-tax bargain purchase gain of $2.7 billion recorded in other income, reflecting net assets exceeding purchase price.
- The Firm and FDIC have up to one year to finalize settlement of purchase price and identification of assets/liabilities; measurement period adjustments (e.g., to loans, commitments, intangibles, leases) may change the bargain purchase gain.
- Two shared-loss agreements with the FDIC were established:
  - Commercial Shared-Loss Agreement: 80% coverage of credit losses on a pari passu basis over 5 years plus a 3-year recovery period for certain commercial loans/OREO.
  - Single-Family Shared-Loss Agreement: 80% coverage for 7 years for certain primary residence mortgage/co-op loans.
  Related indemnification assets reflecting expected FDIC recoveries were recognized at fair value within other assets.
- The $50 billion Purchase Money Note is secured by certain acquired loans and is prepayable upon notice to the FDIC; issuance of this note, settlement of JPMorgan’s $5 billion deposit and $447 million of securities financing with First Republic, and the $3.7 billion payable to the FDIC were treated as non-cash transactions.
- JPMorgan’s prior $5 billion deposit placed on March 16, 2023 as part of a $30 billion consortium was effectively settled at closing; the Firm subsequently repaid the remaining $25 billion (plus accrued interest) to consortium banks on May 9, 2023.
- Valuation methodologies:
  - Core deposit intangible ($1.3 billion) valued using the favorable source of funds method based on after-tax funding cost savings; customer relationship intangibles ($187 million) valued via multi-period excess earnings. Key assumptions included growth/attrition, fee income, servicing costs, and discount rates.
  - Intangibles are amortized over approximately 7 years; as of June 30, 2023, carrying values were $1.2 billion (core deposit) and $183 million (customer relationships), with accumulated amortization of ~$30 million and ~$4 million, respectively.
  - Indemnification assets measured at fair value based on timing of forecasted losses underlying related allowances.
- Additional details note the presence of tax-oriented investments and lease right-of-use assets/liabilities within other assets/liabilities, with references to related notes for further information.

- CCB metrics and definitions:
  - Debit and credit card sales volume: purchases net of returns.
  - Deposit margin: net interest income as a percentage of average deposits.
  - Home Lending revenue split:
    - Net mortgage servicing revenue: servicing fees, MSR fair value changes, related risk management, securitization of excess servicing, and gains/losses on certain repurchased government-insured loans.
    - Production revenue: fees and income from loans originated for sale, pipeline/warehouse risk management, gains/losses and lower of cost or fair value on held-for-sale loans (excluding certain government-insured repurchases), and fair value option changes.
  - Mortgage origination channels:
    - Retail: direct-to-borrower via branches, internet, phone, and third-party referrals.
    - Correspondent: closed loans sold to the firm by other financial institutions.
  - Credit card business: issuing cards to consumers and small businesses.
  - Net revenue rate: annualized Card Services net revenue as a percentage of average loans.
  - Auto loan and lease origination volume: dollar amount originated.
- CIB revenue definitions:
  - Investment Banking: all IB-related revenue net of inter-LOB sharing.
  - Payments: cash management solutions including merchant acquiring, cross-border/domestic payments, liquidity/account services, and global trade services.
  - Lending: net interest income, fees, gains/losses on loan sales or received securities, and credit portfolio risk management results.
  - Fixed Income Markets: market-making revenue in FX, rates, credit, and commodities.
  - Equity Markets: market-making revenue in cash equities, derivatives, convertibles, and prime brokerage.
  - Securities Services: custody, fund accounting/administration, securities lending, collateral management, and depositary receipts services.
- CIB business metrics:
  - Assets under custody (AUC): assets safeguarded/serviced that generate fees.
  - Investment banking fees: advisory, equity and bond underwriting, and loan syndication fees.

nodes.summary:

- CCB metrics and definitions:
  - Debit and credit card sales volume: dollar amount of cardmember purchases, net of returns.
  - Deposit margin: net interest income as a percentage of average deposits.
  - Home Lending revenue components:
    - Net mortgage servicing revenue: servicing income on third-party loans, fair value changes of MSRs, related risk management results, securitization gains/losses of excess servicing, and gains/losses and lower of cost or fair value adjustments on certain repurchased government-insured loans.

    - Correspondent: closed loans sold to the firm by banks, thrifts, mortgage banks, and other institutions.
  - Credit card business: primarily issues credit cards to consumers and small businesses.
  - Net revenue rate: annualized Card Services net revenue as a percentage of average loans.
  - Auto loan and lease origination volume: dollar amount of auto loans and leases originated.

- CIB revenue categories and business metrics:
  - Investment Banking: all investment banking revenue, reported net of amounts shared with other lines of business.
  - Payments: cash management solutions including merchant acquiring, cross-border and domestic payments, liquidity and account services, and global trade for corporates, e-commerce/marketplaces, and financial institutions.
  - Lending: net interest income, fees, gains/losses on loan sales, gains/losses on securities from restructurings, and credit portfolio risk management results.
  - Fixed Income Markets: market-making revenue across FX, interest rates, credit, and commodities.
  - Equity Markets: market-making revenue across equity cash, derivatives, convertibles, and prime brokerage.
  - Securities Services: custody, fund accounting/administration, securities lending, collateral management, and depositary receipts services.
  - Assets under custody (AUC): activities tied to safekeeping/servicing of assets on which fees are earned.
  - Investment banking fees: advisory, equity underwriting, bond underwriting, and loan syndication fees.

nodes.title: COMMERCIAL BANKING (“CB”)
nodes.heading: 10.3 COMMERCIAL BANKING (“CB”)
nodes.start_phrase: Commercial Banking provides comprehensive financial solutions, including lending, payments, investment banking and asset management products across three primary client segments: Middle Market Banking, Corporate Client Banking and Commercial Real Estate Banking.
nodes.summary:
- Defines Commercial Banking (CB) and its comprehensive offerings: lending, payments, investment banking, and asset management products.
- Outlines CB client segments:
  - Middle Market Banking: small/midsized companies, local governments, nonprofits.
  - Corporate Client Banking: large corporations.
  - Commercial Real Estate Banking: investors, developers, and owners of multifamily, office, retail, industrial, and affordable housing.
  - Other: amounts not aligned with a primary client segment.
- Details CB revenue categories:
  - Lending: secured financing (term loans, revolvers, bridge loans, asset-based structures, leases, standby letters of credit) with collateral such as receivables, inventory, equipment, real estate, or other assets.
  - Payments: cash management (merchant acquiring, cross-border/domestic payments, liquidity and account services, global trade solutions).
  - Investment banking: capital raising, advisory, equity underwriting, loan syndications, and revenue from fixed income/equity market products used by CB clients.
  - Other: tax-equivalent adjustments from Community Development Banking and principal transactions.
- Defines key Asset & Wealth Management (AWM) terms:
  - Assets under management (AUM), including committed capital not called.
  - Client assets (AUM plus custody, brokerage, administration, and deposits).
  - Multi-asset and alternative assets (hedge funds, currency, real estate, private equity, and other nontraditional strategies).
- Describes AWM lines of business:
  - Asset Management: multi-asset solutions across equities, fixed income, alternatives, and money markets for institutional and retail clients.
  - Global Private Bank: retirement, brokerage, custody, trusts and estates, lending, mortgages, deposits, and investment management for high-net-worth clients.
- Specifies AWM client segments:
  - Private Banking: high- and ultra-high-net-worth individuals, families, money managers, business owners.
  - Global Institutional: corporate/public institutions, endowments, foundations, nonprofits, governments.
  - Global Funds: financial intermediaries and individual investors.
- Explains Asset Management performance measures:
  - Focus on the percentage of mutual fund AUM in 4- or 5-star funds.
  - Star rating methodologies: risk-adjusted rankings (5-star top 10%, 4-star next 22.5%, down to 1-star bottom 10%); Morningstar overall rating weighted across 3-, 5-, 10-year periods and assigned at share-class level for U.S. funds; Nomura rating based on 3-year risk-adjusted performance; funds under three years excluded.

nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines how mutual fund performance rankings and related assets under management (AUM) metrics are compiled and reported. Rankings and asset values come from external fund rating providers, with asset values redenominated to U.S. dollars where applicable. For star ratings, AUM is calculated at the share-class level for U.S.-domiciled funds, at a “primary share class” level for most non-U.S. funds, and at the fund level in Japan using Nomura ratings. For quartile rankings (1st or 2nd quartile over one, three, and five years), calculations are based on net-of-fee absolute returns, with AUM measured by share class in the U.S., by primary share class for the U.K., Luxembourg, and Hong Kong, and by fund level elsewhere. The text cautions that results might differ if all share classes were included and reiterates that past performance does not guarantee future results. It defines “primary share class” as the C share class for European funds and the Acc share class for Hong Kong and Taiwan funds; if unavailable, the oldest share class is used.
